items.text:
Russian warship hit by suspected Ukrainian drone at Benghazi naval base, Libyan officials say
A Russian navy corvette docked at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya was hit on Sunday by a suspected Ukrainian sea drone, according to local officials. The strike severely damaged the warship and ignited a fire at the facility in what appeared to be the latest attack in Libya linked to the Russia-Ukraine war.
A suspected Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship Sunday at a naval base in Libya, officials said, the latest attack in the North African nation linked to the Russia-Ukraine war.
The strike at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, and ignited a fire at the facility, two Libyan military officials said.
They said that several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, they said.
The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.
Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Muammar Gaddafi, who was later killed, in 2011. A UN-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.
Read moreRussia turns to Libyan ports after Assad's ouster in Syria
The eastern Libya-based government said in a statement that the strike on Sunday caused an explosion and fire at the base, which was later extinguished.
The vessel had docked at the base for refueling and supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said, without providing details on the vessel or its cargo.
A joint investigation was launched with Russia to “uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it,” the statement said.
No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack. There was no immediate comment from either Russia or Ukraine.
On Sunday evening, local media said that another sea drone hit a commercial vessel off the port of Benghazi in a separate attack. No further details were given. The Almasar satellite television channel said that naval and air forces destroyed at least 12 other sea drones off the Mediterranean city.
The western Libya government expressed concerns about “dragging Libyan ports and civilian facilities into external conflicts,” in an apparent reference to the war in Ukraine.
“The government reaffirms its categorical rejection of turning Libya into an arena for international conflicts or a theater for external powers to settle scores,” it said in a statement.
In March, Ukrainian forces operating in western Libya under a covert deal struck a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in a suspected sea drone attack near Maltese waters, Libyan officials said at the time.
The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, operated mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also at other military facilities in the capital, Tripoli, and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

The Listening Post
Cockroaches, dissent and a paradigm shift in India
The rise of Cockroach Janta Party and what it reveals about the future of politics and journalism in India.
A youth-led movement born as online satire has unsettled Indian politics. Named after a dismissive remark by the chief justice, the Cockroach Janta Party has mobilised some of the country’s biggest protests in years. They have been driven by anger over exam leaks, unemployment and a lack of political accountability.
The demonstrators have been met by heavy police crackdowns and clashed with mainstream media outlets they accuse of serving the government.
As young Indians turn to social media and independent outlets to tell their stories, this film examines the growing divide between India’s youth and mainstream media and what it could mean for the future of politics and journalism.
Contributors:
Manisha Pande – Editorial director, Newslaundry
Ashutosh Ranka – Co-convenor, Cockroach Janta Party
Rajat Sethi – Visiting fellow, India Foundation
Priyanshi Sharma – Cofounder, Peek TV

On China, is Trump bucking the US national security establishment?
On China, US is torn between the fears of the national security establishment and the prospect of expanded trade.
For decades, China was considered the top threat to continued US global primacy, and President Donald Trump’s moves to expand trade with Beijing – even on advanced technology – are rattling Washington’s national security establishment. So when former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang argued that the US should sell advanced chips to China to maintain dominance over the AI market, the traditional national security hawks baulked. items.text:
Sudan: Drones strikes hit UN building in residential area of Khartoum
November 22, 2026
The United Nations reported on Sunday a drone attack on a residential area in Khartoum, Sudan's capital.
A UN building located in a civilian neighborhood was damaged in the attack, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
"It is unacceptable that we are put at such risk," said the UN's Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown.
What do we know about the attack?
The AFP news agency reported that explosions were heard around Khartoum Airport and in other parts of the city from approximately 2:00 a.m. to 4:30 a.m. local time.
According to a witness, a drone strike completely destroyed a house. There were no immediate reports of casualties.
Meanwhile, a Sudanese army source said the drones had been launched from Ethiopia.
Sudan has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of allowing attacks to be launched from its territory. However, Addis Ababa has denied these accusations.
Drone strikes are intensifying in Sudan
Sudan has been engulfed in a civil war since April 2023. The army of de facto ruler Abdel-Fattah al-Burhan and the RSF militia led by Mohamed Hamdan Daglo have been fighting for control of the country.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced more than 14 million.
According to UN data, the use of drones has dramatically altered the course of the war this year, killing more than 1,100 people in the first six months.
The UN also said that of the hundreds of child casualties this year, two-thirds were killed or injured by drone strikes.
Just days ago, a Sudanese army drone strike killed 15 people, including four children, in a West Kordofan village. The army was advancing through the state and recapturing territory from the RSF.

items.text:
Aber Kawas becomes first Palestinian in New York state Senate history
Kawas, a democratic socialist, won with 74.5 percent of the vote, championing progressive politics.
New York City, United States – “You have all elected the first Palestinian in New York Senate history!” Aber Kawas shouted over cheers to hundreds of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members at a bar on election night.
As chants of “Aber! Aber! Aber!” filled the patio of Bohemia Beer Garden on November 3, media cameras flashed against her shiny blazer, embroidered with traditional Palestinian tatreez in gold and red.
Kawas, 34, made history as the first Palestinian, and the first Muslim woman, in the New York state Senate and the state legislature. She won the seat representing district 12 in northwest Queens, home to one of New York City’s largest Arab communities, where nearly half of residents were born outside the United States.
As her speech ended and chants of “Free, Free Palestine” rang through the garden, Stylianos Karolidis, a DSA organiser on Kawas’s team, stepped up to remind supporters that she really, really had not wanted to run for office. The DSA had to “hound her non-stop” until she acquiesced, he said.
Kawas had worked with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani when he was in the state legislature, so they knew her organising skills.
Kawas said she did not initially think it was possible to run for office without compromising her commitment to Palestinian liberation. Her victory, with 74.5 percent of the vote against Republican Han Khon To, was part of a broader tide of wins for pro-Palestine and democratic socialist candidates in the midterm elections, including Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Mayor-elect Nithya Raman in Los Angeles, California.
“This midterm election showed a politics of human rights that includes Palestinians is a winning platform,” said Institute for Middle East Understanding policy project executive director Margaret DeReus. “For millions of Americans, holding Israel accountable for genocide and supporting Palestinian freedom are the litmus test.”
Days after the election, Kawas reflected on the DSA’s first approach and her doubts about entering a political system she had long distrusted. In her Queens home, a poster honouring Palestinians who had been killed hung above shelves of books on Islamic liberation, the Palestinian movement and US politics. But she ran because the political climate had shifted, she told Al Jazeera.
“It felt like being pro-Palestinian was the most important thing to run on.”
Kawas’s parents were uprooted from their homes in Palestine during the mass expulsions. Her father was uprooted in 1948 and her mother in 1967. They grew up as neighbours in Jordan before falling in love, marrying and moving to the US with their infant son in the 1990s. They later had three daughters. Aber is the third child of the four, sandwiched between her two sisters. “Which is why I have a lot of politician skills,” she said, laughing.
But when she was in the seventh grade, her father was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which her mother described as a regular occurrence in New York’s post-9/11 Muslim community. His detention meant weekend visits to prison, and it left the family struggling.
“I had to work whether I wanted to or not; you have to become both man and woman, father and mother,” her mother, Manal Abu Samaha, told Al Jazeera.
When Kawas was a teenager, she said she travelled to Albany to tell her family’s story, hoping to expand opportunities for undocumented students like her older brother, who was ineligible for a college scholarship. Lawmakers seemed uninterested, Kawas recalls.
The state senator-elect credits the experience with launching her advocacy career and shaping her goals as a politician. “It’s not upending systems, but it’s meeting real, immediate material needs for people,” she said. “That’s maybe a little kernel of what got me to run.”
Backed by Mamdani and the DSA, Kawas’s campaign said it mobilised more than 1,000 volunteers to knock on doors, make calls and campaign on affordable housing, healthcare and public transport, as well as the Palestinian solidarity work that has shaped her life.
Kawas recalled that, while Mamdani was warned that supporting Palestine would end his political career, the stance instead helped him earn voters’ trust. Seeing this, she said, made her less wary that entering politics would require her to compromise her beliefs.
“I voted for Aber Kawas because Palestinian liberation is not separate from the everyday survival and basic needs that Americans and New Yorkers struggle with,” said community organiser Doreen Mohammed. “Aber Kawas’s vocal support for Palestine is what we need more of everywhere.”
Kawas told Al Jazeera she believes her stance on Palestine helped her earn trust from local leaders. Whether it can change US policy is a harder question.
“Many of us are rightfully cautious, if not outright sceptical, when it comes to electoral politics,” said Samee Sulaiman, an anthropologist at Columbia University who studies the Middle East. “Can we build and use this nascent power to finally end American support of Israel in every way? This will be the real test.”
Kawas acknowledged that a lot will depend on the political will of legislative leaders.
“The challenge, truly, is going to be the political will of the leadership,” she said. “We [the DSA] are still a minority in the legislature.”
Her first priority is reviving the Not on Our Dime! bill, which she drafted with then-Assembly member Zohran Mamdani in 2023 to prohibit New York non-profits from supporting illegal Israeli settlement activity in the occupied Palestinian territory. Rejected at the time, it is now back before the New York state Senate.
Kawas said she remains convinced change is possible, pointing to the activists who helped bring an end to apartheid in South Africa.

items.text:
‘Horrific’ and ‘chilling’: Officials condemn ICE arrests at Seattle airport
Video shows masked immigration agents forcibly detaining two people at Seattle airport, raising concerns over tactics.
Democrats and state officials have denounced a now-viral immigration arrest in Washington state, which took place on an airport jet bridge as passengers were boarding a flight to Los Angeles.
“What we’ve seen happening in Washington is atrocious,” said Nevada’s Governor-elect Aaron Ford, a Democrat, in an interview with the news outlet MS NOW on Sunday.
He added that he supported safeguards to restrict the actions taken by United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.
“ We need some control over these vigilante ICE agents who come en masse in terrorising neighbourhoods, at airports included,” Ford said.
The two arrests unfolded on Saturday morning at Seattle-Tacoma international airport, as passengers boarded Alaska Airlines Flight 1306.
Videos recorded by passengers showed immigration agents in masks surrounding a man and a woman on the narrow jet bridge, forcing them to the ground as other travellers looked on.
Passengers could be heard asking the officers to identify themselves, while a woman repeatedly shouted that she and her family had work permits.
In one video, a young girl can be heard screaming as officers remove a man through a side door. In another part of the footage, an officer appeared to shove a bystander who tried to intervene.
The flight was delayed, eventually departing about three hours later than expected.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) defended the operation, saying ICE had conducted a targeted enforcement action to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who the agency said had overstayed his visa.
DHS alleged that other travellers began obstructing and assaulting officers during the arrest, including one passenger who allegedly “hurled hot coffee on the officers”.
The woman who was arrested, identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was also found to have overstayed her visa, the department said, adding that she would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.
The agency did not say where the two were taken.
Officials demand answers
The footage prompted sharp condemnation from Washington Governor Bob Ferguson, who called ICE “completely and totally out of control” and described the video as “horrific” and “chilling” at a news conference on Saturday.
Ferguson also questioned whether the agents violated a Washington state law he signed in March that restricts law enforcement officers from wearing facial coverings.
“Masked agents who do not identify themselves drag screaming individuals off a jetway as they’re about to do something very ordinary in our country: board a flight. There is no justification for this brutality,” Ferguson said during the news conference.
He added that state officials were investigating the circumstances of the arrests, including how the agents accessed the jet bridge.
Ferguson also urged Alaska Airlines and other carriers to demand that federal immigration agents leave airports.
Alaska Airlines said it did not receive advance notice of the enforcement operation and was working with Ferguson and the Port of Seattle to determine whether established protocols had been followed.
The Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, said in a statement that it has raised its concerns with the relevant federal authorities about whether regulations were breached.
At Saturday’s news conference, Port of Seattle Commissioner Hamdi Mohamed characterised the arrests as particularly distressing because of when they took place.
“We are entering the holidays. That is one of the most heartbreaking things about this moment today. There are so many people in that airport that are travelling to go and connect with their families,” Mohamed said. “And that family is separated.”
Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson also condemned the operation, describing the agents’ tactics as “unacceptable and un-American”.
Protesters gathered at the airport on Saturday evening, in the hours after the confrontation, to condemn the arrests and call for accountability from federal authorities.
Disapproval of Trump’s immigration crackdown
The arrests come as President Donald Trump continues to pursue what he has promised will be the largest deportation effort in US history.
But voters have expressed concern about the tactics used during his immigration crackdown. Some experts believe the topic became a political liability for Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections.
A Fox News poll from September found that 53 percent of registered voters believed the administration’s immigration enforcement had gone too far. The figure rose to 60 percent among independent voters and two-thirds of Hispanic respondents.
In a November 8 interview with the CBS News television programme 60 Minutes, Trump acknowledged that his administration’s deportation policies may have been too aggressive, saying, “I think it might be too tough, yeah.”
In the midterms, the Democratic Party won majorities in both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, flipping both chambers from Republican control.
In the wake of that victory, several high-profile members of the left-wing party have pledged to seek reforms to immigration enforcement operations in the US.
Senators Alex Padilla and Jacky Rosen, for instance, have introduced legislation that would prevent ICE from carrying out arrests at or near airports without a judicial warrant first.
Patty Murray, another Democratic senator, also said she was demanding answers from DHS and warned in a post on X that the administration would face consequences when the incoming Congress is sworn in early next year.
“Trump answers to a Democratic Congress on January 3rd – there WILL be accountability,” she wrote.

items.text:
From conceding seven to Hull heroics - how Tzolakis recovered to defy Brighton
- Published
Hull boss Sergej Jakirovic used one word to describe the performance of his goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis in Sunday's 2-0 Premier League win against Brighton.
"Unbelievable," he told Match of the Day.
"Especially after the international break, which was very difficult for him."
Tzolakis' previous outing had been for Greece against the Netherlands in the Uefa Nations League, where he and his side were humbled 7-0 by the hosts in Amsterdam.
Nine days later, his contribution to the Tigers' first league victory since 29 August was every bit as important as that of striker Oli McBurnie, who netted both goals in second-half stoppage time against the second-placed Seagulls.
Tzolakis made a series of top saves to keep the highest scorers in the top flight at bay and, when Brighton full-back Costinha was sent off in the 89th minute for a second bookable offence, the hosts seized their opportunity to clinch only their third win following their Premier League return.
McBurnie said the 24-year-old stopper had "kept Hull in a few games" this season and the club were "lucky to have him", while Tzolakis told Sky Sports: "We are a unit and a team.
"We play for each other. We showed a good team effort and we deserved the three points."
'Always in the right place at the right time'
With the opportunity to move three points behind leaders Arsenal, Brighton looked most likely to score for long spells of Sunday's game, but just could not find a way past former Olympiacos goalkeeper Tzolakis, who joined Hull in August for a reported £20m fee.
He got down to make a vital block early on to deny Diego Gomez, who had slid in to meet a low cross from the left wing. It was the first of several occasions the Paraguay international would be frustrated in front of goal.
Tzolakis then raced out spreadeagled to foil Georginio Rutter with an outstretched left hand - a stop that BBC Radio 5 Live pundit and former striker Clinton Morrison described as "Peter Schmeichel-esque", referring to the legendary Denmark keeper.
Second-half efforts from distance by Pascal Gross and Lewis Dunk were dealt with, too.
Yasin Ayari went close with a thumping strike against the bar and when Brighton substitute Charalampos Kostoulas pounced on a short backpass to go through one-on-one, Tzolakis got a hand on his Greece team-mate's shot and Regan Slater was back on the goalline to head the ball to safety.
Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy, a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, said: "We saw again how important Tzolakis is for Hull. He had one of those days where he was always in the right place at the right time.
"When you are a Hull player and you see the kind of saves Tzolakis made when he spread himself and kept it out with his foot, you start thinking that it could be your day.
"It happens a lot in football and, on the flip side, Brighton will have been thinking, 'are we ever going to score here?'."
Hull made a superb start to the campaign after being promoted via the Championship play-offs in May.
They followed victories against Manchester United and Coventry with a draw against Aston Villa - all without conceding a goal.
The Tigers had not won since that 1-0 success at Coventry until beating Brighton - but they are one of four top-flight sides still unbeaten at home and have not lost any fixture by more than a one-goal margin.
They lost 1-0 to champions Arsenal before the international break and Scotland forward McBurnie told Match of the Day: "We know we can make it difficult for the top teams in the league and we've proved that in the past two games.
"We want to make it as difficult as we can for teams to come here and make the MKM Stadium a tough place to come. It's proving that way so far, so long may it continue."

items.title: 'No chance!' - Poch and Mainoo fume at 'unfair' Yoro red card
items.summary:
Leny Yoro red card: Man Utd boss Mauricio Pochettino and Kobbie Mainoo angry at sending off for foul on Liverpool's Alexander Isak
Manchester United were thumped 4-0 by Liverpool following Leny Yoro's red card after eight minutes; one of the considerations regarding a red card for Denying of an Obvi
items.text:
Leny Yoro red card: Man Utd boss Mauricio Pochettino and Kobbie Mainoo angry at sending off for foul on Liverpool's Alexander Isak
Manchester United were thumped 4-0 by Liverpool following Leny Yoro's red card after eight minutes; one of the considerations regarding a red card for Denying of an Obvious Goalscoring Opportunity (DOGS), is the likelihood of the attacking player "keeping or gaining control of the ball"
Sunday 22 November 2026 19:46, UK
Mauricio Pochettino felt Manchester United were given an "unfair" red card in their 4-0 defeat at Liverpool - with Kobbie Mainoo replying "no chance" when asked whether Leny Yoro should have been sent off.
Pochettino's first United game started in dismal fashion as Yoro was given his marching orders in the eighth minute for bringing down Alexander Isak as the last defender outside the box.
Dominik Szoboszlai then scored from the resulting free-kick and Florian Wirtz doubled the lead after 13 minutes. Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz put gloss on the scoreline after half-time.
- Liverpool 4-0 Man Utd - report and reaction
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- No Sky? Get Sky Sports or stream with no contract on NOW 📺
However, Yoro's sending off was doused in controversy as Isak took a heavy touch into United goalkeeper Senne Lammens before going down under the challenge.
Under the laws, one of the considerations regarding a red card for Denying of an Obvious Goalscoring Opportunity (DOGS), is the likelihood of the attacking player "keeping or gaining control of the ball".
Pochettino felt that not only did Isak lose control of the ball with his touch, but also that United should have been given a penalty for Jeremy Jacquet's challenge on Bryan Mbeumo at the opposite end just moments before.
"So painful. So disappointed," Pochettino told Sky Sports. "It's not ok to start a game in the Premier League with this situation.
"The game changed completely after six minutes. Now we can explain everything but the damage is done, it's so painful.
"The players are so, so feeling the pain of the result. I told them to be calm: it was an unfair situation that happened. We need to accept that reality. We need to try to increase our focus, concentration and make better decisions on the field.
"We also need to be critical on ourselves but some situations happened in the game that we are not happy."
Pushed on whether he was unhappy with Isak's heavy touch, the United boss replied: "The ball was for the goalkeeper.
"In that situation, if you review the VAR you can see for sure, [Yoro] never had the intention to connect with Isak. When the control was long with the striker, the ball was going to the goalkeeper, he runs and goes down.
"In Leny's case, it wasn't intentional."
But then Pochettino added: "If you look before, on the sixth minute. Jacquet on Mbeumo. Similar? No. If you compare the actions, that was a penalty.
"How that changes life, if you score after six minutes. Now, for sure, we are talking in a different way. We have to take responsibility, I take the responsibility. We keep pushing."
Pochettino was seen speaking to the officials at full-time and when asked on that, the United boss said: "It's not going to change what happened. Being respectful is the most important.
"At the same time, I have to defend my club. And tell what I feel. That was an action that everyone who plays football, it was clear that a situation that was not a red card."
Mainoo: No chance it's a red card
United midfielder Mainoo was equally angry at the call. "The game's been taken out of our hands by a red card that I don't think can be a red card," he said.
"No chance. The ball's already with the goalkeeper. They're both running full speed. What can we do? It is what it is.
"It's 10 vs 11, you come to a place like Anfield, it's a tough game anyway. Then you lose a man, it makes it hard. I can't fault the boys for their fight in the game. We take the pain and move on.
"I wouldn't say it all goes out the window. You can still take the things you did in training into the game, but it makes it 10 times harder with one less man in a situation like that.
"It's hard, it's painful. But no one's coming to save us. We have to work hard, keep digging, keep working, keep fighting. It will all come round."
Keane: Isak is not getting the ball
There was comical defending for the Yoro red-card incident, with United defender Matthijs de Ligt - playing his first Premier League minutes of the season - letting a long ball drop that allowed Isak to run through.
That then led to the Yoro 'foul' - but Roy Keane felt it was unfair on United, even despite their poor defending.
"Isak's not getting the ball," he said. "There's no way he's getting the ball.
"It's clumsy from United. Obviously it's one straight ball over the top. You shouldn't be in so much trouble.
"But there's no way he's getting that ball. Absolutely not. I know Isak is quick and he's sharp, but we've looked at it again.
"It's really poor defending. Players not smelling danger. But Isak is not getting that ball. Absolutely not."
Pochettino defended United's defending - as they became the worst defence in Europe when it comes to goals conceded across all competitions this season.
"I wasn't in the past," said Pochettino, referring to United's defensive record under his predecessor Michael Carrick.
"I take responsibility for today, and today we concede four goals with 10 men, and in a circumstance after playing 80 minutes on Anfield with 10 men.
"Of course I take responsibility about that, no worries, but I don't want to compare situations in the past."
Pochettino defends De Ligt selection call
When put to him that United did not have to go and concede four goals after the sending off, he replied: "It's so easy to talk in this way.
"It's about the team, always it's about balance. It's not about one line, the defensive line, the midfield, the offensive. I think when the team concede it is because the balance is not so good,

items.text:
What's next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?
The COP31 climate summit in Turkey has officially come to an end after countries failed to come to a consensus on a new deal.
The European Union and some other countries rejected a fourth draft agreement over its failure to mention a need to phase out fossil fuels, the largest driver of global climate change.
An EU representative accuses some oil states of hijacking talks, as Russia defends opposing the inclusion of such a commitment and levels direct criticism at the EU in its speech.
The talks have been the longest-running in the summit's history, with negotiations breaking down two days after they had been due to end.
BBC climate and science reporter Esme Stallard reports from Antalya, in Turkey.

Leny Yoro’s red card for Manchester United after just eight minutes paved the way for a 4-0 football defeat at Anfield.
Mauricio Pochettino endured a nightmare start to his Manchester United reign as the 10-man Red Devils were humb
items.text:
Liverpool thrash 10-man Man United in nightmare start for Pochettino
Leny Yoro’s red card for Manchester United after just eight minutes paved the way for a 4-0 football defeat at Anfield.
Mauricio Pochettino endured a nightmare start to his Manchester United reign as the 10-man Red Devils were humbled 4-0 by old rivals Liverpool at Anfield Stadium.
Leny Yoro’s red card eight minutes in set the tone as Andoni Iraola’s side raced into a 2-0 lead after just 13 minutes and spurned a host of chances before adding to their advantage after the break.
United have now conceded 34 goals in all competitions – the most of any top-flight team in any of Europe’s major leagues. But in truth, the hosts could well have matched, or even surpassed, their famous 7-0 victory in 2023 in this fixture.
Pochettino’s side sit 19th, a point off the bottom of the table, in English football’s Premier League, with eight points from 11 games. Meanwhile, the Reds are up to fourth, seven points behind leaders Arsenal.
Liverpool were already well on top when the game turned after eight minutes as Matthijs de Ligt – who struggled throughout after being handed his first Premier League start in 357 days in Pochettino’s first selection – was caught out by a long ball down the left channel which allowed Alexander Isak to race towards goal.
Yoro chased him back and, despite a heavy touch from the Swede on the edge of the box, his clumsy challenge just outside the area led to a straight red card for denying a goal-scoring opportunity.
Matters got immediately worse for the visitors as Dominik Szoboszlai whipped home the low free kick, beating Bruno Fernandes on the end of the wall and the dive of Senne Lammens in goal to find the bottom corner.
It was 2-0 just three minutes later, when the lively Rio Ngumoha glided into the box on the left and fired a cross into the middle, which Florian Wirtz pirouetted to turn home with a close-range volley off the underside of the bar.
With United in disarray at the back, Pochettino brought on Harry Maguire in place of Bryan Mbeumo to form a five-man defence.
Although the visitors found a foothold in the game, the home pressure continued as Isak and Ngumoha fired narrowly past the post while Alexis Mac Allister was denied by a smart save from Lammens and Isak’s shot on the turn was somehow deflected over the top by the diving Maguire.
Szoboszlai saw a long-range effort tipped over by the flying Lammens shortly after the turnaround and saw another effort saved soon after.
Bradley Barcola spurned a glorious chance of a third just before the hour after beating the offside trap, but dragged a tame effort well wide with only Lammens to beat.
Isak missed another wonderful chance after de Ligt misjudged a bouncing ball to allow him another clear run on goal, but the Swede lashed wildly past the near post when one-on-one with Lammens.
Barcola fired over the bar after spinning away from de Ligt on 65 minutes, but the Frenchman nipped past Lisandro Martinez and burst in behind the defence before squaring neatly for Ngumoha to slam home the third a minute later.
Martinez denied Barcola a fourth with a last-ditch block at the far post while Lammens dived to turn around a powerful Isak strike and clawed a curling Szoboszlai shot around the upright with 15 minutes to go.
Virgil van Dijk headed inches wide from a Wirtz cross, but Victor Munoz swept a sublime fourth eight minutes from time after a lovely reverse pass into the box from Wirtz.
United had the chance of a consolation in stoppage time as sub Joshua Zirkzee broke away and found Fernandes. But the United skipper’s shot was turned wide by Allison.

items.title: Liverpool hand Pochettino nightmare Manchester United start after Yoro sees red
items.summary: Green shoots of recovery have lasted longer in a blast-furnace than in the Mauricio Pochettino era at Manchester United. On another abysmal Anfield day for the fallen giants of Manchester, Pochettino’s debut descended into an ordeal after merely eight minutes when Leny Yoro was sent off for denying
items.text:
Green shoots of recovery have lasted longer in a blast-furnace than in the Mauricio Pochettino era at Manchester United. On another abysmal Anfield day for the fallen giants of Manchester, Pochettino’s debut descended into an ordeal after merely eight minutes when Leny Yoro was sent off for denying Alexander Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity. Liverpool would not be denied anything else.
Andoni Iraola indulged in his first fist-pumps towards the Kop after a comfortable, utterly dominant win peppered by Rio Ngumoha and Florian Wirtz brilliance plus goals from Dominik Szoboszlai, Victor Muñoz and the two creative forces. “Poch is at the wheel” was the mocking, merciless soundtrack that accompanied the end of the former Tottenham, Chelsea and USA coach’s first traumatic day in the job.
The latest calamity in United’s worst start to a season for 40 years cannot be pinned on a head coach who only met his new charges on Wednesday. There can be no genuine takes on Pochettino’s vision for United either, given how quickly he was forced to turn his first game into a damage limitation exercise. But there was one firm conclusion to be drawn. His first big call in the job proved a serious mistake, and one that contained destructive repercussions for the entire United team and their performance.
That ill-fated decision was to hand Matthijs de Ligt a first Premier League start in 12 months at the expense of Harry Maguire. Maguire may be a symbol of United’s inertia himself but his replacement at centre-half was heavily responsible for the chaos that unfolded. The Netherlands international was ultimately at fault for three goals. Liverpool, under instruction from Iraola to start strong and “make them feel pressure from the beginning”, could hardly believe their luck at the mishaps in the visitors’ central defence.
De Ligt lost both the flight of the ball and his man, Isak, when Ronald Araújo pinged a routine pass down Liverpool’s right-hand channel. Isak was suddenly away, De Ligt all at sea, and to compound matters Yoro was slow to react to the danger unfolding around his fellow centre-half. By the time United’s covering defender was across to challenge Isak it was too late. Yoro clattered into the back of the Sweden international just outside the area and was shown a straight red card by the referee Sam Barrott. Isak’s heavy first touch could not save him. The free-kick could not save United from double jeopardy. Szoboszlai swept a powerful set piece into Senne Lammens’ bottom right-hand corner from 19 yards.
A simple detail showed the extent of the job that Pochettino has on his hands: the United wall that lined up to face Szoboszlai’s free-kick. Just getting that right was beyond this group of players. White shirts lined up to protect the left side of Lammens’ goal but, with the stranded exception of Bruno Fernandes, there was no one covering the spot where the ball was ultimately placed.
Liverpool seized on the gifts. When the hosts doubled their lead three minutes later thoughts of another 7-0 humiliation for United at Anfield did not seem unreasonable. Ngumoha, starting on the left with Cody Gakpo out injured, tormented Diogo Dalot from the first whistle, as everyone inside the ground expected he would. Having been found by Isak’s cross-field pass the teenager breezed past Dalot to the byline and lifted a cross slightly behind Wirtz. The German playmaker, left in space by De Ligt, improvised brilliantly to hook a volley into the roof of the net while floating in mid-air. United were sinking into the abyss.
The first chants of “Sacked in the morning” flowed from the Kop towards a disbelieving United head coach. There were 14 minutes on the clock. It was of course a ludicrous chant. It might be months before United’s hapless owners are seeking another scapegoat.
Pochettino responded in the only way he could to the onslaught and introduced Maguire into a rejigged five-man defence. Whether in the knowledge that United possessed neither the ability nor the inclination to hurt them, Liverpool eased off for the remainder of the first half although Isak and Alexis Mac Allister could have extended the lead further. Lammens denied both and Maguire threw himself in the way of another Isak shot to deflect over.
Iraola must have had a word during the interval as Liverpool did not let their rivals off so lightly after the restart. Bradley Barcola could and should have provided Wirtz with a hat-trick of assists but squandered three beautiful touches from the £116m recruit. Virgil van Dijk put a free header wide from another fine delivery from Wirtz. Barcola turned provider in devastating style, however, to create the goal that Ngumoha’s display richly deserved. The France winger burst away from Lisandro Martínez and Fernandes with one flick of the ball before rolling an assist on a plate for the teenager to convert at the back post.
Iraola’s thoughts started to drift towards the Champions League trip in Brugge in midweek and he made a triple substitution to rest players in the 72nd minute. But Liverpool were not done. Another mistake by De Ligt, this time a sloppy pass infield, enabled the hosts to pounce and Wirtz released Muñoz free inside the box. The Liverpool substitute stroked an emphatic finish past Lammens. All Sir Alex Ferguson could do in the directors box in the closing stages was laugh with his friend, the actor James Nesbitt. The alternative is too bleak for a proud United man to contemplate.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding commu
items.text:
US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
- Published
The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.
"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."
The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.
The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.
In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.
"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.
It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".
The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.
Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.
Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.
On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.
The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".
One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.
"There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement.
The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a new motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing.
The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.
The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.

items.text:
Yoro sees red as Ngumoha shines - Liverpool v Man Utd player ratings
- Published
Mauricio Pochettino's reign as Manchester United manager got off to a dismal start as his side were beaten 4-0 by rivals Liverpool after playing 82 minutes with 10 men.
Here's how BBC Sport rated the players - and you can see how you scored them below.
- What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean? 
  - Published21 August
Liverpool
Alisson Becker: Caught one cross and took a few goal-kicks. Made a good save to deny Bruno Fernandes in stoppage time. Had little else to do. 6
Ronald Araujo: Never really tested defensively. Made a few contributions going forward. 7
Jeremy Jacquet: Went shoulder to shoulder with Bryan Mbeumo in the box at 0-0, although a penalty against the French defender would have been harsh. 6
Virgil van Dijk: Organised the defence well. Also had a header well-saved at 0-0 and nodded another wide in the second half. 7
Milos Kerkez: Always keen to drive Liverpool up the pitch. Had some nice link-ups with Rio Ngumoha. 7
Dominik Szoboszlai: Fantastic driven free-kick to open the scoring. Went close a few more times with long shots and generally bossed the midfield. 8
Alexis Mac Allister: Did all the simple things right and allowed others to shine around him. Forced Senne Lammens into a top save in the first half. 7
Bradley Barcola: Missed a few chances to score his first league goal for Liverpool when through one-vs-one. Showed his electric pace to set up his side's third. 7
Florian Wirtz: Readjusted well to net Liverpool's second and assisted their fourth. Five goals in four games for club and country now and looks close to his creative best. 8
Rio Ngumoha: So direct and skilful. Scored Liverpool's third with a calm finish. Also set up their second after easily beating Diogo Dalot. Club and country have a real talent on their hands. 9
Alexander Isak: Led the line well but missed some big chances. Won the free-kick that resulted in Szoboszlai's goal and led to Leny Yoro's sending off. 6
Subs:
Victor Munoz (on 72, Barcola): Good cameo and took his goal well, curling it into the far corner. 7
Trey Nyoni (on 72, Mac Allister): Looked bright. Had a shot go just over. 6
Jeremie Frimpong (on 78, Ngumoha): 5
Joe Gomez (on 85, Araujo) 5
Lewis Koumas (on 85, Isak) 5
Subs not used: Chiesa, Mamardashvili, McConell, Tsimikas.
Manchester United
Senne Lammens: Could he have done better with the opener? Good save to deny Mac Allister and some decent stops after that. 6
Leny Yoro: Did he have to make the tackle on Isak? It was almost as though he thought about whether he should and decided the answer was yes. Given Liverpool scored from the free-kick it was a bad decision. 4
Matthijs de Ligt: First Premier League start in almost 12 months in middle of a back three turned into a nightmare with the early error that led to opening goal and Yoro red card. Struggled from that moment on. 4
Lisandro Martinez: Fully extended by Liverpool's attack. The least bad of the visitors' starting defence, but that isn't saying much. Exposed completely by Barcola for Liverpool's third. 5
Diogo Dalot: Given a torrid time by Ngumoha, which prompted Pochettino to bring on Maguire. Tries hard but it's not enough. 5
Youri Tielemans: Concerns about a midfield partnership with Mainoo emerge again. Not having the sustained impact required for a player of his experience. 4
Kobbie Mainoo: Twenty-one-year-old being asked to shoulder so much responsibility in an ailing team. New midfield recruits have not helped him. 5
Bryan Mbeumo: Couple of decent bursts came to nothing, then sacrificed after Yoro red card. Received consoling pat on the head from his new boss. 5
Bruno Fernandes: Early free-kick just wide and shot straight at Alisson. Given the carnage at Old Trafford this season, no wonder contract talks on hold. Furious at free-kick given against him when he thought he was through. 5
Patrick Dorgu: Asked to do an awful lot, initially as wing-back, then further back. Lucky Barcola fluffed his lines or his failure to keep an offside line would have been exposed. 5
Matheus Cunha: Tried to keep simmering frustration in check. Not easy in a losing side with no service. Replaced at the break. 5
Subs:
Harry Maguire (on 22, Mbeumo): Couldn't have expected to be called on so soon. Went into middle of back three and immediately blocked an Isak effort to prevent a third goal. Tried hard. 5
Joshua Zirkzee (on 46, Cunha): Pre-match rumours of a rare start proved unfounded. Replaced Cunha at half-time and asked to bring a different skillset to the number nine role. More physical but not as good and lost possession too easily. 4
Mason Mount (on 65, Tielemans): Only on for a couple of minutes when attempted crossfield pass went to Liverpool player and eventually a third goal. 5
Noussair Mazraoui (on 65, Dorgu): Not really sure what he was supposed to do. Tried to push forward as United's poor control brought more pressure. 4
Andrey Santos (on 87, Mainoo): 5
Subs not used: Heaton, Amad Diallo, Heaven, Lacey.

Liverpool 4-0 Man Utd: Mauricio Pochettino endures nightmare start as Leny Yoro's early red card sparks collapse
Report and free match highlights as Manchester United are routed by Liverpool at Anfield in Mauricio Pochettino's first game; Leny Yoro received early red card before Liverpool ran riot; defeat keeps Man Utd in relegation zone, one point off bottom
Sunday 22 November 2026 18:30, UK
Mauricio Pochettino endured a horror start to his Manchester United tenure as his 10-man side were thrashed 4-0 by Liverpool at Anfield following Leny Yoro's early sending off.
Yoro saw red in the eighth minute when he was adjudged to have made a last-man foul on Alexander Isak, with Dominik Szoboszlai slamming home the resulting free-kick.
The decision was contentious, with Isak having seemingly lost control of the ball when he was fouled, but the double blow left the visitors in disarray and Florian Wirtz added an acrobatic second only two minutes and 46 seconds after the opener.
Liverpool fans taunted Pochettino with chants of 'you're getting sacked in the morning' following the second goal.
- As it happened | Teams | Stats
- Live Premier League table | Watch FREE PL highlights
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱

The Argentine's decision to hand Matthijs de Ligt a first Premier League start in 357 days backfired spectacularly, with the 27-year-old misjudging a high ball in the lead-up to Yoro's red card before the hosts punished more shambolic defending after the break.
Rio Ngumoha added the third when he converted Bradley Barcola's low cross following a rapid counter-attack, becoming the youngest scorer in the history of the fixture, with substitute Victor Munoz netting the fourth from a through ball by the excellent Wirtz.
The four-goal defeat showed Pochettino the size of the task ahead and kept Manchester United in the Premier League relegation zone, only a point off the bottom. They have conceded more goals than any other side in Europe's major leagues in all competitions, with 34.
The defeat was the heaviest in a Manchester United manager's first game since Lal Hilditch was beaten by the same scoreline a century ago, in 1926. It is the first time in 40 years that United have been in the bottom two at this stage of a season.
For Pochettino's counterpart Andoni Iraola, the result represents his first statement win since taking charge. Liverpool move back into fourth place, only a point behind Manchester City in third and seven points behind leaders Arsenal.
WATCH: Yoro's red and all the goals
Keane: Liverpool should have scored eight or nine
Sky Sports pundit Roy Keane said: "United were desperate. So bad.
"Gary Neville's okay with 4-0? Are you telling me they could have done better? Four-nil is not too bad with 10 men? Has anyone ever got a result with 10 men? It can be done!
"People who played for the club said 4-0 is not too bad? Wow. Fans are applauding. Applauding what?
"We're blaming the board, blaming ownership, blaming managers. When do the players take responsibility for some decision-making?
"Liverpool probably should have scored eight, probably eight or nine. It's unbelievable chances they had.
"And everyone's coming off the pitch saying four is not too bad? I feel like swearing."

items.title: COP31 climate talks fail to reach major deal amid deep divisions
items.summary:
COP31 climate talks fail to reach major deal amid deep divisions
- Published
Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into
items.text:
COP31 climate talks fail to reach major deal amid deep divisions
- Published
Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.
But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.
UN secretary general Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".
He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".
After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday morning to try to break the deadlock.
But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.
The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".
"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.
Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.
A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.
Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.
Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".
Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.
Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.
But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.
"Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.
The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".
"This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".
Climate talks in an age of 'overshoot'
While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.
Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said that there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.
He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.
The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.
And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.
In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.
The UN says that the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.
Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.
But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.
Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.
The COP31 president also said that more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035
But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.
The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.

items.title: Why data centers are at the center of the Big Tech backlash
items.summary:
In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.
The book is well-timed, to put it
items.text:
In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.
The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections. And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power.
In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.”
“It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.”
He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.”
During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center.
I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in?
Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so.
I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself. And the thing that struck me most was the level of security.
Obviously, you would expect that this is an infrastructure that is really securitized, because the data inside needs to be kept safe, obviously [they] have these big fences and all the security cameras around the data centers. But to go inside, I had to send my passport in advance. Then when I got there, they had to check the passport, and then as we were going through the data center itself, every single door in the data center was locked unless you had a key card to unlock it.
Then, when you get inside of the server room itself, where all this computer hardware is stored in tall racks that look like cabinets — you can imagine, in your mind, that this would be kind of a sinister location, with some eerie lighting or something like that. But in truth, it’s just quite utilitarian. It’s a warm room with some air conditioning blasting into the servers from vents that are nearby.
It was really loud as well, because you have all these fans running from all these servers, it was really kind of piercing. To be inside of this room, if you were going to be in there for a while, you’d probably want earplugs or something like that.
Before I read your book, I thought of data centers as something that’s important, but a little bit boring. How did you decide they were interesting and rich enough to sustain an entire book?
I felt the same. I was aware that data centers had been out there, but it was not something that I was paying particularly close attention to. But then there were a number of stories that of tipped me off to the fact that there might be more here, and that it was worth looking deeper into what was going on — the first being hearing about the water pressures created by data centers in Chile around the capital of Santiago, where companies like Google and Microsoft were building data centers, and communities were concerned about their access to water and started organizing around that.
And then hearing about how much electricity data centers were consuming in Ireland, to the point that now they consume more than 20% of the country’s electricity, and that was obviously pushing up power prices. It was putting pressures on the grid, such that the grid operator actually put a moratorium in place for grid connections for data centers around the Dublin area, back in 2022. This was even before the generative AI moment that caused a surge in construction of data centers.
And then the other one was in The Dalles, Oregon, where Google had actually built its first company-owned data centers about 20 years back. In that case, its water deal was coming up for renewal. It wanted to build more data centers there, so it needed more water. And when the residents started asking, “How much water is Google actually using?” a journalist at The Oregonian went to the city and essentially asked, “Hey, how much water is Google using? Our readers would like to know this,” he was hit with a lawsuit instead of being given that information. Because Google did not want it to be public. And then, of course, when it did come out about a year later, Google revealed that it was using 29% of the city’s water,

Rafael Camara: Haas confirm Brazilian will race in final two rounds of F1 season rather than chase F2 championship
Rafael Camara will race again for Haas at the Qatar Grand Prix and Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ahead of joining full-time for the 2027 season; Camara leads the Formula 2 standings but will not feature in the final rounds
Sunday 22 November 2026 18:48, UK
Haas have confirmed that Rafael Camara will continue to feature for the team in the final two races of the season, rather than challenge for the Formula 2 championship.
Camara made his debut at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix earlier this month, following Esteban Ocon's departure ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix and reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa stepping in for that race.
He also raced alongside team-mate Ollie Bearman at the Las Vegas GP, finishing 16th, with the Brazilian now retaining his place for the remainder of the season.

The 21-year-old will feature at the Qatar GP from November 27-29 and the Abu Dhabi GP the following week, ahead of taking up a full-time seat with Haas from next season.
In a statement, Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu said: "We're excited to be able to finish the season with Rafa driving and building on his first two race starts with the team in Brazil and America.
"I'm delighted that Rafa's embraced every track session as a learning opportunity and embedded himself further within the team.
"We now get to finish the season together, which is advantageous to us all ahead of a relatively short off-season and as our 2027 preparations get under way."
Camara leads the F2 standings by seven points over Red Bull reserve Nikola Tsolov ahead of the final two rounds of the season, although would be unable to compete in both events on the same weekend.
Invicta Racing, Camara's F2 team, shared on X: "What a journey it's been Thank you for everything Rafa and best of luck for the rest of the @f1 season with @haasf1team."
For Camara to claim the F2 title, a year on from winning the Formula 3 championship, he would need Tsolov to score less than seven points from the final four races and no other driver to move above him in the standings.

Al Jazeera World
Cox’s Bazar: Rohingya Life in Exile
Inside the world’s largest refugee camp, Rohingya families fight hunger and loss as aid dries up, clinging to faith, each other and the hope of returning home.
For more than a million Rohingya refugees, Cox’s Bazar was meant to be a place of safety. Instead, it has become a life on hold. Filmed entirely inside the camps in Bangladesh, this film follows six people: a widowed mother newly arrived from Myanmar, a father supporting his family through a small betel-leaf business, a student and advocate, an artist, a musician and a young man forced to conceal his identity for protection. Together, they face shrinking food aid, restricted opportunities, separation from loved ones and no clear route home. The Islamic holy month of Ramadan forms the backdrop, bringing moments of faith, family and communal ritual into sharper relief amid mounting hardship. Made with a Rohingya producer and director of photography living in the settlement, the film offers an intimate view from within: people working, studying, creating and caring for their families while fighting to preserve their dignity.

NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Jubilee Party presidential hopeful Fred Matiang’i has dismissed claims of competing political camps within the opposition, insisting that the movement is united and will field one candidate against President William Ruto in the 2027 General Election.
Matiang’i, who is positioning himself for the opposition’s presidential ticket, said leaders should not be distracted by claims of internal divisions but instead focus on consolidating their political bases and building a united front ahead of the polls.
Speaking during a church service attended by Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua and Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro, Matiang’i explained his association with the two leaders, saying they shared a common approach to leadership and a desire to provide solutions to Kenya’s challenges.
He described Karua as a leader he admired for her straightforwardness and firm approach to issues, adding that their shared values informed their political relationship.
“First of all, my elder sister Mother Karua is someone I always look up to because we have a lot of things in common. I like her a lot because she is also no-nonsense. She’s also focused on the things we do; that’s why I keep her company,” Matiang’i said.
He also praised Nyoro, describing the legislator as straightforward and focused on finding practical solutions to the problems facing the country.
“You stay with people when you see that as you start planning, you move in one direction. And Ndindi is like that straightforward. We know the solutions that are needed; we want to provide the solution. We are not here for stories. We are here for solutions,” he said.
Matiang’i dismissed suggestions that the opposition was divided into competing political formations, saying there was only one team working towards removing the current administration from power.
He argued that debates about rival camps were unnecessary and risked diverting attention from the bigger political contest ahead of the next election.
“All of us are one. We are one group of people. You say I am no-nonsense, so let me put it this way: You know we spend a lot of time in our country on things that don’t matter. You know this nonsense about competition, I don’t know which team is which,” he said.
The former CS maintained that the 2027 elections would present Kenyans with two political choices: the government and a united opposition.
“We have one team in Kenya in the opposition, and we have a government in power that has failed in its job. So when we go to the election, there will only be two lines: Kasongo’s line and the line of the people of Kenya,” he added.
His remarks come as opposition figures intensify political engagements, consolidate their respective support bases and build networks ahead of the 2027 General Election.
Nyoro rules out rival opposition camps
Nyoro, who also addressed the congregation, echoed Matiang’i’s position, dismissing reports of competing forces within the opposition and insisting that the political movement was united.
The Kiharu MP said opposition leaders were working towards a common objective and would eventually settle on one candidate to challenge the government in the next General Election.
He said the presence of different opposition leaders in separate parts of the country should not be interpreted as evidence of political divisions.
“Lastly, I want to inform you that while the three of us are here, our colleagues are in Embu and others are elsewhere,we as the opposition are united as one,” Nyoro said.
He added: “Today I saw a newspaper claiming there are competing forces within the opposition; there is only one force of the opposition, and that is the unity of all of us in the opposition, and we will produce one united candidate to fly the flag.”
The question of competing political camps has emerged amid growing discussions about opposition leadership, possible alliances and who will eventually carry the movement’s presidential ticket.
Matiang’i, however, insisted that political relationships should be guided by shared objectives rather than individual ambitions, pointing to his association with Karua and Nyoro as an example of leaders who agree on the direction they want the country to take.
He also outlined some of the policy changes he would pursue should the opposition form the next government, promising reforms in security, healthcare, education and taxation.
Drawing from his experience as Interior Cabinet Secretary, Matiang’i promised a firm approach to insecurity, particularly the circulation of illegal firearms and the activities of armed gangs.
He said Kenyans needed a peaceful environment to pursue economic opportunities and development, promising to restore order if given the opportunity to lead.
“In the past, I was the Cabinet Secretary for Security, and that is why people used to say I couldn’t tolerate games like these where armed thugs and guns are walking around here. If we get the opportunity, you will not hear the word ‘gun’ even once,” he said.
On healthcare, Matiang’i pledged to scrap the Social Health Authority (SHA), arguing that Kenyans should not continue struggling to raise money to access medical treatment.
He also promised to address challenges in the education sector and review taxation, particularly deductions affecting civil servants whose take-home salaries have been reduced.
“We will throw away this thing called SHA so that people won’t suffer searching for medical money the way they are searching today,” he said.
Nyoro also used the occasion to outline his education agenda, saying the opposition had a clear plan for the country should it secure power.
Citing the education model in his Kiharu constituency, where day secondary school fees stand at Sh500 per term, he said the opposition wanted to eliminate school fees for all learners in day secondary schools.

A young child has died in Virginia, m
items.text:
Virginia reports first measles-linked death of 2026 in child younger than 5
The death comes within days of health experts stripping the US of its measles elimination status, amid an uptick in cases.
US loses measles-free status after 26 years in historic setback
A young child has died in Virginia, marking the first case of a measles-related death in the southern state for the year 2026.
The Virginia Department of Health made the announcement on Friday, just days after the United States lost its designation as having eliminated the highly contagious virus.
State authorities declined to provide details about the child’s death, citing the family’s privacy. It was disclosed, however, that the child was younger than five.
Virginia has reported 220 cases overall this year, most of them in the central part of the state. The vast majority of the cases were among people not vaccinated against the virus.
They include 40 children ranging from infants to age four, and another 75 children aged five to 12, according to state health department data as of November 19.
“Virginia has not had a measles-related death since 1978,” according to Frederic Bertley, an immunologist and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry, a research centre in Ohio.
He added that the spread of measles is evidence that the virus is gaining a foothold and becoming a growing problem for the US.
Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, reported its eighth measles-related death of the year last week and confirmed 1,631 measles cases, as of November 20.
Wisconsin also reported two deaths in 2026, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated death of 2026 in early November.
In that case, the victim was reportedly a seven-month-old child. It was the state’s first measles-related death in more than three decades.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, though it does not specify the states where the deaths were recorded.
It has also tracked more than 5,800 cases nationally in 2026, the most of any year since 1991.
In August, President Donald Trump issued an executive order reducing the number of recommended childhood vaccinations, falsely suggesting that the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine could be dangerous.
“You have the MMR; we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together, there could be a possibility they are quite lethal,” Trump said.
The CDC has said it remains committed to stopping measles outbreaks and regaining the country’s elimination status.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC director Erica Schwartz said.
The CDC has provided approximately $100m in additional funding to state and local health departments since August to strengthen vaccination efforts, surveillance and outbreak response.
