items.title: McBurnie’s late double snatches shock win for Hull to crush 10-man Brighton
items.summary:
Oli McBurnie’s injury-time brace helped Hull to a dramatic victory over Brighton but the Tigers had the heroics of their goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis to thank for a result which continued their unbeaten home start since returning to the Premier League.
Fabian Hürzeler’s side were much the strong
items.text:
Oli McBurnie’s injury-time brace helped Hull to a dramatic victory over Brighton but the Tigers had the heroics of their goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis to thank for a result which continued their unbeaten home start since returning to the Premier League.
Fabian Hürzeler’s side were much the stronger of the teams on an afternoon they largely dominated. However, a string of chances in both halves passed them by without the goal their play deserved, thanks largely to Tzolakis, with the Greek international producing a string of sensational saves in both halves.
But after Brighton’s João Costinha was sent off for a second yellow card in the final moments, Hull pressed forward for an unlikely winner which they ultimately found, as McBurnie bundled home before tapping in a second two minutes later. It was a damaging afternoon for Brighton’s title hopes, who missed the chance to close the gap to Arsenal to three points.
How they did not secure at least a point is anyone’s guess. The Seagulls should not only have been in front at half-time, but ahead by such a margin that the game could have been over inside the opening 45 minutes.
Tzolakis was called into action early on, with a superb point-blank save to deny Diego Gómez from converting Maxim De Cuyper’s low cross. Gómez, De Cuyper and Yasin Ayari were causing mayhem on a frequent basis, with Ayari then next to miss a gilt-edged opportunity to open the scoring – but he could only fire a tame shot at Tzolakis.
Hull’s keeper was called into action again two minutes later; another slick Brighton move led to Ayari hitting the crossbar and from the rebound, Tzolakis reacted fastest to deny Georginio Rutter from inside the box before Gómez was next to miss a clearcut chance, with Tzolakis making another wonderful save with his foot to keep it goalless.
Half-time did little change the flow of momentum. Pascal Gross’ shot produced another reflex save from Tzolakis before Gómez then fired wide from six yards out, when it appeared easier to hit the target. You began to wonder if those missed opportunities were going to become costly, with Hull starting to become a threat at the other end, too.
On two separate occasions they countered Brighton attacks with wonderful breaks, but Mohamed Belloumi fluffed his lines both times after initially doing well to work the space for shots. Bart Verbruggen, mostly on a watching brief to that point, saved one before breathing a sigh of relief as the second squirmed wide of his post.
Hürzeler had seen enough. Three substitutes were introduced to try and find the breakthrough and one of those, Charalampos Kostoulas, finally beat Tzolakis with a clever chip over the Hull goalkeeper, but Regan Slater was on hand to hack the ball off the line and keep the game level heading into the final 10 minutes.
And all those Tzolakis saves ultimately proved crucial. When Costinha was shown a second yellow for a foul on the impressive Sorba Thomas, Hull surged forward with belief they could perhaps find a winner.
McBurnie then scrambled the ball past Verbruggen after Lucas Gourna-Douath was set free before, two minutes later, the Hull striker repeated the trick to double the Tigers’ lead and seal an incredible victory for the hosts.

items.text:
Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
- Published
An explosion has occurred on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port after a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.
It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS said the country was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Seperately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

Punchestown: Final Demand battles back to win thrilling John Durkan Memorial Punchestown Chase
In a John Durkan Memorial Punchestown Chase dominated by Willie Mullins-trained runners, Final Demand showed real determination to fend off last year's runner up Fact To File
Sunday 22 November 2026 16:04,
items.text:
Punchestown: Final Demand battles back to win thrilling John Durkan Memorial Punchestown Chase
In a John Durkan Memorial Punchestown Chase dominated by Willie Mullins-trained runners, Final Demand showed real determination to fend off last year's runner up Fact To File
Sunday 22 November 2026 16:04, UK
Final Demand emerged best of the army of returning Willie Mullins stars on show after a thrilling finish to the John Durkan Memorial Punchestown Chase.
With Henry de Bromhead's mare The Big Westerner a non-runner due to unsuitable ground, the champion trainer saddled each of the nine remaining runners, with last year's winner and subsequent Cheltenham Gold Cup hero Gaelic Warrior the 10/11 favourite in the hands of Paul Townend.
Kitzbuhel and Daniel King took the field along for much of the two-and-a-half-mile journey, closely pursued by 8/1 shot Final Demand and Patrick Mullins, with Fact To File and Gaelic Warrior next in line.
With the latter unable to quicken sufficiently to get himself into a challenge position, it was the 2024 winner and last year's runner-up Fact To File who looked most likely to prevail when taking over the lead on the run-in, but Final Demand battled bravely to get back up by a neck.
"It was a fantastic race. Very few of my horses were disappointing, they all ran well enough and I was happy with them," said Mullins.
"What a result, for the Mullins family, not just Closutton. To see Patrick riding a Grade One winner and dare I say it, maybe outriding Harry Cobden from the last home.
"Patrick said he thought he had the race won but he just missed the last and he had to win it a second time. So that just shows how much this horse has improved from last year.
"In against those top-class horses, he was good the whole way around. I was amazed at what turn of foot he showed from the last home. I thought when he made that little error that was enough and Fact To File would go on and win. He got down and ground it out. For a second season novice, that's a huge result."
Bookmakers cut Final Demand's Cheltenham Gold Cup odds to 7/1 from 14/1, while easing Gaelic Warrior to 5/2 from 13/8.
Gaelic Warrior's owner Rich Ricci was not too disappointed with the defeat of his star chaser.
He said: "Paul was happy enough, he obviously needed the run. He said he blew up a couple of times and got boxed in a little bit, but couldn't go fast enough to keep with them.
"He rides like more of a three miler these days, but Paul was very positive and said he wouldn't swap him for anything yet. Let's see how it goes.
"For him it's all about the spring, I think. Last year he won here, lost at Christmas, lost at the Dublin Racing Festival and then won the last two at Cheltenham and Punchestown, so hopefully he can repeat his spring successes."

items.text:
PSG's Doue to have surgery on ruptured ACL
- Published
Paris St-Germain forward Desire Doue will have surgery later this month after rupturing the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee.
The 21-year-old was in tears as he was taken off on a stretcher towards the end of the first half in the Ligue 1 champions' 3-2 victory over Nice on Saturday night.
Doue, who has arguably been PSG's best player this season, twisted awkwardly and went down under no contact.
The match was stopped for five minutes as Doue - who was visibly in pain - received treatment before he was applauded off by the crowd at the Allianz Riviera Stadium.
It is a huge set-back for the France attacker, who missed 13 games in 2025-26 with calf and hamstring injuries.
The European champions have been plagued with injury issues so far this season and are already without Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, who sustained an ACL injury of his own against Barcelona in October.
PSG return to action on Wednesday, when they host Roma in the Champions League.

items.text:
Everybody knows the pattern. Performances fade. Results falter. A title challenge becomes clinging on for the last Champions League spot becomes mid-table. Or a promising start becomes a troubling dip, becomes a full-on battle against relegation.
Fans begin to grumble. The media wonder whether the spark has gone. Players look disaffected. A dressing room, once lost, is seldom rediscovered, and few managers are given the opportunity to find it again. A crisis in football, once acknowledged, is only ever resolved in one way: by the sacking of the manager.
With hindsight, Michael Carrick’s dismissal was probably inevitable from the moment Manchester United lost at Hull on the opening weekend, just as Ruben Amorim was doomed from the moment cameras picked him up fiddling with magnetic counters on a tactics board in the rain at Grimsby. The message for Mauricio Pochettino is clear: don’t go playing badly on the east coast.
It’s generally acknowledged that Carrick, while he may not have been the ideal manager for United, was a long way down the list of the biggest problems at the club. So what was the point of sacking him? As Pochettino begins his United career at Anfield on Sunday, what realistically can any manager hope to achieve?
Mauricio Pochettino has called on Manchester United to have “no fear” when they travel to Anfield for his first game. The Argentinian does not want his players to take a backward step as he targets a fast start.
United are 19th in the Premier League and Liverpool fifth but the head coach will not accept any self-doubt. Pochettino is known for being attack-minded and is keen to instil those ideals, but will have had only three days with the players since replacing Michael Carrick.
“We are going to Anfield with the idea to win and be brave and to be Manchester United,” Pochettino told the club’s website. “The history talks for us, and what we need to expect. We need to be sure that we are brave and we are protagonists and go there with no fears and challenge a very good team like Liverpool.”
No big surprises in Mauricio Pochettino’s first Man Utd XI. The most notable selection is probably the centre-back pairing of Matthijs de Ligt (starting his first Premier League game since November 2025) and Lisandro Martinez.
There are three changes from the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa in Michael Carrick’s final game: De Ligt, Martinez and Patrick Dorgu replace Noussair Mazraoui, Harry Maguire and Amad Diallo.
Liverpool bring in Rio Ngumoha for Cody Gakpo, the only change from their win at Crystal Palace before the international break.
The first day in a new job is supposed to be gentle and relaxed: small talk, smaller admin, a few bits of work and some lamentably awkward handshakes. Mauricio Pochettino’s first day* as Manchester United manager is the polar opposite. Liverpool away, the ultimate domestic challenge for any United manager.
This quirk of employment opportunity and fixture list might be a good thing for Pochettino. It’s a free hit, with nobody of sound mind expecting his brave new world to begin until he has had months on the training ground. And if United do win, it’ll increase the length of the free pass that every new manager receives.
Andoni Iraola only joined Liverpool in June, yet he’s already their 11th longest-serving manager. Iraola has made a promising start, including some rousing victories in Europe in particular.
In the Premier League, Liverpool’s main problem has been their home form. They’ve taken five points from five games, but it’s a bit early to lament the demise of Fortress Anfield. Three of those five matches were against the top three of Manchester City, Arsenal and Brighton.
Today, almost unbelievably, Liverpool are playing the team in 19th place: Mauricio Pochettino’s Manchester United.
Kick off 4.30pm.
* Yes, yes, I know this isn’t actually his first day in the job, but you know exactly what I mean so let’s not allow semantics to undermine a perfectly half-arsed preamble.

items.title: Matiang’i opens up on Karua and Nyoro alliance as opposition eyes 2027
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i has opened up about his political association with Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua and Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro, describing the two leaders as people who share his approach to leadership and desire to provide practical solutions
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i has opened up about his political association with Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua and Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro, describing the two leaders as people who share his approach to leadership and desire to provide practical solutions to Kenya’s challenges.
The Jubilee party leader and presidential hopeful said his relationship with Karua was anchored on shared values, particularly their preference for firm leadership, discipline and a no-nonsense approach to public service.
He described Karua as a leader he admires and looks up to, saying their common outlook on governance explains why they have maintained a close association.
The former CS also praised Nyoro, describing him as straightforward and focused on finding solutions rather than engaging in political rhetoric.
Their growing association comes as opposition figures seek to consolidate their respective political bases, strengthen networks and establish a common front ahead of the 2027 General Election.
Speaking about his relationship with Karua, Matiang’i referred to her as his elder sister and said he appreciated her commitment to the issues they believe need to be addressed in the country.
“First of all, my elder sister Mother Karua is someone I always look up to because we have a lot of things in common. I like her a lot because she is also no-nonsense. She’s also focused on the things we do; that’s why I keep her company,” he said.
Matiang’i’s remarks offer an insight into the political relationships he is building as he positions himself within the wider opposition movement ahead of the next election.
He also sought to explain why he associates with Nyoro, saying political relationships should be informed by shared objectives and a common understanding of the solutions required to address the country’s problems.
“You stay with people when you see that as you start planning, you move in one direction. And Ndindi is like that straightforward. We know the solutions that are needed; we want to provide the solution. We are not here for stories. We are here for solutions,” he said.
The former CS dismissed suggestions of competing camps within the opposition, insisting that leaders should concentrate on challenging the government instead of engaging in internal political contests.
He argued that the opposition should be viewed as one political formation despite the different leaders, parties and political interests represented within it.
“All of us are one. We are one group of people,” Matiang’i said.
He criticised what he described as unnecessary competition among opposition politicians, arguing that such debates diverted attention from the task of presenting Kenyans with an alternative government.
Matiang’i maintained that the 2027 General Election would effectively be a contest between the current administration and an opposition seeking to replace it.
“You know we spend a lot of time in our country on things that don’t matter. You know this nonsense about competition, I don’t know which team is which. We have one team in Kenya in the opposition, and we have a government in power that has failed in its job,” he said.
He added that the political contest would ultimately present Kenyans with two choices.
“When we go to the election, there will only be two lines: Kasongo’s line and the line of the people of Kenya,” he said, using the term Kasongo, a political nickname used by government critics to refer to President William Ruto.
Beyond opposition unity, Matiang’i used the engagement to outline some of the policy changes he would pursue if given an opportunity to lead the country.
Drawing from his experience as Interior Cabinet Secretary, he promised a firm approach to security, particularly the circulation of illegal firearms and the activities of armed gangs.
He said his previous experience in charge of the country’s security apparatus had shaped his approach to public safety, insisting that Kenyans should be able to go about their daily activities without fear of armed criminals.
Matiang’i argued that insecurity undermined development and economic progress, promising to prioritise peace and stability under a government led by his political formation.
“In the past, I was the Cabinet Secretary for Security, and that is why people used to say I couldn’t tolerate games like these where armed thugs and guns are walking around here,” he said.
He added that if given an opportunity to lead, his administration would move decisively against the circulation of firearms and other security threats.
“If we get the opportunity,if I were to get that opportunity,you will not hear the word ‘gun’ even once. Life in Kenya, our country, will remain peaceful so we can move forward,” he said.

UpFront
Can we build a more ethical AI future?
Marc Lamont Hill speaks with tech entrepreneur Anil Dash about AI’s risks and the fight for ethical technology.
The artificial intelligence boom is transforming the global economy and concentrating enormous power in the hands of a few technology companies. But a series of developments is raising new questions about the industry’s stability and accountability from the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy to a wave of technology outages affecting the US government, major banks, companies and aviation systems alongside reports of hacked refrigerators across Europe. Concerns are mounting over the economic risks, mass layoffs, privacy and environmental impact of AI. And as AI company Anthropic began trading publicly, reaching a $2 trillion valuation, questions are mounting over whether the extraordinary levels of AI investment are sustainable. Is there a future where AI can be used for the collective good?
This week on UpFront, Marc Lamont Hill speaks with Anil Dash, former adviser to the White House Office of Digital Strategy in former United States President Barack Obama’s administration, about the risks of the AI boom, Silicon Valley’s growing political influence and the urgent need for greater accountability.

items.title: Blackburn earn derby draw for Mowbray and extend Burnley’s wait for home win
items.summary:
Todd Cantwell’s penalty earned Blackburn a 2-2 draw at Burnley in their first match since head coach Tony Mowbray stepped back because of health issues.
In a gripping, physical East Lancashire derby, the home side led twice, through Largie Ramazani’s rising first-half drive and Jaydon Banel’s steere
items.text:
Todd Cantwell’s penalty earned Blackburn a 2-2 draw at Burnley in their first match since head coach Tony Mowbray stepped back because of health issues.
In a gripping, physical East Lancashire derby, the home side led twice, through Largie Ramazani’s rising first-half drive and Jaydon Banel’s steered finish after the break. But Andri Gudjohnsen scored Blackburn’s first equaliser, then earned the penalty which Cantwell converted.
Burnley remain deep in relegation trouble, without a home league victory for 400 days, having once again failed to hold on to a lead. They have now dropped 25 points from winning positions in the Championship this season.
Blackburn wanted a victory not just for local pride, but to honour Mowbray, who turned 63 on Sunday, and for whom this was to be a 900th match in management before his announcement on Tuesday that he would be stepping back. Their players warmed up in T-shirts bearing the message “We’re with you, Tony” on the back and the number 900 on the front.
Coaches Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds have taken charge in Mowbray’s absence and had to reshuffle the defence when Tom Atcheson was concussed after receiving a boot to the face in the third minute.
Stand-in goalkeeper Aynsley Pears, playing after Balazs Toth sustained a broken hand on international duty with Hungary, pushed over a fierce deflected shot from Banel, but was at fault when Ramazani gave Burnley a 27th-minute lead.
The on-loan Leeds winger cut in from the right and fired a shot that flew into the roof of the net right by Pears, who was too slow to react.
But Gudjohnsen equalised four minutes later, racing on to a Harry Pickering long ball that drifted over Burnley centre-back Max Alleyne, and steering a sweet shot beyond goalkeeper Max Weiß for his 12th goal of the season. The Icelander celebrated by grabbing a T-shirt paying tribute to Mowbray from a photographer and displaying it for the cameras.
Blackburn finished the first half strongly, with Cantwell firing over a good chance, before Banel restored Burnley’s lead six minutes into the second half, running unchallenged to place a shot into the far corner as defender Hayden Carter backed off.
The home side were fortunate to escape a strong penalty appeal just before the hour mark as Cantwell burst into the penalty area and saw two attempted crosses both strike the arm of Igor Julio.
Blackburn did get a penalty with 16 minutes left as Josh Laurent, attempting to clear a low cross, failed to spot Gudjohnsen darting in from behind him and caught the striker’s leg. Cantwell drove the penalty straight down the middle to make it 2-2.
Gudjohnsen thought he had given Blackburn the lead two minutes later, when he controlled and drove a low shot against the base of the post with Weiß a spectator, but neither side could find a winner.

Israel's Eisenkot condemns 'Jewish terrorism' in West Bank

items.text:
Israel's Eisenkot condemns 'Jewish terrorism' in West Bank
November 22, 2026
Israeli authorities were on Sunday investigating arson attacks and vandalism against Palestinian properties and vehicles in the occupied West Bank which Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot condemned as "Jewish terrorism."
Images posted on social media showed vehicles in flames and slogans written on walls reading: "In blood and fire Judea has fallen, in blood and fire Judea will rise again," using a biblical name for the West Bank.
"Settlers attacked the northern area on the outskirts of the village at around two in the morning," Jihad al-Qaq, a local activist, told the AFP news agency.
"They set fire to around eight vehicles and wrote racist slogans on the walls of houses."
Israeli soldiers and police were deployed to the towns of Deir as-Sudan, Deir Abu Mashaal, Kafr Malik and Al-Tuwani following the reports, with the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) saying it "strongly condemns" the acts.
Eisenkot condemns 'Jewish terrorism'
The suspected arson attacks were condemned by Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who is engaged in post-election negotiations to form a government to replace that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"The night of arson … is Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word, and it must be called what it is," he said.
"Sabotage by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermines regional stability, endangers lives, and severely damages the national security and foreign relations of the State of Israel," he said. Eisenkot used the biblical terms, Judea and Samaria, to refer to the West Bank territories in question.
More than 500,000 Israelis live in West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law, alongside around 3 million Palestinians.
The West Bank has been occupied by Israel since 1967 but attacks against Palestinians have surged in the wake of Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack on Israel. Since then, more than 1,100 Palestinians in the West Bank have been killed by Israeli soldiers or settlers, according to data from the Palestinian Health Ministry.
Local resident Ahmad Ghneimat told the Associated Press that violence had increased after several Israeli settler outposts sprang up in the area. He said settlers have stolen sheep and violently harassed olive harvesters.
"We woke up at 2:30 at night to the sound of explosions [and] seven cars on fire," said Muntasir al-Malik, another resident. "We came out of the houses and panicked."
Eisenkot called for "severe sanctions" to be imposed on the individuals responsible.
Eisenkot's labeling of the violent settlers as "terrorists" follows the use of the same term by the United States' ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, in September. US officials usually reserve the term for Palestinian militants.

items.text:
Drone attacks kill four near Sudan’s capital, damage UN building
The Rapid Support Forces are blamed as drones reportedly hit United Nations and government buildings, as well as Khartoum’s airport.
Drone attacks blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed four people in and around the capital, Khartoum, and damaged a United Nations building, according to local reports and UN officials.
The attacks early on Sunday struck residential areas as Sudanese air defences responded to drones reportedly targeting government buildings and Khartoum’s airport.
The strikes have raised fresh concerns about the growing danger to civilians and aid workers as Sudan‘s war increasingly relies on drones.
Explosions were heard across the capital between approximately 2am (00:00 GMT) and 4:30am (02:30 GMT), according to witnesses cited by the AFP news agency, as the army attempted to intercept the drones.
Al Jazeera’s AlMigdad Alruhaid reported from the city of Omdurman, across the Nile from Khartoum, that three people were killed and nine wounded when a drone struck a home in northern Omdurman.
A child was also killed in a separate attack south of the capital.
In the village of Jebel Aulia, about 45km (28 miles) south of Khartoum, a witness told AFP that a drone hit the home of a mosque official who calls worshippers to prayer. Residents searched the wreckage for trapped relatives.
The UN’s humanitarian coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, said on Sunday that one of its buildings had been damaged while staff were inside.
The UN’s humanitarian office, which coordinates emergency relief, condemned the danger to its personnel in a civilian neighbourhood, calling it “unacceptable”.
A Sudanese army source told AFP on Sunday that the drones had been launched from neighbouring Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar airport. The allegation could not be independently verified.
Ethiopia has previously denied Sudanese accusations that it allows the RSF to carry out attacks from its territory.
Sudan has also lodged complaints with the UN Security Council, the body responsible for international peace and security, and the African Union, a continental organisation, over alleged drone operations originating in Ethiopia.
Soldiers executed
Separately on Sunday, Sudan’s government accused RSF fighters of executing captured soldiers in southeastern Blue Nile state, near the Ethiopian border.
The government condemned the alleged killings as violations of international humanitarian law. The accusation has not been independently verified.
Both the RSF and the Sudanese army are relying more frequently on drones to hit enemy targets. More than 1,100 were killed by drones in the first half of this year, according to the United Nations.
The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has said that drone attacks account for about two-thirds of children killed or injured in Sudan from the period of January to September.
The war in Sudan between the army and the RSF began in April 2023. It has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with 13 million people displaced and some regions facing famine.

items.title: Manchester City’s WSL title bid hit by Spurs after Vinberg and Naz’s late double
items.summary: This most unpredictable and evenly-contested Women’s Super League campaign took another unexpected twist as Manchester City missed the chance to return to the top of the table as they suffered a second successive WSL defeat, by virtue of a terrific away performance from a Tottenham side who moved wi
items.text:
This most unpredictable and evenly-contested Women’s Super League campaign took another unexpected twist as Manchester City missed the chance to return to the top of the table as they suffered a second successive WSL defeat, by virtue of a terrific away performance from a Tottenham side who moved within three points of the European places.
The shock result came just 24 hours after City’s title rivals Chelsea had dropped points at Liverpool. It was the first time Manchester City had failed to win a home league match during Andrée Jeglertz’s 16 months in charge, let alone lose. Nevertheless, the victory was fully deserved for Tottenham, who made Khadija “Bunny” Shaw wait to equal her teammate Vivianne Miedema’s all-time WSL goalscoring record of 97 goals.
Jeglertz described the defeat as a “wake-up call” for his team, adding: “Tottenham were a little bit more urgent than us. Each duel counts, each moment counts, each ball counts. That was something that I missed with our players, especially in the second half where we needed to score and we needed to beat them in one-versus-one situations. I missed a little bit of that urgency, which I think is the most important in a team, and if we drop a little bit in that, this league is so tight and tough and the teams are so good, you will drop points and lose games.”
Before the game, the anticipated storyline felt almost too obvious. Shaw, needing three goals to surpass Miedema, was facing a club against whom she had previously scored four hat-tricks, including on Tottenham’s most recent visit to this stadium in March, when she recorded the WSL’s fastest treble. Persistently their tormentor, Shaw has scored more goals against Spurs than any other player has managed against a single opponent in the competition.
When Shaw opened the scoring inside 10 minutes, everything seemed to be following the expected script. Jade Rose, pressing very high up the pitch for a centre-back, won the ball and played a precise low pass across to Shaw, who tucked into the bottom corner from inside the box to record her 96th WSL goal and her 16th against Tottenham.
That, however, proved to be the only effort at goal – on or off target – that Manchester City would register during the opening 45 minutes, as Tottenham impressed. Kirsty Hanson drew a good save from Ayaka Yamashita and Hanson also felt she had a very strong claim for a penalty when Carlotta Wamser appeared to foul her inside the area, but it was not long before the visitors were deservedly level as Cathinka Tandberg expertly turned home Hanson’s cross with a clinical near-post finish.
Tottenham continued to threaten after the break, although Rose scooped over the bar to spurn a huge City chance on the rebound after a Lauren Hemp free kick had been parried by Lize Kop. Some very effective counterattacking football then deservedly won the game for Tottenham as they scored twice to stun the defending champions.
First, in the 74th minute, an exquisite Drew Spence through ball found the run of Matilda Vinberg – who was a late addition to the starting side after the withdrawal of Olivia Holdt during the warm-up because of stomach pains – and Vinberg showed her quality to turn Rose and fire past Yamashita. Vinberg turned provider five minutes later, to set up Jessica Naz for another good finish.
Martin Ho, the Tottenham head coach, hailed his team’s “outstanding” display, saying: “Every time we play a team who has been in the top three consistently, the conversation is ‘can you get one over the line?’ And, for the players, they need to feel what that feels like and enjoy that. Today we nullified a lot of their threats. That will give us a lot of confidence.”
Manchester City had won 12 of their 13 previous WSL games against Tottenham, and all of their past 17 WSL home games, but this defeat added a further dent to their title challenge after their loss at Stamford Bridge last weekend. Chelsea, held to a goalless draw by Liverpool on Saturday, remain two points clear.
Jeglertz continued: “We will bounce back, I’m not worried about that. I know the qualities in this group. But it’s the good habits, the small details that matter. Those are the things that win titles – this was actually the first time that I missed that in a game and I’m pretty sure it’s not going to happen again.” With just seven points now separating the top five, his team can ill-afford for it to happen again.

The Drugs Don’t Work

The challenges posed by antimicrobial resistance show where its impact is most acutely and tragically manifested: infant mortality in the developing world
items.text:
Featured Documentaries
The Drugs Don’t Work
A look at how antibiotic overuse could fuel superbugs, killing eight million people annually by 2050.
The challenges posed by antimicrobial resistance show where its impact is most acutely and tragically manifested: infant mortality in the developing world, specifically in sub-Saharan Africa. This film shows what these bland statistics mean in real terms to the health workers and families affected, following them as they struggle to fight this battle with low-tech solutions.
The Drugs Don’t Work follows the battle to the United Kingdom and examines how and why penicillin, the world’s most successful antibiotic, was invented. It then examines why pharmaceutical companies like GlaxoSmithKline are struggling to produce novel solutions to the problem of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
The film also explores the cutting edge of academic research at British universities and hospitals supported by the power of the UK-based tech company DeepMind, and features academics and advocates who are devoting their lives to solving the problem. Returning to Africa, it shows how local innovation and the tools offered by the developed world are now saving lives and contributing to the global battle against AMR – an effort that could ultimately save millions of lives.

items.text:
Zelenskyy urges US to release Patriot missiles as Russia kills 3 in Ukraine
A Russian drone attack kills at least two people near Kyiv as Russian shelling kills one in Zaporizhzhia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged the United States to approve the delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles after a week of Russian attacks across 20 regions of the country with the latest ones killing three near Kyiv and in Zaporizhzhia.
In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Russia launched about 2,700 attack drones, nearly 1,460 guided aerial bombs and 165 missiles over the past week. A significant share of the missiles were ballistic, he said, including some supplied by North Korea.
“Against this backdrop, it is particularly difficult to understand the delays in the delivery of antiballistic systems to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine is short of US-made Patriot interceptors, which can shoot down ballistic missiles.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s partners had already paid for the missiles through a NATO-coordinated programme that funds purchases of US weapons for Kyiv. However, their delivery is still awaiting Washington’s approval.
Rescuers search rubble near Kyiv
One of the latest Russian attacks hit a five-storey apartment building early on Sunday in the village of Dymer, north of Kyiv, causing part of it to collapse.
Zelenskyy initially said nine people had been evacuated and 14 were unaccounted for.
Rescuers later recovered two bodies as emergency crews searched for 11 people, including two children, who were missing, according to Russia’s Interfax news agency, citing Radio Liberty.
Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the Zaporizhia regional military administration, also said a man was killed in Russian shelling in the city of Zaporizhzhia.
Moscow says it hits cargo ship and power facilities
Also on Sunday, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces struck a cargo ship northeast of Ukraine’s Black Sea port city of Odesa overnight.
The ministry said Russian drones struck the Pravoberezhna electricity facility in Zaporizhzhia, which it said supplied power to Ukrainian arms manufacturers. It reported further strikes on an oil refinery, electrical substations and a data centre operated by MKM Telecom.
In its battlefield update, the ministry claimed Russian forces had taken control of the Ukrainian village of Sosnovyi Bir in the northeastern Kharkiv region and destroyed a launcher for Ukraine’s Neptune coastal missile system.
It also said it struck energy and transport facilities it described as serving Ukraine’s military. The Russian claims could not be independently verified.

items.summary:
Why Bangladesh descended into violence ahead of Hasina’s planned return
Supporters of the ousted PM, who lives in self-imposed exile in India, have protested against rejection of her return.
Bangladesh has deployed paramilitary troops to help contain a wave of violence that erupted after supporters
items.text:
Why Bangladesh descended into violence ahead of Hasina’s planned return
Supporters of the ousted PM, who lives in self-imposed exile in India, have protested against rejection of her return.
Bangladesh has deployed paramilitary troops to help contain a wave of violence that erupted after supporters of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina staged protests against the government’s rejection of the ousted leader’s planned return to the country.
At least four people have been killed and police stations, banks and even the ancestral home of the former interim leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner, Muhammad Yunus, have been attacked in a week of violence.
Violence erupted after supporters of Hasina’s now-banned Awami League party took to the streets as part of weeklong protests that overlapped with the anniversary of the former leader’s death sentence last year. Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in absentia for crimes against humanity related to the 2024 student-led protests.
Earlier this month, Hasina requested a new passport and identity card to allow her to return to Bangladesh. She has been living in self-imposed exile in India after fleeing the country in the wake of the July 2024 student-led uprising.
But the Bangladesh government, led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, says she is a convicted criminal, and she can only return under the extradition treaty with India.
Rahman has blamed India for the unrest. “It is not only that; they have not looked at the interests of Bangladesh and its people. At the same time, the country across the border, where they have fled to, is their master… To satisfy those masters, they have again started conspiring against Bangladesh and its people,” Rahman said in parliament on Friday.
So why does Hasina still want to return to the country, and are the recent protests spontaneous or orchestrated?
Here’s what we know:
What do we know about the deadly protests?
Since mid-November, arson attacks and violence have been reported across 28 districts of Bangladesh.
At least four people have been killed in the political violence since November 14, including three political activists and a bus worker who died when his vehicle was torched, according to local media reports.
Two men from the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) were killed in the Narail district, according to the AFP news agency. In retaliation, BNP supporters set ablaze more than a dozen homes belonging to Awami League supporters in the district.
A Narail resident, who asked not to be identified for fear of reprisals, said as many as 50 houses had been damaged in the district.
“We are terrified by the clashes,” he told AFP. “We have asked our women and children to stay inside unless it is absolutely necessary.”
Late Wednesday, police said the ancestral home of Yunus was set on fire in the port city of Chittagong. It was not immediately clear who was behind the blaze.
“Criminals set fire to the eastern side of the house. The area was being used as a storeroom,” Chittagong Metropolitan Police spokesman Aminur Rashid said, adding there were no casualties.
Yunus, who was targeted by Hasina during her term in power, has faced hostility from her supporters. Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, said 22 of its branches were subject to arson attacks.
State news agency BSS reported that 90 additional platoons of the paramilitary Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) had been deployed nationwide.
National police chief Md Ali Hossain Fakir told BSS that security had been restored in Gopalganj, Hasina’s hometown and a longstanding stronghold of her party.
“I urge the peace-loving people of this area to stand against those involved in sabotage and disorder,” he added.
Khandakar Tahmid Rejwan, lecturer of global studies and governance at the Independent University, Bangladesh (IUB) and contributing analyst at the United States defence think tank Jamestown Foundation, told Al Jazeera that the protests do not appear to be entirely spontaneous in nature.
“If they were genuinely organic and spontaneous, one would arguably expect to see broader public mobilisation and participation across different parts of the country. Instead, what we are witnessing is a concentration of protest activity in areas such as Gopalganj, Faridpur, and Madaripur, which have traditionally served as strongholds of the Awami League’s support base,” he said.
He noted that while sporadic protests and demonstrations have also been reported in other parts of the country, their scale and geographical spread, at least so far, suggest localised unrest rather than a nationwide mobilisation.
“Although these incidents are concerning from the perspective of public order and political stability, the available pattern of mobilisation does not, at this stage, indicate a level of nationwide momentum that could fundamentally challenge the incumbent government’s position,” he added.
What triggered the violence?
The recent protests began soon after the government rejected Hasina’s request for her passport and identity card on November 9. Hasina served as prime minister from 1996 to 2001, and again from 2009 to 2024, but her nearly 15 years of iron-fist rule have been slammed by human rights organisations.
She was sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over her deadly crackdown on the student-led protests in 2024. As many as 1,400 people may have been killed in the violence, according to United Nations estimates.
Hasina has, however, denied these charges and told the Reuters news agency on November 9 that she intended to return to Bangladesh and surrender before a court. Her aides added the date would be announced once various formalities were completed.
But her request has been denied by the current government.
“Bangladesh does not give passports to terrorists who kill thousands of people and flee. It will work under the current extradition arrangements with India to pursue and get the terrorist Hasina handed over,” State M

items.title: Gachagua gives Mt Kenya leaders Christmas deadline to dump Ruto, promises political direction
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has warned Mt Kenya leaders still supporting President William Ruto that they risk being rejected by voters in the 2027 General Election, saying the region will settle its political direction during the Christmas festivities.
Gachagua
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has warned Mt Kenya leaders still supporting President William Ruto that they risk being rejected by voters in the 2027 General Election, saying the region will settle its political direction during the Christmas festivities.
Gachagua said political decisions in the Mt Kenya region are traditionally made during family gatherings over Christmas, when relatives return home and deliberate on the leaders they want to represent them.
Speaking in Embu County, the Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader said discussions held between December 23 and December 26 would determine the political fate of leaders seeking elective positions in the region.
He warned politicians who have remained in Ruto’s camp despite growing political differences with the former Deputy President to reconsider their positions before the festive season.
“Here in the mountain, let me tell those who don’t know: when we go to the election next year, every five years, decisions here in the mountain are made during Christmas. Starting from December 23, 24, 25, by the 26th on Boxing Day, the decision is concluded,” Gachagua said.
He described Christmas as an important political decision-making period, when families assess the performance of elected leaders and agree on those they should support in the next election.
Gachagua said the discussions would cover all elective positions, including the presidency, governorships, Senate, National Assembly, Woman Representative and Members of County Assemblies.
He singled out leaders who have continued working with Ruto, warning that those who fail to return to the community before Christmas could find themselves on the wrong side of its political decisions.
“Those of you who are still with Kasongo, the mountain’s decision on how next year’s election will look, from the seat of President, Governor, Senator, Woman MP, MCA, will be made this Christmas. Therefore, if you are still outside, if you care about your seat, you should return home,” he said.
Gachagua added that leaders who continue supporting the President beyond the Christmas period would risk losing the backing of Mt Kenya voters.
“Anyone who stays with Kasongo by Christmas, his matters are ruined,” he warned.
The former Deputy President also announced that he would issue political direction for the Mt Kenya region before leaders break for Christmas around December 22 or 23, giving residents time to deliberate on his position during the festive season.
He said he expected community representatives to return with feedback on December 27 or 28, when they would report whether they agreed with the proposed political direction.
“And I want to say here in the mountain, my people, before we break for Christmas around the 22nd or 23rd, I must also give political direction here in the mountain so that you go and discuss it when Christmas arrives. When it reaches the 27th or 28th, you bring back a report to me on whether you agree with what I said,” he said.
The remarks signal Gachagua’s intention to consolidate his influence in the vote-rich Mt Kenya region ahead of the 2027 elections, as he seeks to rally voters behind a common political position opposed to Ruto’s re-election.
His latest warning also comes amid growing competition for political influence in the region, with several leaders positioning themselves to shape its political future following his fallout with the President.
Gachagua has repeatedly accused Ruto’s administration of betraying the Mt Kenya region, arguing that residents should not offer their votes to political leaders without negotiating for a stake in the next government.
He has also maintained that the region must negotiate with other opposition formations before settling on a presidential candidate, insisting that its political support should be tied to clear commitments on leadership and development.
In November, he called for negotiations with opposition leaders, saying Mt Kenya would no longer surrender its votes without first agreeing on what the region would gain from a political partnership.
Party hopping deadline
Gachagua’s call for leaders to reconsider their political loyalties comes as the IEBC’s preparations for the August 10, 2027 General Election place specific timelines on political party membership and nominations.
Under the electoral timetable, political parties are required to submit their membership lists to the Registrar of Political Parties for certification from March 16, 2027, with the lists expected to be certified by March 23.
The certified membership registers must subsequently be submitted to the IEBC by April 12, 2027, at least 120 days before the General Election. Aspirants seeking party tickets will need to ensure their membership is properly captured in the relevant party register.
The commission has also set April 8, 2027, as the deadline for political parties to submit the names of aspirants participating in their primaries, alongside the dates and venues of the nomination exercises.
Party primaries and internal nomination disputes are expected to be concluded by May 8, 2027. Independent candidates must also have ceased membership in registered political parties by the same date.
The timelines mean politicians intending to switch political parties ahead of the 2027 elections will need to make their decisions early enough to have their membership properly recorded before the nomination process.

items.title: How El Chapo Isidro, alleged Mexican cartel leader, was captured
items.summary:
How El Chapo Isidro, alleged Mexican cartel leader, was captured
Operation in Sinaloa state resulted in deadly heavy battles between members of security forces and gunmen.
After weeks of careful and detailed planning, Mexican special forces have captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as El Chapo
items.text:
How El Chapo Isidro, alleged Mexican cartel leader, was captured
Operation in Sinaloa state resulted in deadly heavy battles between members of security forces and gunmen.
After weeks of careful and detailed planning, Mexican special forces have captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro, a notorious alleged cartel leader on the FBI’s 10 most-wanted list.
Authorities said on Saturday Meza Flores was arrested at a compound in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa, following a stealth operation that left four members of the security forces and seven suspected gunmen dead.
The capture highlighted the “unwavering determination to curb organised crime activities to protect and safeguard the public’s peace and security”, the Mexican Secretariat of National Defence said in a statement.
Here’s what we know about how the operation went down:
Who is Meza Flores?
Meza Flores, 44, is believed to be the leader of the Los Mazatlecos gang, based in Guasave, an agricultural area in Sinaloa.
The group was formerly part of the now-extinct Beltran Leyva Cartel but has operated independently since 2013. Meza Flores had long been subject to arrest in Mexico on charges of organised crime.
He also faces criminal charges in the United States, which had offered a reward of up to $5m for information leading to his capture.
If he is convicted, he could face the death penalty or life in prison.
How did security forces plan the raid?
The operation to capture Meza Flores took place on Friday, but preparations for it began way before.
The Mexican military said the raid, which came after two previous attempts to detain him, was conducted “following coordination” with US intelligence in the “framework of bilateral cooperation”.
Mexico’s Special Forces of the National Guard, the National Army and US intelligence agencies all collaborated on the massive raid operation, according to authorities.
Mexican officials said they had given US intelligence agencies information to locate Meza Flores weeks ahead.
US officials flew reconnaissance drones over the area where he was believed to be holed up, according to The New York Times. Using live video information from the drones, Mexican military analysts were then able to determine the cartel boss’s daily routines.
They also intercepted his communications, including text messages with his mother, wife and sister, to confirm events and meetings he planned to attend, The Times reported.
On Friday, Meza Flores was tracked to a home in Guasave, thanks to phone and radio communications, as well as drone surveillance. Mexican special forces used his voice, build and how he walked to confirm it was him before moving in.
What happened at the raid?
Prior to targeting the home in Guasave, officials first planned two other diversions in Los Mochis, another city in Sinaloa’s northwest.
As the raids distracted cartel members who exchanged fire with the security forces, more than two dozen undercover soldiers from the Joint Special Force elite army unit stormed Meza Flores’s location, The Times reported. They were covered by a ring of dozens of other soldiers, as well as two Mexican Black Hawk helicopters that engaged cartel members positioned in armoured, mounted pick-up trucks in a firefight.
The operation sparked panic across the surrounding area, with gunfire forcing the suspension of a professional baseball game in Guasave, according to local media. Television footage showed players running off the field as loud bangs were heard.
The heavy gun battles between security forces and cartel members left the streets of Guasave smouldering with burned-out cars and destroyed structures.
How was the cartel leader transported?
After the special forces managed to subdue Meza Flores, the tricky issue of exiting Guasave and Sinaloa remained.
That’s where another distraction measure kicked in: two helicopters hovered over the house and then headed in the direction of Los Mochis, creating the impression that Meza Flores was being transported there.
A third stayed back and continued to engage the gunmen.
Amid the chaos, the special forces bundled Meza Flores into an armoured vehicle and drove out of Guasave.
Footage released on social media showed special forces leading a cuffed Meza Flores onto a military transport plane. Early on Saturday morning, the alleged cartel boss arrived in Mexico City, the Mexican defence ministry said in a statement.
In addition to the seven suspected gunmen killed, another eight suspected to be cartel members were arrested, the ministry said, including a man identified as Meza Flores’s cousin and second in command. Another high-ranking member of the gang was identified as the cartel leader’s brother-in-law and the group’s financial operative.
Several weapons and munitions were also seized.

items.text:
Iran unveils dual-missile launcher, new ‘missile city’: What to know
Military officials tour underground facility in show of military capabilities despite US attacks.
Iran is putting its upgraded missile systems and underground military facilities on display, delivering a defiant message that it still has significant military capabilities despite US-Israeli attacks.
The latest showcase included a dual-missile launcher capable of firing two liquid-fuelled missiles simultaneously, according to state media broadcasting footage of military commanders touring an underground missile facility.
Officials insisted Iran has strengthened its missile and air-defence capabilities since previous rounds of fighting, including the launch of the US-Israel war in late February. Still, Iran is under mounting economic pressure from a naval blockade imposed by the United States that has disrupted its oil exports.
Here’s everything to know about the new dual-missile launcher and Iran’s “missile city”:
What is the new launcher?
Iran has developed a range of ballistic and cruise missiles over the past three decades.
The new dual-missile launcher was unveiled as Major-General Ahmad Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), toured the underground facility on Saturday.
The IRGC aerospace force flaunted its range of upgraded missiles and military equipment, including the launcher, which is designed to carry and fire two liquid-fuelled missiles simultaneously, according to state broadcaster IRIB.
Liquid-fuelled missiles are launched vertically and offer speed-control capabilities, which can aid in overcoming air defence systems, IRIB reported.
State media said the latest generations of Iranian missiles have improved in range, accuracy and guidance capabilities independent of the US Global Positioning System (GPS).
What is known about the underground ‘missile city’?
Vahidi’s tour followed the IRGC aerospace force’s announcement of a new underground facility on November 10, according to the semiofficial Tasnim News Agency.
Tasnim said Iran is constructing underground military complexes able to continue weapons production and storage even under heavy bombardment.
The IRGC has said it transferred its missile and drone production lines from the surface to underground facilities to allow it continuing missile production.
Footage broadcast by IRIB on Saturday showed kilometres of tunnels and hundreds of missiles and launchers, including double launchers, among other systems.
Reporting from Tehran, Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar said it was not clear when the state broadcaster’s footage of the underground site was filmed.
“The IRGC are trying to send a message to the outside world that they are not short of ammunition; they have enough missiles and enough launchers,” he said.
“If the war resumes again, they are going to deploy these capabilities,” he added. “It is a part of their propaganda, but also, Iran is flexing its muscles and trying to restore deterrence.”
Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut, said Iran can safely store spare parts, raw materials and chemicals needed for creating missiles and drones at its underground sites in addition to storing finished missiles and drones.
Iran has been planning for such a scenario for decades, he said. “So there’s no doubt that Iran has stored an enormous amount of all of this,” Khouri, who is also a nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, told Al Jazeera.
“They’ve shown … they’re prepared to stand sanctions and keep fighting.”
What is Iran trying to achieve by showcasing its defence capabilities?
Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer in international security at King’s College London, said Iran is now more emboldened than ever to assert its military capabilities due to the outcome of the US midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffered sweeping losses.
The rising cost of living as a result of the war on Iran was a major factor in how people in the US voted in the elections, which saw Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress.
“So [Trump] looks more like the boy who cried wolf,” Pinfold told Al Jazeera. “There seems to be a feeling that the US has been deterred or disincentivised from escalating the conflict.”
Khouri said Iran has taken a gradual approach to showing its technical and military capabilities as well as its political will to strike back.
“[This is] all designed to show the US and Israel … [that] Iran has very sophisticated capabilities that can both evade the Western defence forces and defence systems … and at the same time reach targets that it wants to hit in the countries that it decides to attack,” he said.
At the same time, Iran is suffering under the US naval blockade of its southern ports, so it feels the need to escalate because it feels backed into a corner, Pinfold noted.
He added that Iran’s economy is already in recession and there are growing fears it could suffer an even bigger hit.
“Very little if any oil is coming out of Iran at the moment,” Pinfold said.

AI claimed another major scalp in maths on Friday, as Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge published what he says is a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a Millennium Prize Problem, in 17 million lines of code that no human has read in full. Physicist Tony Padilla tells Tech 24 that verification could take years, and that Alpöge should share how he got there.
Alpöge says he proved the hypothesis, a conjecture about the distribution of prime numbers that has resisted mathematicians since 1859, by working with Anthropic's chatbot Claude. Brian Conrey, a leading expert on the Riemann hypothesis who reviewed an earlier Claude paper on the problem for Anthropic in August, called the moment "the biggest thing that's ever happened in mathematics".
Speaking to Tech 24, theoretical physicist Tony Padilla of the University of Nottingham said the result would reach "into so many other areas" of mathematics, since a whole host of other proofs rely on it. But he said the mathematical community would need to see a human-readable proof: "This can take years… there may be problems and we don't know. It's very early days."
Padilla also called for transparency. Acknowledging that Alpöge would have "commercial interests at heart", he said: "It's absolutely crucial that everything is shared in a way that the community can follow."

Burnley 2-2 Blackburn: Todd Cantwell penalty earns draw as Rovers players send message to Tony Mowbray
Report and free match highlights from the Championship match between Burnley and Blackburn Rovers at Turf Moor on Sunday; Burnley took the lead on two occasions but Blackburn battled back to draw; Rovers players sent a message to Tony Mowbray, in what would have been his 900th game
Sunday 22 November 2026 14:25, UK
Todd Cantwell's penalty earned Blackburn a 2-2 draw at Burnley in their first match since head coach Tony Mowbray stepped back because of health issues.
In a gripping, physical east Lancashire derby, the home side led twice, through Largie Ramazani's rising first-half drive and Jaydon Banel's steered finish after the break.
But Andri Gudjohnsen scored Blackburn's first equaliser, then earned the penalty which Cantwell converted.
- Watch FREE Championship highlights | Latest EFL news and rumours
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream EFL games with no contract📺
Burnley remain deep in relegation trouble, without a home league victory for 400 days, having once again failed to hold on to a lead. They have dropped 25 points from winning positions in the Sky Bet Championship this season.
Blackburn wanted a victory not just for local pride, but to honour Mowbray, who turned 63 on Sunday, and for whom this was set to be a 900th match in management before his announcement on Tuesday that he would be stepping back.
Their players warmed up in T-shirts bearing the message 'We're with you, Tony' on the back and the number 900 on the front.
Coaches Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds have taken charge in Mowbray's absence and had to reshuffle the defence when Tom Atcheson was concussed after receiving a boot to the face in the third minute.
Stand-in goalkeeper Aynsley Pears, playing after Balazs Toth suffered a broken hand on international duty with Hungary, pushed over a fierce deflected shot from Banel, but was at fault when Ramazani gave Burnley a 27th-minute lead.
The on-loan Leeds winger cut in from the right and fired a shot that flew into the roof of the net right by Pears, who was too slow to react.
But Gudjohnsen equalised four minutes later, racing on to a Harry Pickering long ball that drifted over Burnley centre-back Max Alleyne, and steering a sweet shot beyond goalkeeper Max Weiss for his 12th goal of the season. The Icelander celebrated by grabbing a t-shirt paying tribute to Mowbray from a photographer and displaying it for the cameras.
Blackburn finished the first half strongly, with Cantwell firing over a good chance, before Banel restored Burnley's lead six minutes into the second half, running unchallenged to place a shot into the far corner as defender Hayden Carter backed off.
The home side were fortunate to escape a strong penalty appeal just before the hour mark as Cantwell burst into the penalty area and saw two attempted crosses both strike the arm of Igor Julio.
Blackburn did get a penalty with 16 minutes left as Josh Laurent, attempting to clear a low cross, failed to spot Gudjohnsen darting in from behind him and caught the striker's leg. Cantwell drove the penalty straight down the middle to make it 2-2.
Gudjohnsen thought he had given Blackburn the lead two minutes later, when he controlled and drove a low shot against the base of the post with Weiss a spectator, but neither side could find a winner.

items.summary:
Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
- Published
At least three people have been killed after a fire at a confectionery factory in western Java on Saturday, with the death toll expected to rise.
Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers search
items.text:
Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
- Published
At least three people have been killed after a fire at a confectionery factory in western Java on Saturday, with the death toll expected to rise.
Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for around 36 missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.
Rescuers recovered 24 body bags from the fire as of Sunday evening, as search operations continue to locate missing people.
Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.
The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.
Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.
Local media reported that the search had been called off for the night late on Sunday, and would resume on Monday.
"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.
Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.
Firefighters had been called to the building at 16:30 local time (09:30 GMT) on Saturday - but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.
"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.
The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.
On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

items.text:
What next for Iraq’s push against militias following Jurf al-Sakhar deal?
Thursday’s Iran-brokered compromise may bode poorly for Baghdad’s attempt to curb militia influence.
The entry of Iraqi government forces into Jurf al-Sakhar, a town 60km (37 miles) southwest of Baghdad long held by the Iran-backed armed group Kataib Hezbollah, has raised questions about the future of Iraqi militias in the country.
A deal reached between Iraqi authorities and Kataib Hezbollah about control of Jurf al-Sakhar, where oil smuggling was allegedly taking place, staved off a potential confrontation between the two sides.
It is the latest episode in Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s push to assert federal government control over the country and crack down on corruption, which is allegedly funding pro-Iran militias.
So how does Thursday’s compromise bode for the Iraqi state’s mission to rein in militias and weapons outside its control?
What happened at Jurf al-Sakhar?
Kataib Hezbollah seized Jurf al-Sakhar from ISIL (ISIS) in 2014, renaming it Jurf al-Nasr (“victory”). For the 12 years since then, it has prevented state authorities from re-establishing control and allegedly siphoned oil from local pipelines.
After an intelligence report was released this week about oil smuggling in Jurf al-Sakhar, the government formed a high-level committee to investigate the issue.
After an anti-corruption crackdown was announced, al-Zaidi then gave Kataib Hezbollah until Friday to withdraw from the town. A compromise deal was reached a day before the due date, with government forces entering Jurf al-Sakhar and establishing a joint operations centre in the town. This should see the gradual withdrawal of Kataib Hezbollah units and the phased deployment of an army brigade, a federal police brigade, an energy police regiment and two brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) to the town.
The compromise reportedly came after direct Iranian intervention brokered by Esmail Qaani, head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) elite Quds Force, which once joined the PMF on the front lines against ISIL and maintains deep ties with several of Iraq’s militias.
Why is Baghdad moving against militias?
PM al-Zaidi, a businessman with a Shia background, took power in May, vowing to end corruption and the fragmentation of the country’s security landscape.
Initially, he set a deadline of September 30 for militias to place their weapons under state control, coinciding with the withdrawal of US and allied forces from Iraq. While US forces withdrew, the militias refused to comply, and the deadline was pushed to June 2027.
Of major concern to Baghdad is the use of Iraq by armed groups to launch unauthorised attacks at Iran’s behest. Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, several Iraqi militias have pledged to support Iran’s war effort. Baghdad has acknowledged that attacks targeting neighbours have been launched from its territory and has vowed to put an end to them.
Akeel Abbas, an expert in Iraqi affairs, said Baghdad was the reason for the government’s intervention in Jurf al-Sakhar, not the issue of oil smuggling.
“This area, which the state could not enter since 2014, did actually participate in Iran’s war effort, bombing Gulf countries, bombing US interests in Iraq,” he told Al Jazeera.
“There are other areas, but this one is the strongest, most fortified, and the best weaponry is stored there.”
In July, after Iran-aligned militias attacked Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, the United States and Saudi Arabia launched retaliatory strikes against PMF targets across Iraq, killing at least 20 personnel and drawing condemnation from Baghdad.
By establishing a presence in Jurf al-Sakhr, once the site of former President Saddam Hussein’s military-industrial complex, Baghdad signalled to the US that it was removing it as a potential target.
What next?
Zeidon Alkinani, founding director of the Doha-based Arab Perspectives Institute, said the deal over Jurf al-Sakhar was a positive step, especially as it was secured through negotiation and not armed confrontation.
“The remaining questions are how long this will take and what the armed groups will want in return,” he told Al Jazeera. Kataib Hezbollah may also retain its influence in the area through PMF units, with the process of deployment likely to take weeks to complete.
“How the next phases go will determine whether this becomes a real return of state authority or just a rearrangement of who controls the area,” Alkinani said.
Tallha Abdulrazaq, an Iraq expert and strategy and security consultant, said that the deal was compromised by the presence of militia and pro-militia personnel in the security contingent sent by Baghdad.
“Effectively, we’re changing Shia militias for Shia militias, but in uniform,” he said. “There has been no announcement about them being disarmed and their missile and drone manufacturing facilities set up with Iranian expertise being dismantled.”
Where did Iraq’s militias come from?
Iran-backed armed groups have become some of the most powerful actors in Iraq since the US-led invasion of Iraq overthrew President Saddam Hussein’s government in 2003.
Some of Iraq’s most influential militias – like Kataib Hezbollah and Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq – found their genesis in the resistance to US occupation, many with the alleged support of Iran.
Others were formed in response to the threat posed by ISIL after a fatwa was issued by leading Iraqi Shia cleric Ali al-Sistani, fighting under the banner of the PMF.
The PMF are a recognised component of Iraq’s security forces, granting the militias semiofficial status. However, some Iraqi militias, such as Kataib Hezbollah, still operate outside the framework of the state and have been accused of undermining the government’s legitimacy.
There have also been frequent accusations that militias operate corrupt patronage networks to finance themselves, and that their close relationship with Tehran has frustrated the Iraqi gover

Some important pre-match news for me personally … my significant other has brought a tube of sour cream and onion Pringles into my home office. Huge. Absolutely elite live blogging snack. Less than 10 minutes until KO now.
Fabian Hürzeler sounded a little way of Hull in his pre-match press conference, citing the Tigers’ narrow 1-0 defeat to table-topping (and possible title rivals) Arsenal as a template for how today’s game might go.
“I think they do an impressive job,” Hürzeler said. “They had a brilliant start in the Premier League. They are very structured. Against Arsenal, I think Arsenal suffered. They [Arsenal] didn’t create a lot of big chances, and therefore we need to be patient because we also know that Hull are really good in transition.
“They also have individual quality in their team. Very well structured, very well organised, good in transition, good in set pieces, and I think it’s not an easy place to go to.”
Hull obviously beat Manchester United 2-0 in their opening home game and have drawn four successive matches at the MKM Stadium since, so that proves Hürzeler’s point somewhat.
Well, maybe only City will lose this afternoon, Elisabeth Terland scored for United as I was typing.
Women’s Super League: Both Manchester clubs are in serious danger of suffering shock defeats in the early WSL games this afternoon. The two matches are approaching their denouement, so catch the latest with Emillia Hawkins on our clockwatch blog.
My personal two-pennies-worth is that Brighton will probably fall away from the title race at some stage after Christmas. Their fixture list in the short term is fairly inviting, so I see their lofty position being sustained for a little while.
But realistically, a top five finish and Champions League qualification should be their primary objective. That’s really not impossible when you consider the struggles of Manchester United and Chelsea, and the possible fate of Manchester City if and when a verdict/punishment arrives re their 115s charges.
The fact Fabian Hürzeler could achieve that just after his 34th birthday would be an astonishing feat in itself.
A reminder you can follow The Guardian’s live Premier League Golden Boot tracker here:
The stats don’t lie when it comes to Brighton’s brilliant form. They are well clear as the Premier League’s top scorers with 26, despite many of their rivals having played a game more. They are also level with Arsenal (7) in terms of goals conceded, again having played fewer games than the Gunners.
Pascal Gross also leads way in the league this season for chances created (29).
They don’t have one outstanding goalscorer, but Gross is on four so far this season, with Yasin Ayari, Jack Hinshelwood and Charalampos Kostoulas all chipping in with three.
There’s plenty of time before kick-off to get around this special report on Brighton’s superb start to the season by William Ralston. In it, he analyses exactly what the Seagulls have excelled in so far, what comes next and their chances of remaining in the title hunt in the coming months and weeks.
Go inside a brilliantly run club who are upsetting the traditional Premier League big six:
It looks like Hull could line up in a 4-4-2 today. It remains to be seen where Mohamed-Ali Cho will play, either on one of the flanks or pushed up alongside Oliver McBurnie. Mohamed Belloumi has been their primary creator this season, so watch out for him.
Brighton will surely shape up in their standard 4-2-3-1 formation, fluid as that is, with the likes of Diego Gomez, Yasin Ayari and Pascal Gross rotating between the midfield lines.
Peter Bankes (from Merseyside) is the referee today, with Andrew Kitchen in the VAR booth.
Team news
Hull City: Tzolakis; Coyle, Ajayi, Mendy, Stroud; Belloumi, Crooks, Slater, Iroegbunam; Cho, McBurnie.
Subs: Butland, Giles, Thomas, Hjerto-Dahl, Egan, Norton-Cuffy, Herrington, Gourna-Douath, Vaz.
Brighton: Verbruggen; Costinha, Vuskovic, Dunk, Boscagli; Gross, Andres; Gomez, Ayari, De Cuyper; Rutter.
Subs: Steele, Hinshelwood, Minteh, Osman, Kostoulas, Kadioglu, Wieffer, Svoboda, O’Riley.
Preamble
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the solitary early kick-off in the Premier League today. Many will view Hull City versus Brighton as a mere hors d’oeuvres to the main dish of Liverpool against Manchester United later, but there is plenty riding on it.
Hull have not won a game in any competition since claiming back-to-back victories in a shock opening burst after winning promotion, while Brighton have lost just twice across 17 matches in all competitions. So this is a nailed-on Seagulls win, right?
Maybe, though Fabian Hürzeler will be guarding against complacency, especially because Hull have not lost by more than one goal in any game this season and have not conceded more than two. They are the proverbial hard nut to crack, albeit scoring goals is a problem for the Tigers – despite sitting 14th in the table, only two teams (Nottingham Forest and Sunderland) have scored fewer.
Team news has already dropped so we’ll bring you that in the next post. Kick-off is at 2pm (GMT) so please do stay tuned. I’m predicting this will be a tighter game than many would imagine.
