items.title: NFL’s Jaylen Harrell hospitalised and investigated for assault in car crash
items.summary:
NFL’s Jaylen Harrell hospitalised and investigated for assault in car crash
Police in United States investigating whether Tennessee Titans defensive end assaulted a rideshare driver before collision.
Tennessee Titans defensive end Jaylen Harrell has been hospitalised in Florida after being involved
items.text:
NFL’s Jaylen Harrell hospitalised and investigated for assault in car crash
Police in United States investigating whether Tennessee Titans defensive end assaulted a rideshare driver before collision.
Tennessee Titans defensive end Jaylen Harrell has been hospitalised in Florida after being involved as a passenger in a rideshare car in what the team have called a “serious” accident.
The Tampa Police Department said in a preliminary report that Harrell was riding about 8:45am (13:45 GMT) on Friday in the back seat when “he reportedly assaulted the driver while the vehicle was in motion.”
The driver of the Kia Sorento then swerved, struck a Toyota Highlander and collided with a utility pole, the police report said.
Police investigation under way
Harrell, 24, was thrown from the backseat, hit the windshield and lost consciousness, according to the police report.
Harrell was hospitalised with serious injuries while the rideshare driver, identified as a man in his mid-30s, sustained “minor injuries” and was treated at the scene, according to police. The driver of the Highlander was not injured, the police said.
Detectives are working through the timeline of events in investigating the crash, according to the preliminary report.
The Titans issued a statement on Saturday but did not disclose Harrell’s condition or the injuries he had suffered nor did they mention the assault accusation.
Harrell has not played this season after tearing an ACL in August during the preseason and being placed on the injured reserve list.
“We have been in constant communication with Jaylen’s family and are still working to gather more information,” the team said in its statement.
“At this time, Jaylen remains in the hospital and continues to receive care. We ask that Jaylen and his family’s privacy be respected at this time. We will provide an update when appropriate.”
The accident occurred in Tampa, Harrell’s hometown.
The Titans selected the University of Michigan alumnus in the seventh round of the 2024 NFL Draft. He has appeared in 34 games (two starts) and has 38 tackles, seven tackles for a loss and 4.5 sacks.

items.title: Nyoro: There is no third force; opposition will unite behind one candidate
items.summary:
NAIROBI,Kenya Nov 22 – The People’s Party of Kenya party leader Ndindi Nyoro has dismissed claims of divisions within the opposition, insisting there is no third force and that the leaders are united behind plans to field a single presidential candidate in the 2027 General Election.
The 2027 preside
items.text:
NAIROBI,Kenya Nov 22 – The People’s Party of Kenya party leader Ndindi Nyoro has dismissed claims of divisions within the opposition, insisting there is no third force and that the leaders are united behind plans to field a single presidential candidate in the 2027 General Election.
The 2027 presidential hopeful said the opposition remained united despite reports of competing political camps, arguing that its leaders were working towards a common goal of challenging President William Ruto’s administration.
Speaking during a church service in Kirinyaga county , Nyoro said opposition leaders were committed to presenting one candidate to fly their flag in the next General Election.
He was accompanied by Narc-Kenya leader Martha Karua and former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i, among other opposition leaders.
Responding to reports suggesting the existence of competing forces within the opposition, Nyoro said such claims did not reflect the reality of their political engagements.
“There is no third force. There is only one force of the opposition, and that is the unity of all of us in the opposition, and we will produce one united candidate to fly the flag,” he said.
The MP also sought to counter speculation that a separate political formation was emerging within the opposition following joint political engagements involving himself, Matiang’i, Karua and Siaya Governor James Orengo.
The four leaders have recently stepped up joint political activities, including engagements in the Gusii region, fuelling speculation that they could be building an alternative centre of power within the opposition.
Their growing association has raised questions about whether the opposition is developing competing political blocs ahead of the process of selecting a presidential candidate to challenge Ruto.
The political debate has also been intensified by public exchanges between Gachagua and Matiang’i, exposing differences among some of the leaders seeking to work together against the President.
Nyoro, however, insisted that the opposition’s different political engagements should not be interpreted as divisions, maintaining that leaders would eventually agree on one candidate.
Education pledge
The Kiharu MP used the church gathering to outline his education agenda once elected President, promising to eliminate school fees for learners in day secondary schools if the opposition takes power in 2027.
He cited his Kiharu Constituency model, where day secondary school learners pay Sh500 per term, saying the arrangement demonstrated that affordable education could be achieved through proper planning.
He said the proposed programme would take effect in January 2028 and would ensure learners across the country receive both education and meals at school without paying school fees.
“You know in Kiharu, where education affairs are managed, day school fees are Sh500 per term. And that is why we are saying: if you give us the opportunity in January 2028, we want all students in Kenya at the day secondary school level to learn and eat at school without paying a single shilling in school fees,” he said.
The proposal builds on an education financing plan Nyoro has previously outlined, which envisages contributions from the national government, county governments and the National Government Constituencies Development Fund to support free secondary education and school meals.
He said the opposition also had plans to address challenges in the health and economic sectors, arguing that its campaign should be anchored on policies that directly improve the lives of Kenyans.
IEBC credibility
The Kiharu MP also turned his attention to the IEBC, warning that the commission’s decisions on recruitment and election management systems would have a direct bearing on the country’s stability.
He specifically cited the recruitment of the commission’s chief executive officer and the management of electoral technology, insisting that all processes must be transparent and free from political interference.
Nyoro said Kenyans expected the commission to conduct a credible election in 2027 and warned that any questionable decisions could undermine public confidence in the electoral process.
“Regarding the IEBC, we are watching you closely, and it is vital you know that the work you do will determine Kenya’s peace. So it is important that in everything the IEBC does hiring of the CEO and management of election systems it must be done above board and in an acceptable manner because Kenyans demand free and fair elections,” he said.
His remarks come as opposition leaders intensify pressure on the electoral commission to address concerns surrounding preparations for the 2027 General Election, including voter registration, electoral technology and the integrity of the electoral process.
The opposition has repeatedly called for transparency in the commission’s operations, arguing that public confidence in the electoral body will be critical to ensuring a peaceful transition after the next polls.

items.title: Oluga orders removal of hospital paybills, warns against burdening patients
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – Principal Secretary for Medical Services Ouma Oluga has ordered the removal of payment paybills from public hospitals, directing Social Health Authority (SHA) compliance officers to move in and stop facilities from placing additional financial demands on patients.
Oluga said
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – Principal Secretary for Medical Services Ouma Oluga has ordered the removal of payment paybills from public hospitals, directing Social Health Authority (SHA) compliance officers to move in and stop facilities from placing additional financial demands on patients.
Oluga said public hospitals should not worsen the financial struggles of Kenyans by requiring them to raise money before accessing medical services, warning that such practices could push vulnerable households further into poverty.
The PS issued the directive during a meeting with SHA compliance officers and public hospital officials in Vihiga County, where he instructed the officers to inspect facilities and remove payment paybills.
“Compliance officers, go through any public hospital. Any public hospital. Remove those things called paybills. I will give you security,” he said.
Oluga said hospitals must recognise the economic realities of the communities they serve, particularly low-income earners whose businesses and livelihoods could be destroyed by expensive medical bills.
He cited women operating food kiosks and small eateries in local markets, noting that some rely on working capital of less than Sh30,000 to sustain their businesses.
He questioned how such traders could be expected to pay Sh50,000 for treatment without jeopardising their livelihoods.
“You can imagine when that woman comes to the hospital, you want to put for her a paybill to pay Sh50,000. You are closing the business,” he said.
According to Oluga, hospitals should not become contributors to the poverty they are expected to help communities overcome.
“So the hospital then is now contributing to poverty in the society,” he said.
He argued that access to healthcare should be considered alongside other social and economic factors that determine people’s health and life expectancy.
The PS challenged hospital administrators to look beyond treating individual patients and embrace a broader responsibility of improving the health of entire communities.
He identified quality healthcare, training and research, and population health as key responsibilities of public hospitals.
Oluga further urged health facilities to strengthen community outreach programmes to educate residents about available services and how to access treatment through SHA.
He said compliance officers should ensure patients are guided towards using the health insurance system instead of being required to raise substantial amounts of money at hospital facilities.
The PS also questioned the ability of ordinary residents to meet expensive medical bills, asking officers how many people in Vihiga County could afford Sh200,000 in hospital charges.
An officer indicated that only a small number of residents could raise such an amount.
Oluga said the situation demonstrated why public hospitals needed to reconsider practices that exposed patients to financial hardship.
He assured compliance officers that they would receive security support as they carried out inspections and enforced the directive.
The PS said county commissioners had already been informed about the exercise and would facilitate security arrangements for officers moving into public hospitals.
“And the commissioners have been told, the county commissioners, you will be accompanied, go and remove paybills in any hospital. Public hospital,” he said.

items.text:
Climate talks break down over fossil fuel exit and funding
November 22, 2026
Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.
After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU said it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.
"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time," said Irish climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU on Sunday.
He said adopting a decision that omitted fossil fuels would be "unconscionable" and risked "deepening the chasm between global commitment and the action required."
Panama also rejected the deal, describing it as a step backwards in addressing the climate crisis, and adding that any decision must acknowledge "the truth about the collective failure on 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit]." That is the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avert runaway climate change.
"Those who contributed to this crisis ... must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it," the Panamanian delegation said.
The Marshall Islands, which faces an existential threat from sea level rise, formally objected to the cover decision, saying "we will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests."
Chris Bowen, Australia's COP31 negotiating president said the breakdown in talks was very disappointing.
Russia, however, supported the decision to leave out wording on accelerating a phaseout of fossil fuels, arguing that they are still a necessary power source and that each country should be able to determine its own pathway on how to cut emissions.
Pakistan and Ghana, defended the agreement as a necessary compromise in the spirit of multilateralism. "We need to build bridges not barriers," said the Pakistan negotiator.
Deep divisions over climate finance
The marathon talks, held at a time when the window is rapidly closing to avoid the escalating impacts of climate change, including drought, deadly heat and flooding, also saw major disputes over financing.
Developing states blamed the collapse in talks on the EU and other wealthier nations for failing to scale up financing to help them adapt to climate-linked weather extremes and the damage they cause. The EU is the largest provider of climate finance and has resisted new adaptation finance targets. 
Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign accused wealthy countries of demanding greater climate ambition while refusing to stump up the cash to pay for it.
"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he added.
The final cover decision had proposed further discussions on "an implementation pathway for tripling adaptation finance by 2035" but without mentioning a figure. It noted that developing countries need some $300 billion annually for adaptation until 2035, and expressed concern about "the gap between climate finance flows and needs."
Fossil fuel exit on the sidelines
Outside formal negotiations, a separate initiative to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) has been gaining momentum.
Maina Talia, Tuvalu's minister for climate change and the environment, said TAFF was "moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed plans for a global transformation."
At the same time, a growing number of states, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Finland, have either completed or are working on so-called national roadmaps to wean themselves off fossil fuels.
But Brandon Wu, director of Policy and Campaigns ActionAid USA, dismissed such plans as "meaningless" and "nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy" on the part of rich countries not stepping up on climate finance.
"COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it's because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise. They may as well have come to the COP shouting at vulnerable communities: 'we don't care if you die.'"
The push for global electrification
The rejected cover decision had recognized that electrification can deliver emissions reductions, improve energy security and expand access to energy.
It included a call to increase the share of electricity in final energy demand from around 20% now to 35% by 2035 — a proposal heavily touted by co-host Turkey.
Still, about 75 countries, including solar powerhouse China, adopted the pledge outside of the formal negotiations. It is non-binding and does not specify whether that additional electricity must come from clean sources. Critics say this leaves open the possibility that expanded electricity demand could be met by fossil fuels. 
Hottest ever climate conference
The talks in Turkey marked the first time a COP was taking place under the explicit knowledge that global temperatures will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Countries were split on how to deal with that so-called "overshoot."
The cover decision had called on states to commit to limiting overshoot , acknowledging that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.”
It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid and sustained" emissions cuts and for action on ramping down potent greenhouse gas methane.
Another contenious issue at the talks and in the final draft decision was a call for "increasing" carbon capture and storage technologies that entails capturing CO2 and burying it. The text said the world should aim to reach "gigaton scale" by 2035.

items.text:
Saudi Arabia intercepts drone, missile as Houthis report attack on Sanaa
Houthi media say several people were injured in an attack on an oil company as Saudi air defences down a drone.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen says it has intercepted a drone and a missile launched by the Houthis, while the media affiliated with the Yemeni group reported that at least six people were wounded in an air attack on an oil company’s fuel station in Sanaa.
The Yemen News Agency quoted the spokesperson for the Ministry of Health and Environment, Anis al-Asbahi, as saying on Sunday that Saudi aircraft targeted a fuel station operated by the state-run oil company on 60th Street, “injuring six employees and causing material damage”.
There was no immediate comment on the claim from the Saudi-led coalition fighting against the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).
Separately, the Saudi-led coalition spokesman, Turki al-Maliki, said the country’s air defences destroyed a drone launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh.
Al-Maliki did not provide further details or report any casualties or damage in his post on X.
His statement came hours after he announced that a ballistic missile was intercepted and destroyed as it targeted the country’s western region, on the coast of the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia’s western region has key energy infrastructure, including the Yanbu oil terminal, a facility for crude exports, and the Jazan refinery in the far southwest of the country, which borders Yemen.
The Houthis have attacked oil installations in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, along with airports and military sites.
Meanwhile, clashes continue between the internationally recognised Yemeni government forces and the Houthis on several fronts, amid warnings of worsening displacement and food shortages.
Since seizing Sanaa in September 2014, the Houthis have controlled much of northern and western Yemen, and the internationally recognised government has controlled much of the south. While a United Nations-brokered ceasefire largely halted the fighting in 2022, the conflict flared again this summer when the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports.
The group then carried out a lightning offensive in September, seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline near the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Government forces launched a counteroffensive last month to recapture territory from the Houthis, but forces allied to the government earlier this month said they would withdraw from areas around the strait and focus on defending Aden.
Analysts say the conflict is no longer driven solely by the dynamics in Yemen, and it is intertwined with the wider regional confrontation and the US-Israel war on Iran.
Houthi attacks have killed 26 people in Saudi Arabia since September, including 23 in strikes on airports, according to the kingdom’s authorities.
On Thursday, a tower housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund in Riyadh’s financial district sustained damage on several floors in a Houthi attack, authorities said.
A skyscraper belonging to state oil giant Aramco was also damaged in a strike at the beginning of the month.

items.text:
Children in besieged Gaza struggle to find life-saving insulin for diabetes
As insulin and blood glucose testing supplies become increasingly difficult to obtain, families say they are being forced to make impossible choices to keep their children alive.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – When Amir, a nine-year-old with diabetes, began repeatedly vomiting and complaining of severe abdominal pain, his mother, Nahawand, called an ambulance. He was rushed to a hospital in Gaza City and admitted to intensive care, where doctors found a dangerous build-up of acid in his blood due to insulin poisoning.
Nahawand said last week’s hospital admission was the latest and most frightening consequence of a struggle to find enough insulin to keep Amir alive and his blood sugar under control.
Amir was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes when he was just a year old. His mother has to monitor his blood sugar throughout the day and adjust his insulin according to his readings and meals.
Keeping Amir’s condition under control with diabetes medication has become increasingly difficult due to the high cost of insulin caused by Israel’s crippling siege on Gaza and because her husband is out of work.
After months of being unable to find insulin in Gaza City, 39-year-old Nahawand finally managed to obtain supplies brought from Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, only to discover the medicine had expired.
“I cannot afford to buy it. I am unable to buy insulin for my son at all,” she told Al Jazeera.
Before the war, Nahawand said a single insulin pen cost between 25 and 30 shekels (($7.62 to $9.17), or was free through clinics and aid organisations. Now a pen costs between 50 and 80 shekels ($15.29 to $24.46).
His mother checks his blood sugar roughly every two hours, as well as before meals, to determine whether he needs insulin. Depending on Amir’s readings and what he eats, he may require two or three injections a day.
But the test strips needed for these checks have also become increasingly unaffordable, between 150 and 200 shekels ($45.87 to $61.17) for a box of 50. Before the war, Nahawand could buy two boxes for about 150 shekels ($45).
“Our children are already living with an illness,” she said. They should not have to suffer like this on top of it. Insulin is not too much to ask for.”
The International Diabetes Federation (IDF) said in August that it was “deeply concerned by the severe restrictions on access to insulin and essential diabetes care in Palestine”. It noted that access to diabetes care is particularly severely constrained in Gaza.
Awni Shweikh, executive director of the Haifa Association for Children with Diabetes, said her organisation speaks on behalf of about 800 children with diabetes in Gaza and appealed for urgent supplies of insulin pens and blood glucose testing strips.
Established in 2012 as the first association in Palestine dedicated to children with type 1 diabetes, Haifa used to provide a free box of testing strips every month to as many as 700 kids.
They also supplied insulin pens for children, offered educational sessions for families, provided psychological support and insulin to families not covered by UNRWA services. But since the start of the genocidal war in Gaza in October 2023, children lost their blood glucose monitoring devices and there was a severe shortage of insulin pens, threatening their lives.
“Insulin is not a luxury. It is a life-saving treatment,” Shweikh told Al Jazeera.
Some families have been forced to use expired insulin, resulting in kids being admitted to hospital with dangerously high blood sugar levels and complications involving acidity in the blood.
The loss of testing strips created a second, closely connected problem: even when parents managed to find insulin, they could not always measure their children’s blood sugar or determine the correct dose.
Afraid to eat
Alaa Ghaban, who lives with her family in a school for displaced Palestinians in Jabalia in northern Gaza, said insulin shortages have affected her daughter’s health and appetite.
Fifteen-year-old Janna was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes when she was just eight and needs two types of insulin, one taken during the day and another at night. Her thirty-six-year-old mother said she cannot stop either medication, but with supplies difficult to find and prices rising, securing both is a constant struggle.
One type of insulin that previously cost around 30 shekels ($9.17) now costs about 80 shekels ($24.46). But with no regular income, even reaching organisations that previously helped is becoming unaffordable.
Janna feared that eating without having enough insulin to control her blood sugar could be dangerous, so over the past four months, she has lost seven kilos.
“She has become afraid to eat because she is afraid she will wake up and not find insulin,” Alaa said.
Janna was recently admitted to hospital for eight days, malnourished and dehydrated, with tests showing high acidity levels in her blood and an enlarged liver.
Alaa once had to return to her family home under heavy Israeli bombardment to retrieve life-saving insulin for her daughter. Keeping medication cool is another daily challenge due to electricity shortages.
“My daughter sometimes wishes she were dead because she cannot bear watching us struggle and seeing me exhausted,” she said.

items.text:
Frick delivers on 'heavy metal football' promise
- Published
If "heavy metal football" is what Aberdeen did, indeed, serve up at Kilmarnock on Saturday, Dons supporters will be eager to see more of this type of concert.
New head coach Mario Frick used the phrase in the build-up to his first game in charge and his team did not disappoint.
The 4-2 Rugby Park victory was bombastic, chaotic and end-to-end - just one of six goal-laden Scottish Premiership games on Saturday.
The four Aberdeen strikes - two from Kevin Nisbet and one each from Brad Lyons and Findlay Marshall - showed Aberdeen's attackers at their best with fine finishing.
In the work in progress column, though, is defending, with the visitors lapsing badly for Killie goals scored by Greg Kiltie and Tyreece John-Jules.
All in all, it was an ideal start for former Luzern boss Frick.
'Just the beginning', says new head coach
Frick was not a complete unknown to Scottish football when he was appointed during the international break - but the reference point was somewhat obscure.
Playing for Liechtenstein at Hampden in 2010, Frick gave the visitors a shock second-half lead.
The end of that game was reminiscent of the kind of heavy metal the head coach was talking about pre-match as Stephen McManus headed Scotland's winner after Kenny Miller's leveller.
Speaking after his Premiership bow, the former Luzern boss described himself as "very happy, very proud" of his new team.
"With only three training session, you can see so many attacking patterns in that first half, which was amazing," he told BBC Scotland.
"We struggled the first few minutes with some players that hadn't played in a long long time and the 1-0 lead helped. First half was very good, the second half, complicated, because Kilmarnock played very well. We were very lucky, but at the end, I think it is a deserved victory and we are very happy."
When asked if he was happy with the players trying to show his style, Frick replied: "Yes, for sure, after two training sessions, I saw a lot of it in the first half.
"It is a good start for us, but it is just the beginning."
Former Scotland midfielder Derek Ferguson took in the match at Rugby Park and was impressed with the visitors.
"As an attacking force, I thought they were good to watch," the former Rangers player said.
"They've got a big game on Tuesday night, against Rangers, so Rangers will need to be at their best, on their toes if they're going to get a result.
"It was the perfect result, obviously, for the manager coming in.
"There was more energy, more legs, more running power. They were winning a lot of the duels.
"It's something to build on, but they've got to work on that defence. They've got to be more solid if they're going to go forward."
Next up Ibrox and a season's third meeting with Rangers.
The two previous encounters, in the Premiership and League Cup semi-final, finished 1-0 to the Ibrox side, with the winning goal coming in the second half both times.
Meetings of Aberdeen and Rangers are typically just as fraught as the Rugby Park game on Saturday.
So, more heavy metal? It probably won't be smooth jazz.
'Recovery evident' - Aberdeen fan views
We asked for your views following Aberdeen's 4-2 win over Kilmarnock.
Allan: One simple question. Why was [Ante] Palaversa nowhere to be seen under Stephen Robinson? I think the fans are due an explanation as to why both he and [Nicky] Devlin fell so far down the pecking order.
Brian: Much, much better is probably an understatement. Great entertainment and a big threat going forward and,as long as we score one more (at least) than the opposition then I will be happy. It is very noticeable that Jack Milne is much more steady when Nicky Devlin is playing. I am looking forward to the rest of this campaign.

It's Medicare open enrollment time. Here's what you need to know
Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people. The coverage choices are complex and often consequential.
Open enrollment runs through Dec. 7. The plan you choose takes effect on Jan. 1, for the full calendar year.
Build-your-own Medicare menu
Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn't one plan. It's more like a build-your-own-insurance menu.
Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there's no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn't cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services.
As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D, the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.
Medicare Advantage
This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums.
"People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs," said David Lipschutz, a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.
The hassle saves money
Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It's a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can't find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projects that the average Part D premium will increase less than $1 a month for a standalone prescription drug plan, describing the market as stable. But that average doesn't tell the whole story. An analysis by KFF, the health policy research nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, found that enrollees who stay in their prescription drug plan will see a 50% increase on average, from $34 to $51. About 10.4 million people could pay higher premiums, not including higher deductibles and coinsurance costs.
Some beneficiaries who didn't have to pay monthly premiums in recent years will begin paying for prescription drug Part D coverage in 2027. While that change follows the 2025 introduction of federal caps on out-of-pocket drug expenses, it comes as the Trump administration is ending temporary federal subsidies that helped keep premiums down. The cap on out-of-pocket expenses for prescription drugs in 2027 will be $2,400, a total enrollees can opt tospread out over the course of the year.
Juliette Cubanski, who directs the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said people who don't shop around could be leaving money on the table.
"It is worth it to avoid any unpleasant surprises in the form of either higher premiums or higher cost sharing for covered services in 2027," she said.
Some plans no longer offered
An estimated 4.3 million people now have to look for a new Medicare Advantage or prescription drug plan after private insurers left the market. Those who want to stay in Medicare Advantage must select new coverage, or they'll be moved to traditional Medicare automatically. For those shopping for a new plan, low monthly premiums may be appealing, but it's important to read the fine print and add up the other costs.
"There are going to be, often, increases in cost sharing and copays, increases in out-of-pocket caps, and reductions in the scope of some of the extra benefits that Medicare Advantage plans provide," Lipschutz said.
So ask: Is my prescription covered? Is my pharmacy preferred? Is my doctor in-network? What does the dental benefit actually cover?
And pay attention to the out-of-pocket maximum for the Advantage plans, Cubanski said, so you know how much you might have to shell out in 2027.
"Look at that dollar value specifically," she said.
For those moving to traditional Medicare, it won't come with a drug plan, so enrollees must sign up for a new Part D plan if they want most prescriptions covered. Enrollees who miss that step when they are first eligible may not have drug coverage for the coming year, and they may face a late-enrollment penalty on their monthly premiums for life.
When selecting a drug plan, enrollees must also tell their insurer how they want to pay, either by getting a bill in the mail or by having the cost deducted from their Social Security. If you don't pick a payment plan, you could get dropped from coverage.
If enrollees elect to leave their Medicare Advantage plans for traditional Medicare within their first year of joining Medicare, they have a guaranteed right to buy a Medigap plan, with no health screening. After that, all bets are off: Insurers in most states can turn enrollees down or charge more because of a health condition. Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, and New York are exceptions.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
Large language models can now redesign your TV and upgrade your camera for you. Is the physical world ready to be Claude Code-d?
How it started
Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What is new is that it’s easy now. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of.
For one developer in India who goes by Gathin T, the whole thing started almost on a whim. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. His was a set made by Xiaomi and running Android TV, with so many ads and so much interface chaos it was hard to even change inputs. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?”
Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. An hour and a half later, Gathin had redesigned his TV to his liking — no more onscreen ads, a simpler interface, easier access to his PlayStation on another input. He posted on X about what he’d done and promptly went viral. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. It became one of the most popular repositories on GitHub, got thousands of pull requests and feature ideas, and inspired countless people to point their own chatbot at their big screen.
Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to share the process so widely.) But for vibe hackers everywhere, the good news is that Android kind of runs everything. From dishwashers to digital photo frames to luxury cars, even gadgets that don’t look like Android often run Android. Even when they don’t, odds are good that there’s another way in. If there’s a hidden API, your LLM can find it. If the firmware file lives on a website somewhere, your LLM can unpack it, explore it, and repackage it to your liking.
Again, few of the technical capabilities here are new, and enterprising developers have been doing this kind of work for many years. Some have even been using AI for several years to make the work easier. But when Claude Code first had its “oh my gosh it works” moment in late 2025, developers began leaning on the tools even more — and non-developers began discovering they, too, could build software now. And over the course of 2026, more and more people began pointing that capability at their hardware.
How it’s going
Now, it seems, all hardware is hacker hardware. Camera enthusiasts embraced the possibilities of vibe hacking as fast as anyone, using LLMs to repackage their camera software in all sorts of ways. Firmware hacks like Magic Lantern are a staple of the camera community, but suddenly it seems like everyone is using AI to add new recording capabilities, support higher resolutions, or even add new looks and color profiles to their shots. Many are using the tools to give their old gear new life; other, more enterprising vibe coders are pointing their bots at their brand-new hardware.
The music world is being similarly upended. Budding musicians are turning cheap synths into powerful new kinds of gear, and a cheap gadget known as the M-Vave FM-1 has become a popular target for custom firmware and new features. M-Vave has even released an open-source firmware, embracing the hackers as other companies have tried to keep them out. The FM-1 is cheap, it’s easy to hack, and it’s raising questions about what higher-end manufacturers can even do to compete.
Gamers, who are also using AI to decompile and mod the games they love, are using LLMs to add new features to their consoles. One vibe coder found a way to play PlayStation 2 discs on a PlayStation 5; lots of gamers have built scripts that allow them to use their favorite controllers on other devices.
In the games world in particular, this has caused the industry to fight back. Game makers are looking for ways to protect their work from being decompiled and made available for free and on other platforms. Luke Dicken, a longtime gaming executive who was recently Take-Two’s head of artificial intelligence, recently predicted to Kotakuthat the industry will start to embrace “more invasive DRM, platform-level solutions, and probably more of a push towards streaming solutions since nobody can decompile what they can’t get their hands on.” Hardware makers will push harder to lock down their systems; companies across the board will pursue legal action to protect their intellectual property.
All this hardware access also creates new risks for users. When you install a vibe-coded version of your camera’s firmware, you are now well outside the bounds of what the camera manufacturer is equipped to help you solve. items.title: Gachagua gives IEBC Jan ultimatum, threatens mass action over election concerns
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has given Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) chairman Erastus Ethekon until January to address opposition concerns over preparations for the 2027 General Election, warning that Kenyans could b
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has given Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) chairman Erastus Ethekon until January to address opposition concerns over preparations for the 2027 General Election, warning that Kenyans could be mobilised to confront the commission directly.
Speaking in Embu, Gachagua accused President William Ruto’s allies of panicking after the opposition raised questions about the commission’s preparedness and electoral safeguards.
He said the opposition had raised specific concerns during its engagement with IEBC commissioners, insisting that the questions were directed at the commission’s leadership and not political allies of the President.
Gachagua said one of the key issues was the planned audit of the voters’ register to remove names of deceased persons and establish the integrity of the electoral roll.
He also demanded the removal of voters he alleged had been registered from Uganda and Somalia, arguing that the commission must ensure that only eligible Kenyan citizens participate in elections.
The former Deputy President said the opposition was concerned about the elections management system, questioning the commission’s preparedness following the expiry of the contract with Smartmatic.
He argued that the matter was particularly urgent because mass voter registration was expected in February, yet the contract issue remained unresolved and was subject to court proceedings.
“We want to know when the audit of the voters’ register will be conducted so we can remove the names of deceased people,” Gachagua said.
He added: “The contract with Smartmatic expires on November 24th and you haven’t bought another system, while the matter is in court and it takes five to six months. What will happen?”
Gachagua further accused Interior Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo of interfering with voter registration, claiming that the IEBC was taking instructions from the Interior Ministry on how the exercise should be conducted in different parts of the country.
He alleged that voter registration was being conducted differently in regions perceived to support the President, compared to areas considered opposition strongholds.
According to Gachagua, residents in Ruto’s political strongholds were being registered through door-to-door mobilisation, while those in other regions were being required to travel to designated registration centres.
He also claimed that young people in the President’s backyard were receiving national identity cards within days, while applicants in other regions waited several months.
Gachagua alleged that the disparities were intended to disadvantage young voters who do not support the President, demanding that the IEBC and relevant government agencies address the concerns.
“On voter registration, we also want to know why you, Erasto, take instructions from PS Interior Raymond Omollo. At Ruto’s home, voter registration is done door-to-door, while elsewhere you tell people to board vehicles to go to registration centres,” he said.
The former Deputy President also challenged the commission over the presidential vote tallying and announcement process, insisting that results should be declared at constituency level.
He argued that the Constitution provides for presidential elections to be conducted across the 290 constituencies and that constituency results should be final.
Gachagua said the opposition would not accept a National Tallying Centre, arguing that the arrangement was not provided for in the Constitution and had created opportunities for electoral manipulation.
“We want announcements made at the constituency level, and we will tally the votes ourselves. We don’t want Bomas matters, because that is where election fraud takes place,” he said.
He warned that the opposition would mobilise Kenyans to engage the electoral commission directly if its concerns were not addressed through consultations with political leaders.
Gachagua issued Ethekon with a January deadline, saying the IEBC chairman had to choose between engaging political leaders or facing direct pressure from members of the public.
“So Erastus, you have a choice to make by January: You either talk to the leaders or you talk to the people directly,” he said.
He invoked the 2024 Finance Bill protests as an example of the public’s capacity to mobilise, warning that the demonstrations were only a glimpse of what could happen if Kenyans felt their concerns over electoral credibility were being ignored.
“What you saw during the 2024 Finance Bill protests was just a party. You don’t know what is happening in this country. Kenyans are quiet, waiting for us to blow the whistle, and when we blow the whistle, they will come and address these issues with you directly,” Gachagua said.
He further accused the commission of risking its credibility if it allowed political interference in preparations for the next election, insisting that Kenyans must be guaranteed a free, fair and credible electoral process.
Gachagua maintained that the opposition would not allow the electoral process to be manipulated in favour of Ruto, urging Ethekon to address the concerns before the country heads into the 2027 election period.
He said Kenyans were demanding political change and warned that the opposition would resist any attempt to undermine the integrity of the polls.
The latest demands come days after Gachagua, Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka and Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna led opposition leaders in a walkout from an IEBC consultative meeting in Nairobi on November 19, 2026.
The opposition leaders walked out of the meeting chaired by IEBC chairman Erastus Ethekon after disagreeing with the agenda, arguing that the commission had failed to prioritise electoral reforms and concerns raised by Kenyans.
They wanted discussions on proposed electoral reforms to take precedence over the commission’s presentation on its preparedness for the 2027 General Election

items.text:
COP31: Climate deal 'not adopted,' summit president says
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 22, 2026
What you need to know
- Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey
- The summit's president acknowledges that a deal was 'not adopted'
- The draft declaration omits any mention of fossil fuels
- The EU says it cannot accept a deal that 'greenwashes fossil fuels'
- Fossil fuels are a major flashpoint at this year's summit, which comes amid soaring energy prices and tensions over the US-Israeli war with Iran
These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 through Sunday, November 22:
COP31 fails to agree climate deal amid fossil fuel rift
The COP31 climate summit has failed to agree on a final joint declaration.
During a plenary session, the summit's Turkish president acknowledged there would be no climate deal.
"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," Murat Kurum, who is also Turkey's environment minister, told a closing plenary in the Mediterranean city of Antalya.
The rift centered on whether to include the phaseout of fossil fuels in the final declaration. Scientists say the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas is the main cause of global warming.
European nations, smaller island states and climate activists have criticized oil-producing countries for the omission.
Ghana says COP presidency has not 'shown respect'
Several nations continued to raise serious objections to the draft.
Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, took a shot at the presidency for how it has handled the negotiations.
"With all due respect Mr. President, you have not shown respect to a group of 54 countries (from Africa) and my country (Ghana) for that matter," Amoah said.
Panama rejects draft decision, saying it 'should be based on science'
Panama's representative said the Central American nation was amongst those who suffer most from the consequences and issue of climate justice.
Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks were being held hostage by a "petroleum mafia" and need to be reformed.
He said science must be the basis for the cover decision, adding that those who contributed to this crisis must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it.
"We are running out of time," Navarro told attendees. "Panama cannot support this decision. The planet cannot continue to wait."
EU cannot accept deal that 'greenwashes fossil fuels': Irish minister
Ireland's Climate Minister Darragh O'Brien has said the European Union is "profoundly disappointed" with the current draft deal on the table at COP31 because it "fails to meet the moment" and that the bloc will not agree to it.
"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5°C within reach," O'Brien said.
"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time. And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels," he added.
Former Greenpeace chief says no deal is better than current deal
Former Greenpeace executive Jennifer Morgan said it would be better to end the COP31 summit with no deal than a watered-down declaration.
Her remarks come amid deep divisions over the omission of fossil fuels from the draft declaration.
Morgan rejected the notion that it would be better to accept the current draft than have no resolution at all, as the Turkish COP president has suggested.
"I think this is the day for the first time in my 31 COPs that I thought it was better not to have a decision that sets us back, that goes against what small islands and vulnerable people are saying," Morgan added.
She praised Germany for standing up to pressures to accept the current deal.
"Of course it would have been better to have a strong outcome here with everyone moving forward, but I agree with the German minister who just said if the text stays the way that it is, then it should not be accepted," Morgan said.
The US climate activist blamed oil-producing nations for the impasse.
"Saudi Arabia's fingerprints are all over" the current draft proposal, she said.
The omission has created a deadlock at COP31, which was due to conclude on Friday but has been extended as delegates seek consensus.
Morgan also blamed this year's Turkish presidency for failing to bring everybody together and instead letting countries that rely on fossil fuels dictate the terms of the agreement.
"Last year we had Brazil with a very strong presidency. They worked all year to bring countries together and they managed. It was not easy last year," Morgan said.
"This year we had presidencies that, in my view, were not well prepared. They did not bring countries together (...) it's been shuttle diplomacy with no text for four days. That's not the way you get an agreement here," she added.
Germany rejects 'unacceptable' draft deal
German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider has said the latest version of the draft agreement is "not acceptable."
Schneider said that the draft decision "not only fails to provide an adequate response but actually takes a step backward. A step backward from previous decisions on climate protection is the last thing Germany can support."
Schneider said that delegates had been working hard for days to reach a unanimous decision on "the world's greatest challenge: human-induced climate change," noting that this summer had "shown that the nature of this warming not only costs lives — as in Nepal — but also changes our world for the worse."
"It is up to us, as humanity, to do something about it. That is why a conference dedicated to climate protection

If that had been given, I don’t think anyone would’ve had any complaints. City perhaps lucky to get away with that.
Birmingham City 1-0 Manchester United: Big chance for United as Park plays the ball through to Terland, who rattles the underside of the crossbar with her shot before Birmingham scramble it away.
It feels like it’s only a matter of time before we see an equaliser.
Manchester City 1-0 Tottenham: Dijkstra is booked for pulling the shirt of Hemp.
Birmingham City 1-0 Manchester United: The visitors are seeing much more of the ball now. They are putting the pressure on the Birmingham defence.
Manchester City 1-0 Tottenham: You may be wondering why goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita is playing today following her red card against Chelsea last weekend…
In case you missed it, City successfully appealed the red card earlier this week.
Birmingham 1-0 Manchester United: Chance for Manchester United to go level as Janssen attempts a volley from around 18 yards out, but Thomas makes a good save.
Birmingham 1-0 Manchester United: A huge chance for Birmingham to double their lead! Hurtré plays a fantastic pass through to McKenna, who meets it after cutting into the box from the right. She goes for the shot but Tullis-Joyce gets a foot to it.
Manchester City 1-0 Tottenham: The conditions here today are like a section from a textbook on the perfect English setting for a game of football. The air is fresh, the temperature feels crisp, the playing surface looks spotless and is shimmering slightly in the low, bright sunlight, so much so that the Tottenham goalkeeper Lize Kop has her arm raised to her forehead to try and shield her eyes from the sunshine. There is just the faintest ripple of wind. It’s almost like something from a painting.
GOAL! Manchester City 1-0 Tottenham (Khadija Shaw, 10)
Shaw strikes for City!
Rose wins the ball high up the pitch before passing to Shaw, who is left in plenty of space in the box. The striker then has plenty of time to slide the ball home.
Shaw is now just one goal away from equalling the WSL all-time top goalscoring record. Can she do it today?
Manchester City 0-0 Tottenham: Blakstad receives a yellow card for pulling Fujino back just outside the box. Manchester City have a free kick but nothing comes of it.
Birmingham 1-0 Manchester United: What a start that is for Birmingham. There is still a long way to go, however, and they have struggled with retaining a lead at times this season.
GOAL! Birmingham 1-0 Manchester United (Lee Geum-min, 4)
Lee fires Birmingham into an early lead!
Her initial shot is blocked, but she is first to the volley and fires the ball into the bottom-left corner.
Birmingham 0-0 Manchester United: The visitors are first to have an attempt at goal as a corner is sent into the box. However, Zigiotti heads it over the crossbar.
Kick-off
Here we go! Both games are under way.
Olivia Holdt was set to start for Tottenham this afternoon, but she has been forced to withdraw from the squad due to illness. The attacking midfielder was visibly emotional while speaking to Martin Ho during the warm-up, she is understandably devastated about not being able to play.
Matilda Vinberg has stepped in to replace her.

items.text:
US Congress helped end the Vietnam War. Can it stop the Iran war?
Congress forbade funding for the Vietnam War, contributing to the fall of the South Vietnamese government in Saigon.
Democrats plan to force United States President Donald Trump to end the war on Iran as early as December although there’s worry their approach could trigger a government shutdown and pile on to soaring food and petrol prices.
Before this month’s midterm elections, the party promised to end the conflict, and its antiwar stance contributed to its sweeping wins at the polls as public anger has grown over the war.
After Democrats flipped multiple seats, including in deeply Republican strongholds, and seized majorities in both the Senate and House of Representatives, many lawmakers said they would refuse to pass new war appropriations once they take control of both chambers on January 3.
However, some in the party are preparing to use the “power of the purse” to stop US attacks even before the new Congress begins its work. They are eyeing a December 11 deadline by which Congress must pass a critical bill to extend funding for some federal agencies.
Here’s what we know:
What have Democratic senators said about ending the war?
Democrats have already tried multiple times through resolutions to end the US-Israel war on Iran without success.
In a joint statement last week, Representatives Yassamin Ansari and Ro Khanna called on Democratic lawmakers to leverage a funding deadline to ensure “not another cent of taxpayer money” goes to prolonging the conflict.
They were referring to a continuing funding package that Congress must deliberate on and pass by December 11. The package is meant to maintain government operations across defence and other sectors. The representatives said Congress should “oppose any funding package that does not explicitly prohibit funds from being used for offensive operations” in Iran.
Failure to pass the package would halt funding for federal agencies and trigger a government shutdown from December 12.
“The American people were loud and clear on November 3rd: they want an immediate end to Donald Trump’s reckless war in Iran,” they wrote in the open statement to their colleagues. “Passing such a measure would defy the demands of Americans who want this war to end – now.”
In an accompanying video, Khanna recalled that Congress ended the Vietnam War using the same approach.
Senator Chris Van Hollen, who is gunning for the Senate majority leader position in the new Congress, also said in a statement last week that any bills passed “must include language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran”.
Senators Tammy Duckworth, Michael Bennet and independent Bernie Sanders also signed the statement.
Did lawmakers force the end of the Vietnam War?
Indirectly, yes, by cutting off US financial support.
The 1955-1972 war was between communist North Vietnam and South Vietnam. The US supported the South and initially sent only military advisers and aid.
In 1964, a US Navy contingent positioned in the Gulf of Tonkin alleged direct attacks by North Vietnam. Congress thereafter passed a resolution granting President Lyndon B Johnson power to send troops without declaring war. The US deployed more than 500,000 soldiers and launched a scorched-earth bombardment.
But as the conflict dragged on and morale among US soldiers began to suffer amid high casualties, the war grew unpopular. Reports of US Army atrocities, including mass rape and massacres, further dampened public support. Congress repealed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in 1973 and ordered US forces to withdraw.
President Richard Nixon’s administration began handing over US military authority to South Vietnamese forces, but it also continued bombardments.
In June 1973, Congress passed the Case-Church Amendment, which forbade approved federal funding from going directly or indirectly to the war. More than two-thirds of lawmakers in both chambers supported it, meaning Nixon could not override it with a presidential veto.
Lawmakers also passed the War Powers Resolution (or War Powers Act), which mandated that the president seek congressional approval before declaring war except in emergencies. Nixon vetoed it, but Congress overrode his veto in November 1973.
With US funding cut off, South Vietnam’s government in Saigon eventually fell in April 1975.
Are all Democrats willing to cut government funding?
The Trump administration irked Democrats when it failed to seek approval to declare war on Iran, a power that is constitutionally vested in Congress.
But not all Democrats support a government shutdown to end the war.
Democratic Representative Rosa DeLauro, who in the new Congress will chair the influential House Appropriations Committee, which can block funding, told CBS News before the midterms that she would support “cutting off the funds” for the war.
However, she has not backed a shutdown and said she would rather approve a short-term funding extension rather than a funding package meant to run for a year.
“I think that the American people would like to see us end the war,” she told reporters on Wednesday. “I also believe that the American people may not believe that shutting the government down ends the war.”
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is likely to become speaker of the House in January, as well as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, have not yet taken a stance.
Can the president use his veto power?
Yes, because Republicans still control Congress for another six weeks and Democrats, in the current Congress and the next, do not have the two-thirds majority required to override a presidential veto.
The two-thirds supermajority in the Senate requires 67 votes when all 100 senators participate. Even in the new Congress, in which Democrats will have a 56-44 majority, they will be 11 votes short.
Likewise, a two-thirds majority in the 435-member House requires 290 votes, but Democrats

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes says the club has offered him a new contract, but discussions
items.text:
Bruno Fernandes says contract talks on hold as Man United battle poor start
The Manchester United captain’s current deal expires at the end of the season, though the club has an option to extend.
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes says the club has offered him a new contract, but discussions have been put on hold as the team focuses on turning around their poor form.
“Yeah, the club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay. And as you said, there are no negotiations going on,” Fernandes told Sky Sports in an interview published on Sunday.
Fernandes’s current deal expires at the end of this season, although United hold an option to extend the midfielder’s contract by a further year until June 2028, giving the club more time to reach an agreement on new terms.
“We spoke about the contract at the end of last season; we came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but because of the context of the team and the club, I just put that to one side because I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations,” Fernandes said.
“The most important thing now is that the club gets back to winning games.”
The Portugal international also addressed comments claiming he had demanded more money and a longer deal, saying his priority was to remain at Old Trafford and help restore the club’s fortunes.
United are third from the bottom of the Premier League standings, having won only one of their opening 10 league matches, their worst start to a season in 40 years.
“I’ve seen people saying that he’s asked for more money; he’s asked for more years. If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here. I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United,” Fernandes said.
“I could have been in a place that’s much warmer than Manchester.”
New manager Mauricio Pochettino, appointed after Michael Carrick was sacked earlier this month, will take charge of his first game when United face fifth-placed Liverpool on Sunday.

items.title: 🔴 COP31 ends without deal as EU rejects text for omitting mention of fossil fuels
items.summary:
COP31 ends without deal as EU rejects final text for omitting mention of fossil fuels
EU member states on Sunday objected to adopting an 11th-hour deal that omitted explicit references to fossil fuels, the bloc's presidency said. The issue remains a major point of contention at the summit, which is
items.text:
COP31 ends without deal as EU rejects final text for omitting mention of fossil fuels
EU member states on Sunday objected to adopting an 11th-hour deal that omitted explicit references to fossil fuels, the bloc's presidency said. The issue remains a major point of contention at the summit, which is taking place amid soaring energy prices and geopolitical tensions fuelled by the war in Iran.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
COP31 President Murat Kurum acknowledged on Sunday a failure to reach agreement on an overarching deal at the UN climate conference after countries objected to the text.
"This text was not imposed on anyone," Kurum, who is also Turkey's environment minister, told a closing plenary in the Mediterranean city of Antalya.
"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted."
The COP31 presidency proposed an 11th-hour deal Sunday that again failed to mention fossil fuels – an omission that deepened a tense standoff at the UN climate talks.
The last offering by summit co-hosts Turkey and Australia published deep into overtime left unresolved tensions over planet-heating fossil fuels but retained a much-sought goal to electrify the global economy.
The European Union presidency said it would "object" to adopting the contentious final deal.
"We will not endorse a cover decision... that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change," Ireland's Climate and Energy Minister Darragh O'Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, told the closing session of the conference.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The proposal needed consensus approval from nearly 200 nations at a closing session Sunday but they struggled to bridge differences during two weeks of grinding negotiations.
The EU and other nations pushed for strong language on transitioning away from fossil fuels, a call that faced resistance from oil-rich Saudi Arabia.
France called the latest proposal a "backward" step.
"Time is ticking and we are not there yet," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said in a statement.
"The situation is difficult, and the outcome is uncertain. The oil-producing countries are putting up a fierce fight," a German official said.
A Saudi official declined to comment.
Fossil fuels are a flashpoint at the climate talks and the summit comes against a difficult backdrop of soaring energy prices and geopolitical tensions stemming from the war in Iran.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase out of fossil fuels but a second, pared-down version released Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas.
Threats of a walkout prompted Turkey and Australia to convene a hurried meeting between the EU and Saudi Arabia in a bid to broker a compromise.
The latest text introduced a reference to a previous global deal in 2023 to shift the world away from fossil fuels – but stopped short of naming them explicitly.
And it retained a contentious push to expand carbon capture and storage, a technology championed by the fossil fuel industry but criticised as costly and ineffective in cutting emissions.
"We are very disappointed with how the text looks," the environment minister of Antigua and Barbuda, Michael Joseph, said after leaving the COP31 presidency's offices.
"I can't honestly say that I'm okay with it passing" in its current state, Joseph said, adding that the draft was "quite silent" on fossil fuels.
Read moreCOP31 climate talks go into overtime as nations wrangle over fossil fuels omission
Goal to electrify
The draft also called for global efforts to boost the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035 and the expansion of "clean energy".
The summit had been under pressure to show progress in tackling soaring greenhouse gas emissions in a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal and Indonesia.
Facing blowback over fossil fuels, Turkey and Australia pointed to "electrification" as a way to cut heat-trapping emissions and bolster energy security.
This works by replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels directly – like diesel cars and gas heating – with electric alternatives.
But some nations had demanded an explicitly "clean" target to ensure the electrification push was powered by renewable energy and not fossil fuels.
Around one-third of global electricity is produced using coal and another fifth using fossil gas.
Attempts by Saudi Arabia, India and Kenya meanwhile to delay the next set of reports by the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) have been another major source of friction at the talks.
The draft text "highlighted the importance" of these reports for an upcoming stocktake of global carbon-cutting efforts in 2028.
Dozens of countries across Europe, Africa and the Pacific wanted these assessments by the global scientific authority on climate change published in time for that crucial stocktake.
Countries also disagreed at COP31 over how to respond to the looming breach of the 1.5C warming target set under the Paris climate accord.
One of the latest drafts expressed "deep concern" that global warming would cross 1.5C above pre-industrial levels in the next few years.
The talks also jammed over long-running complaints that rich nations are shirking their obligations to help developing nations confront climate change.
The removal of a $120 billion target for climate adaptation angered developing nations.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Israeli settlers have attacked several Palestinian towns and villages in the central occupied West Bank,
items.text:
Israeli settlers attack several Palestinian villages in occupied West Bank
Attacks in Ramallah, el-Bireh provinces included the burning of 12 vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on homes.
Israeli settlers have attacked several Palestinian towns and villages in the central occupied West Bank, burning cars and damaging property.
The attacks early on Sunday included the burning of 12 vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on the walls of homes in Ramallah and el-Bireh provinces, reported the Palestinian news agency Wafa. The incidents were reported in Kafr Malik village, Deir Abu Mash’al village, and Deir al-Sudan village.
“Residents were awakened around two in the morning by sounds of fire and explosions. They realised the settlers had set fire to cars,” reported Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Odeh from Kafr Malik.
Israeli settler violence has surged across the occupied West Bank since Israel launched its genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza. At least 1,222 people, including 255 children, have been killed in attacks there since Israel launched its war in October 2023 in response to the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.
The Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said there was a significant increase in the number of attacks throughout the Palestinian territory last month.
According to the Palestinian Authority body, there were 3,133 attacks in October, with Israeli forces responsible for 1,764 of them and Israeli settlers 1,369.
The commission said the total number of attacks increased by 53 percent compared with September when 2,051 attacks were recorded. Settler attacks alone rose from 647 in September to 1,369 in October – a 112 percent increase.
‘Jewish terrorism’
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar Party, who has been tasked with forming a new government after Israel’s general election last month, criticised the latest attacks on Sunday.
He wrote on social media that the attacks were “Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word, and it must be called what it is”.
“Sabotage by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermines regional stability, endangers lives and severely damages the national security of the state of Israel and its foreign relations,” he posted on X.
“The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy,” he added, referring to far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
Ben-Gvir rejected the allegations and said Eisenkot was rushing to conclusions. He wrote on social media that Eisenkot’s stance represents a “down payment” to Arab Knesset member Ahmad Tibi in preparation for forming a government with the support of Arab parties.
Settlers are often “escorted by Israeli squads and they do nothing to stop the attackers,” Shai Parnes of the Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem told Al Jazeera.
The Israeli military said it was sending police officers and investigators from the Criminal Identification Unit to the attacked areas “to collect evidence as part of the ongoing investigation”, the military wrote on social media.

The 46-year-old Italian was appointed in June after the departure of Ed Still, who himself lasted only three months
items.text:
Watford sack boss Dionisi after 18 games
- Published
Watford are looking for their sixth manager in 18 months after they sacked head coach Alessio Dionisi following 18 games in charge.
The 46-year-old Italian was appointed in June after the departure of Ed Still, who himself lasted only three months at Vicarage Road.
Still, Javi Gracia and Paulo Pezzolano were all also given full-time contracts after Tom Cleverley left in May 2025.
Dionisi was Watford's 12th head coach, not including interim bosses, since the end of the 2020-21 season, and leaves the Hornets searching for a 25th since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.
The club have had 57 permanent managers in their 145-year history.
The decision to replace him comes after Saturday's crushing 4-0 defeat by Sheffield United at Bramall Lane.
Dionisi's dismissal caps an underwhelming start to the season, with the Hornets having won just four league games to leave them 21st in the table.
"We thank Alessio and his staff for his professionalism and their efforts," sporting director Luke Dowling told the club website., external
"As I'm sure the supporters have seen, Alessio is a really good guy and we wish him the best for the future.
"The process has started for a replacement and we hope to be in a position to announce that shortly."
Dionisi was sacked by Serie B club Empoli in March after only five months in charge following a run of five wins in 22 matches.
His spell in charge of the Hornets was his first outside his homeland and started promisingly when his youthful side beat Southampton in their opening league game.
But they won only two of their next 12 in all competitions, and despite deservedly beating Charlton on 17 October, reverses at Wolves and Norwich followed, before four points from Dionisi's final three games in charge of the Hertfordshire side and his dismissal means further upheaval for the Hornets.
Since sacking Cleverley at the end of the 2024-25 campaign, the club has now been through four permanent head coaches, as well as interim boss Charlie Daniels' two-game spell in charge.
Of those four, only Gracia, in his second spell at Vicarage Road, took charge of more than 20 games.
On the morning of their final-day drubbing by Coventry last season, chief executive Scott Duxbury wrote a statement on the club website saying Watford had made mistakes, labelling their end to the campaign "unacceptable" and "truly disappointing in the extreme".
