items.title: What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf?
items.summary:
What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf?
Tehran has ramped up attacks in recent days as the US naval blockade and sanctions campaign hurt the country economically.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have targeted radars at a United States military base in Bahrain,
items.text:
What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf?
Tehran has ramped up attacks in recent days as the US naval blockade and sanctions campaign hurt the country economically.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have targeted radars at a United States military base in Bahrain, as Iran has intensified attacks over the past week, hitting tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, and downing US drones.
At least 25 tankers have been hit in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes, in the past seven days, causing the Gulf oil flow to drop sharply.
The escalating attacks come as Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country is facing what he called a “silent economic war” amid US sanctions and a naval blockade.
So what is behind Iran’s latest escalation, and will it trigger a new round of hostilities between Tehran and Washington or force the two sides to sit down for talks to end the war that has caused a global energy crisis?
Where have the latest attacks been?
Bahrain has faced the brunt of Iran’s attacks in recent days.
On Saturday, Manama said an Iranian strike hit a civilian industrial facility, starting a fire, as it thwarted several other attacks that day.
The IRGC said it had carried out a combined missile and drone operation targeting US military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain, claiming to have destroyed two US Patriot air defence radars at the bases.
Iranian state media reported that an interceptor missile launched from the US Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain crashed on Sitra Island near Manama, sparking a large fire.
The IRGC said the operation was retaliation for a US strike on a radar installation on Iran’s Hengam Island. Iran has justified the attacks as a response to continued violations of its airspace, including by US MQ-1 and MQ-9 reconnaissance and combat drones.
Bahrain has faced three drone attacks in recent days after a lull in fighting for several weeks.
Iran’s army on Saturday said its air defences fired a missile at a US F-16 jet over the Gulf the previous evening, damaging the aircraft, the IRNA news agency reported. However, US Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the claim, stating that “all US fighter jets in the Middle East are safe and accounted for”.
Iranian forces on Sunday also said they shot down another MQ-1 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC claimed it was the 20th US drone of this type to be shot down since the war began in late February and the fourth in the past 24 hours.
Meanwhile, British maritime authorities reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz near Oman.
Al Jazeera correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week, with about 25 since November 14.
Last week, the Iranian army also said it targeted US drone and missile installations at Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem base. The attack came after the US struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which remains under effective Iranian control.
How are attacks affecting oil exports through Hormuz?
Oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz has seen a considerable dip as Iran has escalated attacks on a near-daily basis.
According to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), 263 ships passed through the key waterway between November 12 and 18, which is 15 percent fewer than the previous week and 20 percent fewer than the week before that.
Of those vessels, 37 were oil tankers, down from 52 the previous week, UKMTO reported on Friday.
The figures, however, could be higher as vessels passing through as part of shadow fleets are not officially registered.
About 135 ships passed daily through the vital strait before the war began in February.
Last week, the US maritime agency warned that the Iran blockade was adding to rising Gulf premiums, with insurance rates up from 0.10-0.25 percent before the war to 3.5-7.5 percent.
Oil prices have spiked, crossing $100 a barrel before settling down to $83, still more than $15 from before the war.
Cumulative losses from the conflict have now reached 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas supply from the Gulf, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday.
The IEA, however, added that the conflict could cut world oil demand by more than 4 percent by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response.
Why is Iran escalating attacks?
As Iran has ramped up attacks, senior officials have asked the US to choose between surrendering to missiles or to diplomacy.
The attacks indicate that Iran is using its leverage in the conflict, sending the message that the US allies in the region will continue to bear the brunt of its actions if the war does not end.
The attacks aim to diminish US military capabilities in the region and “also to spread the pain of the war widely to include the entire [Gulf region] and, indirectly, global economies via higher shipping costs and stressed supplies of essentials”, Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut, told Al Jazeera.
The single biggest driver of this strategy, Khouri said, is for Iran to continually ensure that it will no longer “suffer alone from US-Israel-imperial assaults”.
Tehran is hoping to change US policy by revealing its inability to protect its own facilities or those of its Arab allies, which could prompt Arab governments to press US President Donald Trump to end the war, Khouri, who is also a nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, added.
Meanwhile, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told Iranian media that he considers the economic blockade imposed by the US on Iran an act of war.
“We consider the economic siege a hostile act, and we will take any necessary measures to break this economic siege,” Gharibabadi told Iranian reporters.

items.title: Why have UN efforts to regulate ‘killer robots’ stalled?
items.summary:
Why have UN efforts to regulate ‘killer robots’ stalled?
CWC countries agree to ‘elaborate’ on potential accord regulating autonomous weapons in two years, prompting criticism by rights groups.
A United Nations conference has failed to agree on the swift adoption of legally binding rules to regulate
items.text:
Why have UN efforts to regulate ‘killer robots’ stalled?
CWC countries agree to ‘elaborate’ on potential accord regulating autonomous weapons in two years, prompting criticism by rights groups.
A United Nations conference has failed to agree on the swift adoption of legally binding rules to regulate autonomous weapon systems known as “killer robots”.
The member states of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) met in Switzerland this week to discuss developing a new treaty which would regulate how the systems are used amid growing alarm over artificial intelligence (AI)-driven warfare and the lack of transparency and accountability.
But on Saturday, participants fell short of securing a mandate to negotiate a legally binding ban, agreeing instead to “elaborate” on a potential accord regulating such weapon systems by 2028. Rights groups and NGOs called the development “disappointing”.
Here’s what you should know:
What are ‘killer robots’?
According to the UN, lethal autonomous weapons systems are “a combination of one or more weapons and technological components operating together, that is capable of identifying, selecting, and engaging a target in a way that results in loss of life, without intervention by a human being operating the system”.
In simpler terms, they are systems that can identify, select and engage a target without human intervention. They are commonly referred to as “killer robots”, but this is not an established technical or legal designation.
The systems are programmed with a specific “target profile” before deployment, using sensor data such as facial recognition and other technologies to search for and kill matching targets.
“When the weapon encounters someone or something the algorithm perceives to match its target profile, it fires and kills,” the Autonomous Weapons Organisation explains.
According to the UN, not all autonomous weapon systems use AI. At the same time, AI is not necessary for autonomous weapon systems to function, nor does it determine whether a system is autonomous.
“However, when AI is used to identify, select and engage targets, it can amplify the serious legal, ethical, humanitarian and security concerns associated with autonomous weapon systems,” the UN warns.
Despite the concerns, AI-assisted weapons have already been used in the wars in Ukraine and Sudan and conflicts in the Middle East. Israel has used surveillance tools and AI-powered targeting systems in its genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
What is the CCW?
Adopted in 1980, the CCW was established as a key international humanitarian law instrument.
“Its purpose is to ban or restrict the use of specific types of weapons that are considered to cause unnecessary or unjustifiable suffering to combatants or to affect civilians indiscriminately,” the UN says.
There is currently no legally binding instrument under the CCW that specifically regulates autonomous weapon systems.
What happened this week?
The 128 countries that are party to the CCW met in the Swiss city of Geneva to discuss whether to authorise negotiations on curbs and a potential ban on such systems.
Julien Thoeni, the Swiss diplomat who chaired the Geneva conference, said the process should determine which weapons can be banned under international humanitarian law and which can be permitted but regulated.
The week-long conference came after nearly 100 countries agreed last month that it was important to swiftly adopt legally binding rules on the weapons capable of killing without a human making the final decision to fire.
But on Saturday, key arms-producing nations, including the United States, Russia and Israel, opposed the push. Decisions under the convention require the agreement of all member states.
Diplomats told the Reuters news agency that negotiations over the final wording of the treaty had continued all night after Russian objections to rules of procedure forced the cancellation of some formal meetings.
Two EU diplomats told media outlet Politico that the US, the UK, South Korea, Japan, Turkiye and Israel were also countries that resisted an effort to agree on a binding regulation. Others supporting a new convention included the European Union and NATO member states, as well as Ukraine, China and Iran, diplomats cited by The Guardian newspaper said.
In the end, all countries agreed on a watered-down convention which aims to develop new rules to regulate such weapons by 2028.
A diplomat involved in the talks from a country supporting the new laws told Reuters that the outcome was “disappointing but could have been much worse”.
Why did some resist regulating ‘killer robots’?
While most countries support a pact to regulate “killer robots”, major military powers are opposing it, saying that humanitarian law linked to those weapons is sufficient.
As investment in AI warfare and autonomous systems grows, those countries also resist restrictions that could curb their ability to develop, test or use advanced weapons on modern battlefields. So rather than committing to strict legal obligations, they favour flexible, non-binding frameworks or longer timelines for discussions.
Swiss diplomat Thoeni told reporters after the meeting ended that some countries had rejected the word “negotiate”. The agreed text refers instead to the “elaboration” of an instrument.
How have rights groups reacted?
Stop Killer Robots, a coalition of some 300 organisations opposed to the development and use of autonomous weapons, called the mandate “watered down” and said it offered no clear route to legally binding rules.
Its executive director, Nicole van Rooijen, said autonomous weapons were being deployed in combat, including systems that use artificial intelligence to choose targets.
“Delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk,” she told AFP news agency.

items.summary:
Bruno Fernandes has revealed that Manchester United have offered him a new contract, but discussions have been put on hold as the club focus on turning around their terrible start to the season.
Fernandes’s current deal expires at the end of this campaign, although United hold an option to extend th
items.text:
Bruno Fernandes has revealed that Manchester United have offered him a new contract, but discussions have been put on hold as the club focus on turning around their terrible start to the season.
Fernandes’s current deal expires at the end of this campaign, although United hold an option to extend their captain’s contract by a further year until June 2028, giving the club more time to reach an agreement on fresh terms.
“The club offered me a new contract so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay. And as you said, there are no negotiations going on,” Fernandes told Sky Sports in an interview published on Sunday.
“We spoke about the contract at the end of last season, we came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but because of the context of the team and the club, I just put that to one side because I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations,” Fernandes added. “The most important thing now is that the club gets back to winning games.“
The 32-year-old’s future is still up in the air after it was revealed he turned down a second contract offer from the club. Fernandes’s form has dropped off this season, his goal and assist in the 4-4 draw against Aston Villa providing his first goal involvements in the league since scoring a hat-trick against Ipswich in August.
The Portugal international also hit back at rumours he had demanded more money and a longer deal, saying his priority was to remain at Old Trafford and help restore the club’s fortunes.
“I’ve seen people saying that he’s asked for more money, he’s asked for more years. If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here. I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United,” Fernandes said. “I could have been in a place that’s much warmer than Manchester.”
United are second-bottom of the Premier League standings having won only one of their opening 10 league matches – their worst start to a season in 40 years. Their new head coach, Mauricio Pochettino, will take charge of his first game when United face fifth-placed Liverpool on Sunday. The former Tottenham and Chelsea manager was appointed after Michael Carrick was sacked this month.

items.text:
Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments
November 22, 2026
In the space of just two days this weekend, Bayern Munich were held to a 1-1 draw by FC Cologne, saw Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane ruled out until the new year with a serious ankle injury and lost first place in the Bundesliga to rivals Borussia Dortmund.
But even those setbacks – as well as the return of head coach Vincent Kompany to the sideline following health issues – have been overshadowed by explosive public comments made by Bayern club bosses regarding young attacker and Germany international Jamal Musiala.
What is wrong with Jamal Musiala?
Back in July 2025, Musiala suffered a fractured fibula and a broken ankle at the Club World Cup.
Since then, the 23-year-old has been battling to recover not only from that injury but also with a debilitating neurological condition diagnosed as "absence seizures" which led him to collapse on the pitch in two consecutive pre-season games in August this year.
Musiala has struggled to replicate the sort of form which led to a well-remunerated contract extension in January 2025, prior to the ankle injury and the seizures.
The situation has now prompted a series of controversial public remarks from the Bayern hierarchy seemingly questioning the validity of that contract.
What have Bayern Munich officials said?
"It is well known that he has a contract which contains some considerable sums," former chief executive and current supervisory board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told broadcaster Sky on Friday evening following the 1-1 draw with Cologne, in which Musiala had made a 20-minute substitute appearance.
"It's in all of our interest that he comes back, ideally in top form, but what happens if that's not the case?" asked Rummenigge, adding that Musiala's condition "leads us to suspect, unfortunately, that it will be difficult [for him] to return to the level that he has often shown in this stadium" and that "then we of course have to think about the finances."
Rummenigge suggested a need for Bayern to hold talks with Musiala, his family and his representatives because "such sums are, with respect, no longer justifiable."
Asked whether Bayern would consider selling Musiala, Rummenigge said he considered it unlikely that any club would be prepared to buy the player out of his new contract, which is set to run until 2030 and which reportedly sees Musiala earn up to €30 million per year.
"I cannot imagine that Jamal would leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions," said Rummenigge. "And that is a problem."
Rummenigge was not the first senior Bayern official to express such doubts. Earlier this month, former club president Uli Hoeness had told local broadcaster Bayrischer Rundfunk that Musiala's situation presented the club with a "dilemma."
"He has an illness which cannot be cured but which can be somewhat controlled through medication," said Hoeness, who also sits on Bayern's supervisory board, questioning "whether he will ever regain the ability he once had" and stating that "he continues to receive money."
Bayern chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen has also weighed in, telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper last week: "We all have a responsibility towards the club and we all hope that Jamal will come back. Of course this will take time. We will assess the situation and speak to his family and management. Either we'll all be happy that the old Jamal [will return] or, if he becomes a different [player], we'll have to hold talks."
FIFPRO: 'Bayern should know better'
The comments by Hoeness, Dreesen and Rummenigge landed like a bombshell in Germany and beyond.
The global players' union FIFPRO issued a statement on Saturday slamming what they called "a coordinated strategy to put pressure on Musiala and his representatives ahead of any negotiations," highlighting Bayern's "duty of care" towards their player, and stating: "A club of Bayern's standing should know better."
"Across professional football, uncertainty about a player's future can take a toll on their mental health, particularly when they are recovering from injury," the statement continued. "Making Musiala's health and future a matter of public debate adds to that pressure. Contracts are there to be respected. An injury or a dip in form gives a club no grounds to reopen terms it agreed to, just as a run of outstanding performances gives a player no automatic right to a pay rise."
Former Bayern Munich and Germany defender Lothar Matthäus also criticized the club, saying in his role as a pundit for Sky: "I've been a bit shocked throughout the entire week. It started with Uli Hoeness, continued with Jan-Christian Dreesen, and yesterday Karl-Heinz Rummenigge chose the strongest words of all. I have enormous respect for Karl-Heinz. I've known him for over 30 years. But he chose those statements very deliberately. The person who suffers most from all this is Jamal Musiala."
The comments by the Bayern bosses also came just hours ahead of the club's annual general meeting on Saturday, where club members – who hold a majority 70% stake in the club in accordance with German football's "50+1" ownership rule – took to the stand to criticize the club's hierarchy.
One member, professional neurologist Jonatan Hoffmann, expressed his "absolute respect" for Musiala and said that patients suffering from such conditions require "support."
He said Musiala had received such support from head coach Vincent Kompany and director of sport Max Eberl, but said Hoeness', Dreesen's and Rummenigge's comments were "not helpful" and had "little to do with the much talked about Bayern Munich family" – earning considerable applause from fellow members.
Bayern president: 'Musiala will get time and support'

- Published
Rescue and firefighting efforts are continuing for a Russian cargo vessel hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, authorities have said.
The ship - the Sparta II - was bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday that work was ongoing to make sure the cargo ship did not sink but it was not aware of any danger to surrounding maritime traffic.
Water was still being used to douse the ship on Sunday, and Finland said Estonian and Russian assets were also involved in recovery work.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used in the strike, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

items.title: Messi throws ball in opponent’s face, avoids red card as Inter Miami lose
items.summary:
Messi throws ball in opponent’s face, avoids red card as Inter Miami lose
Lionel Messi escapes a red-card booking for a controversial throw-in in Miami’s 3-0 defeat to Columbus in MLS Cup playoffs.
Lionel Messi is at the centre of a controversy after hurling the ball at an opponent during a throw-in
items.text:
Messi throws ball in opponent’s face, avoids red card as Inter Miami lose
Lionel Messi escapes a red-card booking for a controversial throw-in in Miami’s 3-0 defeat to Columbus in MLS Cup playoffs.
Lionel Messi is at the centre of a controversy after hurling the ball at an opponent during a throw-in and after the Columbus Crew coach says the Inter Miami superstar should have been sent off instead of receiving a yellow card.
The incident took place on Saturday during Miami’s 3-0 home defeat by Columbus in the first game of a best-of-three series in the MLS Cup playoffs.
With 10-man Miami 1-0 down at the stroke of half-time, Messi’s frustration boiled over as he aimed a forceful throw-in into the face of Columbus Crew forward Gonzalo Tapia.
Tapia, less than a metre (3ft) away and trying to impede Messi’s actions, threw himself to the ground after the ball hit his face while Messi appealed for a handball.
Referee Allen Chapman showed yellow cards to both Messi and Tapia, but coach Laurent Courtois said afterwards Messi should have been given a red card.
“Everybody knows that he deserved more than a yellow card,” Courtois said in a postgame news conference when asked about the incident.
“It’s just really sad.”
What are the laws and rules about Messi’s actions at the throw-in?
According to the International Football Association Board Law 12, which pertains to fouls and misconduct, the appropriate disciplinary action for such an incident would be both players being “cautioned (yellow card) for unsporting behaviour”.
It adds that the player taking the throw-in could be “sent off (red card) for violent conduct (if the thrower used excessive force)”.
Chapman defended his decision to brandish a yellow card to Messi.
“The force used was negligible, and the offence did not reach the level of violent conduct,” the referee told a pool reporter.
Tapia, who scored twice for Columbus in the win, refrained from commenting on the referee’s decision, saying, “I don’t know if it’s a red card, but I am not the referee to say. It stays there.”
Miami head coach Kily Gonzalez also echoed Tapia’s thoughts, adding that the “card doesn’t change much”.
“The referee saw a yellow, and that is it. We can’t blame the referee,” Gonzalez told reporters. “Sometimes they make mistakes. Sometimes they don’t like each one of us, and we have to accept it.”
The 3-0 defeat means seventh-seeded Columbus, the 2023 champions, could eliminate Messi and Miami from the playoffs with a victory in game two of the series in Ohio on Friday.
“It was a game where nothing went right for us, and we effectively created their chances for them,” Gonzalez said.
“We didn’t produce the great performance we had hoped for. Everything went wrong, but we have to learn from it because next time, if we don’t win, we’re out,” he added.

The suspect, identified as Latif Kinyua Mbaya,
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – The Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) has arrested a suspect accused of assaulting police officers during violent disruptions at this year’s Mashujaa Day celebrations at Githongo Stadium in Imenti Central, Meru County.
The suspect, identified as Latif Kinyua Mbaya, was arrested in Meru Town following investigations into the October 20, 2026 incident that left two police officers seriously injured.
In a statement on Sunday, the DCI said the violence erupted when a group of rowdy youths armed with stones and clubs disrupted the national celebrations.
Anti-riot police officers initially intervened to restore order, but the group reportedly returned on motorcycles and charged towards the stadium, triggering further chaos.
During the confrontation, two police officers sustained serious injuries, while the windscreens of two government vehicles were smashed.
Detectives from Meru subsequently launched investigations to establish the circumstances surrounding the violence and identify those responsible.
Upon completion of the investigations, the case file was forwarded to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) for review.
The ODPP directed that Mbaya be charged with grievous harm, contrary to Section 231 of the Penal Code, among other offences.
Acting on the prosecution’s directions, detectives tracked down and arrested the suspect in Meru Town.

items.title: Murkomen accuses opposition of fighting 2027 vote transparency
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has accused opposition leaders of resisting transparent presidential vote tallying ahead of the 2027 General Election.
Murkomen questioned why opposition politicians would allegedly oppose an open verification process, insisting t
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has accused opposition leaders of resisting transparent presidential vote tallying ahead of the 2027 General Election.
Murkomen questioned why opposition politicians would allegedly oppose an open verification process, insisting that the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) must tally presidential results transparently in the presence of candidates’ agents.
Murkomen also warned politicians against threatening to take over election processes or declare their own results, describing such remarks as reckless and potentially dangerous to national unity.
“I am surprised that for the first time in Kenya, it is the opposition leaders who don’t want transparency. It’s the opposition leaders who are telling the IEBC chairman to go and do his own tallying in his room, not in the presence of the rest of Kenya,” Murkomen said.
He maintained that presidential results should not be calculated and announced by the IEBC chairman working alone, arguing that the process must be open enough for political parties and Kenyans to follow.
Murkomen explained that election results are first declared at polling stations, followed by the tallying of votes at ward, constituency and county levels, depending on the elective positions.
He said the final presidential tally should be conducted at the national tallying centre in Nairobi, with the IEBC chairman working alongside presidential election agents.
“That tallying of presidential elections cannot be done by the IEBC chairman alone. It must be done in a transparent manner, in a manner everybody can follow in the presence of agents,” he said.
The CS further cautioned politicians against threatening protests at constituency tallying centres or suggesting that they could appoint their own returning officers.
“We want transparent tallying and verification of national elections for the sake of the unity of our country,” Murkomen said, adding that Kenya must be able to move forward after the elections.

items.title: 87% of the Anthropic power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028
items.summary: In The AI Gas Rush: Risks and Implications of “Bring Your Own Power”, we dug into how data centers are increasingly securing their own dedicated primary power generation rather than relying solely on utilities to procure power (“BYOP”). We identified 177 GW of planned BYOP gas capacity—enough to pow
items.text:
In The AI Gas Rush: Risks and Implications of “Bring Your Own Power”, we dug into how data centers are increasingly securing their own dedicated primary power generation rather than relying solely on utilities to procure power (“BYOP”). We identified 177 GW of planned BYOP gas capacity—enough to power 65% of all US homes. Conversely, we found renewables are much less common than gas for BYOP: we estimate that for current proposals, less than 20% of energy generation will come from renewable sources by 2032.
But BYOP projects aren’t the only new fossil sources that are coming online to meet the skyrocketing energy demands of AI data centers. Another 200 GW of new fossil power plants is being built on the grid to meet growing demand, due in large part to data centers.1
As a case study of how the AI buildout is driving both new BYOP and grid fossil infrastructure, we analyzed the compute commitments of a single company: Anthropic.
Map of Anthropic’s data centers and associated power plants. See our full dataset for details of each site.
Finding 1: Anthropic has made no direct commitments to renewable energy in the U.S. Though Anthropic has stated “We’re also working to broaden our energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar, and emerging technologies”, its only publicly disclosed commitments, contract, or investments in renewable power are in Norway and Canada (as of November 2026). In contrast, Anthropic is directly procuring fossil power equipment—it recently “bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty [gas] generators for $3.4bn”.
Finding 2: Anthropic’s currently contracted data centers in the U.S. will be overwhelmingly powered by fossil fuels in the near term. By considering on-site gas and the grid power plants which are likely to meet Anthropic’s added load (i.e. marginal generators), we estimate about 87% of the company’s power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028. As of October 2026, Anthropic has contracted 15 GW of compute; of this, about 5.9–9.6 GW is contracted to specific data center sites. For a sense of scale, 9.6 GW could power about 7 million homes or cover 18% of the peak power demand of California—the world’s 4th largest economy.
This demand will be met with a mix of new on-site gas, new grid gas, and existing grid gas, coal, and nuclear. In the short term, no grid renewables are attributed to Anthropic’s power use, because—without commitments to new renewable capacity—new load on the grid will be met by dispatchable, marginal fossil resources.2 For more details, see our full dataset and our methodology below.
Finding 3: Total CO2 emissions from Anthropic’s power use at these sites could reach 17–38 million MtCO2e per year in 2028, when this capacity is expected to be online. This range reflects uncertainty in Anthropic’s average power use, due to factors such as cooling needs and average utilization (see methodology below). In our mid-case, Anthropic will emit 32 million MtCO2e in 2028. These totals will continue to grow—possibly doubling by 2030, as some analysts expect Anthropic to secure 30 GW by 2030.
To put these figures in context, Anthropic’s CO2 emissions from power use in 2028:
- could exceed the emissions of all of California’s power generation (31.1 MMtCO2e in 2024, not including imports).
- could exceed Meta, Microsoft, and Google’s combined Scope 2 emissions from 2025 (their location-based emissions, before renewable energy offsets, were 5.9 million, 12 million and 15 million MtCO2e, respectively)3
- would represent a 16–36% increase over 2024 levels of the entire U.S. data center sector (105 MMtCO2e).
- would increase the entire U.S.’s power sector emissions (1,485 MMtCO2e in 2025) by 1.1–2.5%.
Finding 4: Anthropic’s data centers are sited in areas where the grid mainly uses coal and gas. We estimate the average carbon intensity of Anthropic’s power to be 1,033–1,076 lb CO2e/MWh, 35% higher than the U.S. grid average (767 lb CO2e/MWh).4
Finding 5: 80% of on-site power uses inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines. About 25% (2.5 GW) of Anthropic’s contracted power will come from on-site, behind-the-meter gas. 80% of this on-site capacity consists of inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines, which emit more pollution per unit of electricity than modern combined cycle plants (see our report for more details on the types of power generation being used for on-site gas).
Finding 6: Based on EPA’s nationally-averaged benefit-per-ton estimates, air pollution from Anthropic’s on-site and grid power use could cause $2–3 billion in annual health damages, with total emissions of over 13,000 tons per year (tpy) of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and 2,000 tpy of fine particulate matter (PM2.5).
In October 2026, Anthropic outlined its “approach to responsible data center development”, stating: “We follow the air permitting process everywhere we operate and require the same of the plants powering our data centers. Those plants must also use emissions control technology, including selective catalytic reduction [SCR].” However, Anthropic has used compute capacity at SpaceX’s Colossus 2 facility since May 2026, which still receives most of its power from temporary, unpermitted turbines, the majority of which are not equipped with SCR. Anthropic will use as much as 600 MW of power from Colossus 2 by the end of 2026 (see methodology below).
Anthropic has also contracted 460 MW (and is in talks for up to 920 MW) of power from Nscale’s Monarch Compute Campus in Mason, West Virginia. This facility will be powered by inefficient reciprocating engines which have significant formaldehyde and hazardous air pollutant (HAP) emissions compared to conventional gas power plants.
For more, see our full dataset on Anthropic’s compute and our report on BYOP.

The 32-year-old midfielder is out of contract at the end of
items.text:
'Not the right time' - Fernandes pauses Man Utd contract talks
- Published
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes says he has been offered a new contract by the club but feels it "is not the right time" for discussions about his future.
The 32-year-old midfielder is out of contract at the end of the season, though the club have the option to trigger a 12-month extension until 2028.
He was left out of the side under previous manager Michael Carrick but says he has no issues at the club and has chosen to stay at Old Trafford despite offers elsewhere in recent seasons.
He told Sky Sports:, external "The club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay.
"There's no negotiations ongoing, but I've seen people saying that 'he's asked for more money, he's asked for more years'. If I wanted more money, I wouldn't be here.
"I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.
"Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here."
United chief executive Omar Berrada recently spoke about Fernandes' contract situation, saying: "It's true that we're having conversations about his new contract, but I prefer to keep that private."
Fernandes has scored 75 Premier League goals since signing from Sporting in 2020 and last season set a record for the most assists in a Premier League season.
His form has tailed off this season in a poor start for the club as a whole.
United are 19th in the Premier League table going into Mauricio Pochettino's first game in charge against rivals Liverpool on Sunday afternoon.
"We spoke about the contract at the end of last season," Fernandes said.
"We came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side because I don't think it's the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.
"The most important thing now is that the club gets back to winning games."
- 'He will see what Man Utd are made of' - Pulis on Pochettino's first game 
  - Published2 hours ago
No fallout with Carrick
Fernandes was dropped for the Premier League defeat by Bournemouth last month after being critical of United's approach in their heavy defeat against Como in the Champions League.
But Fernandes says he did not fall out with Carrick, who was sacked on 12 November.
"The manager came to speak to me before the Bournemouth game, to say: 'Look, I'm not going to start you tomorrow. There's nothing to do with the words of Como, I know people will make it around that. I just want to tell you that we need to change something, I need to make a change, performances have not been great, so I just want you to know that there's nothing to do with that'," Fernandes said.

items.title: Robins ‘aims for the stars’ as Stoke dream of Premier League return
items.summary: There have been false dawns before. Plenty of them. So hopeless was their subsequent run that by the onset of spring they wer
items.text:
There have been false dawns before. Plenty of them. This time last year, with Christmas on the near horizon, Stoke sat second in the Championship table and were beginning to wonder whether they might allow themselves to dream. So hopeless was their subsequent run that by the onset of spring they were forced to consider a potential relegation fight.
Experience has taught the benefit of pragmatism, so no one will be getting ahead of themselves just yet. But this weekend was supposed to be the big test for Mark Robins’s team and few considered they would pass it quite so resoundingly.
Facing a Birmingham side who arrived top of the table and with firmly held Premier League ambitions, Stoke dominated for an hour, the hitherto goal-shy George Hirst earning a well-deserved lead to send a bumper crowd into raptures. The hand-wringing that then followed Luca Bombino’s sending-off with half an hour remaining made the victory that followed all the sweeter. The 10 men of Stoke were superb. It was no surprise that it took considerable time to convince those in the stands to depart for home after the final whistle.
You see, it is not just that Stoke are second in the table, kept off top spot by goal difference. It is not even that they are undoubtedly the Championship’s form side, with just one defeat in their past 13 games. It is the whole feeling around the place; the resilience Robins has developed, and the belief that they can take on the big guns and beat them.
“We are a work in progress, but today was that step in quality against different opponents. A step up in class,” said Robins. “I thought we were really, really good. The intensity, bravery and the intent that we showed was everything that we asked for.
“And, on the back of that, you’ve got the support that are absolutely right behind us. They trust the players. That is a really good feeling. It’s a great feeling for the players. It’s a heady mix, really.”
Eight years have passed since Stoke were last in the top flight; eight years spent as the Championship equivalent of a sea sponge, doing the bare minimum to survive and letting defeats wash over them while remaining resolutely attached to the rocks of the bottom half of the table. During that time they have ended every campaign no higher than 14th and no lower than 18th. Now, something altogether different is afoot. And this may well be the win that convinces supporters to trust their upbeat instincts.
There was an unavoidable fact heading into Saturday’s game. Stoke’s four defeats this season had all come when tasked with opponents fighting at the top end of the table in Swansea, Southampton, Wolves and Middlesbrough. They had shown themselves capable against much of the division, but a failure to deliver against another Championship heavyweight would have raised legitimate questions about their realistic aspirations.
The three August defeats at the start of the campaign preceded the departure of their best player, Sorba Thomas. His replacement, Jack McGlynn, has been an inspired signing. That this victory came without the talismanic figure of Ethan Galbraith, who was absent through illness, is considerable.
As well as switching to a three-man defence following those season-opening losses, a key factor in their upturn has been the restoration of a touch of old-school Stoke; a physicality that was frequently evident on a cold Saturday afternoon.
Bobby Madley, the referee, did not always take kindly to such an approach – to the indignation of the home crowd, who frequently made their feelings clear – but there was no complaint over Bombino’s sending-off for a second yellow after a rash challenge that left him head in hands before the card had even been shown. Tears followed on his slow trudge towards the tunnel, but he need not have worried, with Birmingham barely threatening thereafter.
Given just five points separate the top eight in the Championship table, it would come as no great shock to see Stoke drop off at some point. They do not have the financial benefit of recent Premier League parachute payments or big-spending owners, they are not prolific goalscorers, and a look at their expected goals and expected points tallies shows them firmly in the bottom half of the table. But they are finding ways to win and if McGlynn has a habit of scoring from unexpectedly long distances, perhaps it is because he is good at it.
Before this weekend, Robins had revealed that a top-eight finish was the pre-season target. “You aim for the stars and hopefully you land trying to grab hold of one,” he had said, rather poetically.
If promotion is a “P” they dare not yet speak of, another one – playoffs – is becoming an increasingly realistic proposition. No more sticking to a rock. Swim free and prosper.

items.text:
César Azpilicueta looks well. César Azpilicueta always looks well – “ah, Captain Handsome,” one Chelsea fan says when told who’s turning up – but today especially, smiling in the sunshine. Strolling in, he eases into an easier chair, golf course spreading out beyond the terrace, west of Madrid, and orders a detox almost as green. It is nearly 20 years since he played his first game and a few months since he played his last, training kit replaced by bermudas, loafers and a polo, a picture of relaxation. So what’s it like not being a footballer? “Well, different,” he says. Then he laughs, which he does a lot.
It is not a laugh-your-head-off laugh, more a chuckle, a giggle, as if amused at everything he did. And for all the self-deprecation, the lack of triumphalism, he did everything. Now, at 37, it’s not the same, although there remains much to do, Azpilicueta as understated and quietly busy as ever: “square,” he calls himself. He’s completed an MBA, a sports directorship diploma and there are media offers, a life to live. Matches to play still: against his kids the needle is never far away, he says. And although he hasn’t found a seven-a-side team yet he will.
“I get up, take them to school, go to the gym. I do pilates some days. I walk the dogs, play golf, then it’s after-school activities. I read, try to learn new things. I haven’t yet thought: ‘I’m bored,’” Azpilicueta says, although you wonder how long that will last. “Over the last 12 months I could see it. The summer before I already ‘hit the post’ with retirement. It’s natural: a day comes … if only I could play for ever but it is what it is and you have to keep evolving. I’m enjoying it.”
Don’t get the wrong idea. “In terms of controlling your time, playing every three days, always waiting on the next message: ‘Meet at …,’ it’s a release. But it’s not a liberation because you’re delighted to pull your boots on. An important part of your life ends; you kick a ball almost from the moment you walk, live your passion. Even last season – when there were days everything hurt, when you think: ‘How can I get injured like that?’ – I would make demands of myself, my teammates. I always liked that.
“I never thought I’d be a professional. I couldn’t tell you the moment I thought: ‘I’m a footballer,’” Azpilicueta continues, but he can tell you the score on his debut, for Osasuna in 2007. “One-nil win, Getafe.” Celta de Vigo were the last opponents: a 1-0 loss in May for Sevilla. Between those, more than 800 matches, 508 for Chelsea. Only five players have played more for Chelsea; no foreigner has.
“I don’t think anyone who saw me back then could explain how I played 11 years at Chelsea … and nor could I,” Azpilicueta says, and there’s that laugh again.
It’s a long time since he stood before his new teammates and sang an Estopa track. He arrived in London with a labrador and a sausage dog; he left a legend and the captain, with three kids and every trophy, a European and world champion.
Asked to define his career in a word, Azpilicueta goes for: constancia. Perseverance, consistency, commitment. He talks about the cruciate tear with Marseille aged 19 as a lesson, something that “changed my perspective and made me value discipline, preparation … Out of something negative I grew.” About always adapting, always overcoming, becoming what managers need you to be. There’s a laugh at the little lies – of course I’ve played on the left, boss – and the hours spent alone practising, convincing coaches or teammates to stay behind with him and go over it again and again.
“I arrived at Chelsea late in the market [in 2012],” Azpilicueta says. “My representative said: ‘We’ve spoken to Michael Emenalo, the sporting director, and they’re signing younger players.’ Oscar, Eden Hazard, Victor Moses, Marko Marin, Paulo Ferreira. I was 22. Doubts? Pfff … Olympique needed the money. Chelsea had just won the Champions League and I …”
That laugh. “I hadn’t played for Spain. What did Emenalo see in me? It’s hard to work it out. Also, what you are and what you become is different. You think: ‘What’s it going to be like?’ Another country, another pace, but Juan Mata was there, Fernando Torres, Oriol [Romeu]. Doctor [Paco] Biosca, Ivan the physio. Petr Cech spoke Spanish. Hazard and I spoke French together. I could [communicate] with the Brazilians. But it wasn’t just them. I integrated fast, tried to speak English.
“Not long after arriving there was this audience with fans. Fernando, Juan, Oriol and I. A Q&A. One said: ‘Look, your name is very difficult. Can we just call you Dave?’ Juan translated. I said: ‘Yeah, sure,’ thinking that they meant for the evening. And it stuck. Going down the street: ‘Hey, Dave!’ There was the occasional ‘Dave’ in the dressing room but mostly it was fans. I felt the affection.
“You go with an open mind and bit by bit carve yourself a place. Every time a new coach comes you think: ‘Now what? Will I fit?’ I started as a winger in Pamplona. At Chelsea I played right-back, left-back, a line of three which I hadn’t played in my life … lots of systems, lots of coaches.”
Twelve coaches, in fact. Azpilicueta played under all of them. ““You arrive at a historic club like Chelsea and just try to stay as long as you can. That machine makes demands of you every three days. What I really noticed was a hunger to win: either you have that culture or … forget it. At Chelsea a draw was a catastrophe. You see teammates come and go. The reality is the reality. On the pitch, you have to do it. It’s hard? Yes. But you can’t be sunk by a bad game. If you win: very good, done, next. If you can’t perform, you’re out … You have to manage that pressure.
“I’ve had plenty of unpleasant days. I remember a 6-0 loss Manchester City.” So then what? “For me, the first thing would be watch the video. Look at the data. But know that’s not everything. Sleep, get up, turn it round. Get into to training first. And it’s not just about you; some days it’s about lifting up teammat

items.title: 'Completely unacceptable! - Vasseur slams Leclerc for Hamilton collision
items.summary:
Ferrari boss Frederic Vasseur blames Charles Leclerc for 'unacceptable' collision with Lewis Hamilton in Las Vegas GP
The Ferrari team-mates clashed on track once again, just weeks after their costly collision in Mexico City derailed the team’s race; Charles Leclerc punished by stewards and blamed b
items.text:
Ferrari boss Frederic Vasseur blames Charles Leclerc for 'unacceptable' collision with Lewis Hamilton in Las Vegas GP
The Ferrari team-mates clashed on track once again, just weeks after their costly collision in Mexico City derailed the team’s race; Charles Leclerc punished by stewards and blamed by team boss Frederic Vasseur after spinning Lewis Hamilton in battle over sixth place
Sunday 22 November 2026 08:01, UK
Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur blamed Charles Leclerc for a "completely unacceptable" collision with team-mate Lewis Hamilton in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.
The Ferrari drivers made contact when battling over sixth place with 12 laps remaining in a breathless, frenzied race in which the team were attempting to recover from a poor qualifying when both drivers were knocked out in Q2.
Hamilton was spun around in the Turn Seven-collision, dropping to 10th in the order. Leclerc was found to be at fault by race stewards, who imposed a 10-second penalty on him.
- Las Vegas GP race result

That was applied to Leclerc's final race time and dropped him to 10th place in the final classification, with Hamilton ending up seventh.
Two weeks after speaking to both drivers to remind them of their responsibilities to the team after a squabble on track in Mexico had cost them a likely win, Vasseur was left unimpressed. He also revealed they had asked Leclerc not to overtake Hamilton given they did not want the drivers fighting amongst themselves and leave them vulnerable to slip-streaming rivals.
"Clearly, it's unacceptable," Vasseur told Sky Italy.
"A little bit the same message as Mexico because you have to think about the team, about the people working in Maranello. About all the stakeholders, the sponsors and so on.
"We told Charles not to overtake, because in a race like this, you have to focus on your own race rather than risk being overtaken by others. Charles clearly made a mistake, and it has cost the team dearly. What happened today [Sunday] is completely unacceptable.
"Honestly, I am more than upset because that message was clear after Mexico.
"We had a chat all together in Brazil. Today we passed the message to think about the team when they were racing together and the outcome is this one. It's mega frustrating for all of us."
'I'm penalised so it has to be my mistake' - Leclerc frustrated but accepts decision
In their report confirming the decision to penalise Leclerc, the stewards said the Monegasque had started his move on Hamilton from "a considerable distance behind" in the sister Ferrari, Hamilton's car, and had "not earned the right to the corner" by the apex.
They therefore found him to be "wholly to blame".
On Leclerc's cool-down lap back to the pits at the end of the race, Vasseur told him on Ferrari team radio: "Charles, I want to see you just after the race, before everything"
While stopping short of any apology in his post-race interview, instead saying he was "embarrassed for the team", a visibly-frustrated Leclerc said he accepted the stewards' decision.
"I have been penalised so, as a result, I guess the majority and the stewards thought that it was my mistake. I'll accept that," Leclerc told Sky Sports F1.
"I'm not going to say much more. At the end of the day, I'm penalised so it has to be my mistake."
Asked if Ferrari now needed to impose stricter rules, Leclerc said: "Well, I just feel quite embarrassed for the team in general. We'll review."

Max Verstappen says George Russell 'so far below his level' after poking fun at rival for major error during Las Vegas GP
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix and hit out at George Russell after the Mercedes driver said "I'm not going accept somebody to screw me over" after the pair collided in final practice; Russell crashed during Sunday's race and finished down in ninth
Sunday 22 November 2026 07:53, UK
Max Verstappen says George Russell is "so far below my level" in a scathing response to the Mercedes driver after winning the Las Vegas Grand Prix.
Verstappen claimed his fourth win of the season after a stunning defensive drive while Russell crashed in the latter stages and finished ninth, having battled Verstappen for the win earlier.
The pair collided in final practice on Saturday with Verstappen warned for "driving erratically" in the incident but Russell criticised the Red Bull driver.

"There's nothing in the rules to say you cannot overtake someone who is starting a lap but when you do this, you are screwing this person over and he does this week in, week out with many drivers and everybody accepts it," he told Sky Italy.
"I'm not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they're bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody's got to stand up to that guy."
Verstappen was asked about the comments in the post-race press conference following his third Las Vegas Grand Prix victory and hit back at Russell.
He said: "The thing is, he speaks a lot next to the track. And honestly, for me, it doesn't really bother me because he's so far below my level that it doesn't really make any sense for me anyway to try and challenge that. So, it doesn't bother me.
"And today, karma is a b****. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening [when Russell crashed]. I was like, 'fantastic, my day is only getting better.'
"And of course, when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete."

items.text:
Why Arsenal are behind in race for Champions League spots
- Published
Before the 2026-27 season began, Arsenal technical director Jodie Taylor declared: "I'll flat out say it: we want to win the league and want to take that next step."
After finishing second last season, it seemed like a logical statement to make.
However, after 10 games in this season's Women's Super League, they are sixth in the table, trailing leaders Chelsea by 13 points.
They are also nine points behind third-placed London City Lionesses, albeit with a game in hand, and facing stiff competition to qualify for the Champions League again next campaign.
BBC Sport looks at where things have gone wrong for the Gunners, who have not won the WSL since 2018-19.
Poor form at Emirates Stadium
Last term, Arsenal hosted all 11 of their league home games at Emirates Stadium for the first time, winning eight times and drawing on three occasions.
This season, Renee Slegers' side have drawn all five of their home games and will seek their first win at the sixth attempt when they host West Ham on Sunday (14:30 GMT), live on BBC Two.
Two of those draws came against promoted sides Crystal Palace and Birmingham City, where a combined 57 shots yielded just one goal.
Home fans are getting disgruntled and this has been reflected in attendances. Last season, the Gunners had an average attendance of 33,808, better than eight Premier League clubs.
So far this year their biggest crowd was against London City Lionesses last weekend, when 32,588 were in the stands.
Speaking on the Women's Football Weekly podcast, former England striker Ellen White said: "The Emirates seems [like] a bit of an issue for them at the moment - they just can't get that win there.
"A draw might feel like a loss for them because they are so far behind now in terms of the Champions League spots."
Former Gunners striker Vivianne Miedema, who did play at Emirates Stadium for Arsenal but joined Manchester City before the full switch was made, added: "Players always say that the crowd really, really helps you at Arsenal. The fans are amazing - it gives you that extra bit of energy.
"Obviously playing in the Emirates with all the fans should still give them that boost but it doesn't seem to be fully working for them this season so far."
Plenty of shots - but a lack of clinical edge
The Gunners have had 199 shots in 10 league matches but managed just 11 goals. That is just over one goal per game, and their conversion rate of 5.53% is the lowest of any club over the past six seasons.
Part of the problem could be an over-reliance on key goalscorer Alessia Russo.
She has alternated between the number nine and number 10 position during the season but thrives most when she is the focal point in the attack.
This season, the England striker has five league goals and provided two assists, with her form improving in recent weeks.
She was player of the match against Tottenham after scoring and providing an assist in a 2-1 win and similarly against Liverpool, when she scored twice to help Arsenal triumph by the same scoreline.
After Russo, only Lisa Baum (two), Georgia Stanway (two), Smilla Holmberg and Frida Maanum have scored in the league.
Injuries to attacking options Chloe Kelly, Selina Cerci and Stina Blackstenius have also proved costly, while key midfielder Mariona Caldentey is about halfway through an expected 10-week absence with a hamstring injury.
The result is that Arsenal and Brighton are the only teams in the league to have a goal difference of zero after 10 games.
Contrast that with title rivals Chelsea, who have scored 29 goals and have a goal difference of +24, while defending champions Manchester City have netted 27 times.
Slegers' future has been questioned
While Slegers will always be hailed for winning Arsenal's second Champions League title last year against Barcelona, questions have been asked about her future after another slow start to the season.
In three of their home league matches, Arsenal have fallen behind and dropped points. Last Sunday, they went ahead against London City but only held the lead for 98 seconds.
It was a big summer of change in north London with club stalwarts Katie McCabe and Beth Mead among those departing, and seven new signings arriving including Stanway, Cerci and Baum.
Also among the arrivals was Swiss midfielder Geraldine Reuteler, who helped her country reach the quarter-finals of Euro 2025 but has struggled for minutes since signing a four-year deal in the summer.
She has made just four appearances across all competitions, appearing for a total of just 66 minutes in the WSL.
The results have left Slegers vulnerable and a first home win of the season against West Ham would be a much-needed boost for a side that have fallen far short of the lofty targets they set back in September.

items.text:
Argentina midfielder Paredes collapses during TV interview
- Published
World Cup winning midfielder Leandro Paredes collapsed while giving a post-match interview minutes after winning a trophy with Boca Juniors.
The former Paris St-Germain midfielder, 32, was suffering with the heat and humidity in Barranquilla, Colombia, where Boca won the Copa Sudamericana by beating Atletico Mineiro of Brazil 2-0.
He was replaced during the second half, then collapsed while being interviewed on television, with pictures showing a journalist trying to break his fall.
After some treatment Argentine Paredes was able to walk to the dressing room and joined in with his team's celebrations.
"Thanks to everyone for the messages, it was just dizziness," he said on Instagram, external after the match.
Heat was a discussion before the game with forecasts predicting tempertures could reach 32C and humidity around 80%.
Boca manager Rodolfo Arruabarrena said he noticed the midfielder's difficulties during the second half.
"He felt dizzy towards the end of the first half," Arruabarrena said.
"He improved a little during the break, but after 10 minutes in the second half you could see he was struggling."
Paredes started his career with Boca before moving to Europe in 2015.
The victory for Boca ended an 18-year international trophy drought for the Argentine side.
By securing their 19th international cup, Boca also became South America's most decorated club since 1960, overtaking domestic rivals Independiente who have 18.

Audley Harrison doesn't believe Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua has been left too late in their careers; "they're not in their primes but there's still enough there and the animosit
items.text:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have a genuine animosity, says Olympic gold medallist Audley Harrison | 'We need to see it'
Audley Harrison doesn't believe Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua has been left too late in their careers; "they're not in their primes but there's still enough there and the animosity that they have is genuine. So it's a fight definitely I want to see," the Olympic gold medallist said
Sunday 22 November 2026 08:43, UK
Audley Harrison has backed Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury to deliver when they fight on December 11 in Cardiff.
Harrison was one half of an all-British heavyweight grudge match when he boxed David Haye in a 2010 event that was much hyped but ultimately disappointed.
Harrison though doesn't think Fury and Joshua have left their fight too late.
"'Politricks' has always been there in boxing, always unfortunately messing up boxing," Harrison told Sky Sports.
"I will be sitting on the edge of my seat for Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. They're not in their primes but there's still enough there and the animosity that they have is genuine. So it's a fight definitely I want to see. While it's a little late, I can't argue with that.
"It's not going to be them in their primes but it's going to be good enough. We need to see it for sure."
He added: "Look at Mike Tyson-Lennox Lewis, everyone was complaining for that fight, that fight was like five years too late in many people's eyes.
"I was there in Memphis, it was a great fight, great atmosphere, exactly what we wanted.
"Lennox banged him out but the fight was so exciting."
Harrison preceded Joshua as an Olympic super-heavyweight gold medallist for Great Britain. But he did not scale the heights Joshua achieved in the professional ranks. Joshua has twice been a unified heavyweight world champion and has made a habit of selling out stadium shows in London and Cardiff.
"All of these guys came from nowhere. AJ went to the Olympics not as the favourite, same as Deontay Wilder, and they punched their way to glory," Harrison said.
"When Joshua turned pro he was raw as hell, you've got to give him credit he was able to go through.
"When he lost to [Andy] Ruiz they crucified him because he was meant to win, but he was still raw. He's always been really disciplined, he's strong and he's always come into the ring ready.
"Technically and tactically he's been off in some fights, obviously with [Oleksandr] Usyk, obviously with [Daniel] Dubois. But came back in the [Wladimir] Klitschko fight. When you look at his career, you've got to take your hat off. He wasn't perfect, but he's not supposed to be."
Harrison added: "He's still got the power, he's still got the punch but he doesn't have the punch resistance now.
"We're seeing that with Joshua, we're seeing that with Fury. We haven't seen that with Usyk yet. I haven't seen him start to flounder yet in terms of punch resistance.
"To be fair to AJ and Tyson Fury, they've both had a legendary career, when you look at what they've done, not just the money they've made, if you look at their legacy."

items.title: DiBernardo joins Rapinoe, Pulisic in pantheon of great Olimpicos
items.summary:
(Editor's note: This article was originally published on Oct. 2, 2025, and it has been updated after Vanessa DiBernardo's stunner in Saturday's NWSL championship finale.)
For a relatively simple sport, soccer is filled with novelties.
Outfield players don the gloves and go into goal when there's no
items.text:
(Editor's note: This article was originally published on Oct. 2, 2025, and it has been updated after Vanessa DiBernardo's stunner in Saturday's NWSL championship finale.)
For a relatively simple sport, soccer is filled with novelties.
Outfield players don the gloves and go into goal when there's no other option, penalty takers attempt chipped "Panenka" spot kicks to varying degrees of success, goalkeepers sprint the length of the pitch to come up for last-minute corners -- and sometimes they even score. And every now and then, players will score directly from a corner kick.
Highly improbable, sometimes intentional, a goal scored in this way is known as a Gol Olimpico, an Olympic goal.
But how did these goals get their name? The history of the Olimpico is irrevocably intertwined with South American football and with one of its great rivalries: Uruguay vs. Argentina.
- New Premier League record set with eight injury-time goals
- From World Cup Willie to Ciao: Ranking every World Cup mascot
- NWSL has more money than ever, yet its biggest problems remain
On June 9, 1924, Uruguay won the Olympic gold medal in Paris after defeating Switzerland 3-0. Around the same time in June 1924, the International Football Association Board (IFAB) changed the laws around corner kicks, making goals scored directly from the corner legal. But it wasn't until Oct. 2, 1924, that these two pieces of information would combine to create the Olimpico moniker.
Following Uruguay's Olympic victory, they played a two-game friendly series with their South American neighbors Argentina. The teams played out a 1-1 draw in Montevideo in late-September before travelling to Buenos Aires.
The return match was suspended after four minutes due to the large crowd on the sideline and was rescheduled for Oct. 2. Argentina would eventually win the rematch 2-1, but the whole game was filled with controversy. La Celeste withdrew from the match with four minutes remaining and both sides accused the other of excessive aggression.
But the important part of this story happened in the 15th minute, when Argentina's Cesareo Onzari whipped in a corner and scored.
The audacity of the goal and La Albiceleste defeating the Olympic champions was the catalyst for local journalists to dub the goal an Olympic one. From then on, whenever other goals were scored in this fashion, they were described as like the one scored against the Olympians, and soon the label Gol Olimpico was applied to all such goals.
The Olimpico is stunning when it's intentional and sometimes comical when it's not. It really has no right to work considering where players are standing on the field, how much of the target they can see from that position and what they need to do to the ball to make it curve into the back of the net. Whether they dribble through at the near post or sail past everyone into the far corner, there's beauty in the curl of ball, the audacity, the incredulity. It's glorious.
Take Vanessa DiBernardo's opening goal in Saturday's NWSL championship game. The Kansas City Current were set on course for their first NWSL title thanks to DiBernardo's Olimpico in the 54th minute, with the ball curling over everyone's head to nestle into the far corner of the next.
From regular-season matches to finals, the Olympics and even the World Cup, here are some of the very best Olimpicos.
Vanessa DiBernardo, Kansas City Current vs. Washington Spirit | 2026 NWSL championship
Vanessa DiBernardo opens the scoring to give the Kansas City Current a 1-0 lead in the #NWSL Championship Final! 🔥 https://t.co/oK4ommtzBt
— TSN (@TSN_Sports) November 22, 2026
Kansas City fans will never forget how the Current's first NWSL championship was secured thanks in large part to DiBernado's kick from the corner. Hang it in the Louvre.
Marcos Coll, Colombia vs. USSR | 1962 World Cup
The most impressive part of the first Olimpico to be scored at a World Cup is who Coll beat in the USSR goal: the legendary Lev Yashin.
Megan Rapinoe, United States vs. Canada | 2012 London Olympics
When it comes to scoring an Olimpico at the Olympics, only one player in soccer history has managed the feat: USWNT icon Rapinoe.
Elise Kellond-Knight, Australia vs. Norway | 2019 Women's World Cup
The Matildas may have got knocked out of the 2019 Women's World Cup on penalties, but they'll always have Kellond-Knight's amazing Olimpico at the Allianz Riviera in Nice.
Leandro Carvalho, Ceará vs. Corinthians | 2019-20 Brazilian Serie A
Vai bater no @MuseeLouvre, este vídeo. Oui?
📽️ Premiere#CearáTimedoPovo pic.twitter.com/Jqq2ivy7m0
— Ceará Sporting Club (@CearaSC) September 7, 2019
Carvalho's Olimpico was cunning and spectacular, catching the defence sleeping and using the outside of his foot. What's more, it was scored in the 92nd minute to level the scores at 2-2 against São Paulo giants Corinthians.
Megan Rapinoe, United States vs. Australia | 2020 Tokyo Olympics
Remember when we said that Rapinoe was the only player in soccer history to score an Olimpico at the Olympic Games? Well she's did it twice, repeating her 2012 stunner over eight years later in Tokyo.
Hakan Çalhanoglu, Internazionale vs. AS Roma | 2020-21 Serie A
1️⃣ | CALHA @hakanc10
⛳⛳#ForzaInter #RomaInter pic.twitter.com/TscYbCUxOS
— Inter ⭐⭐ (@Inter_en) December 5, 2021
Why is Çalhanoglu's goal against AS Roma -- in Rome -- so memorable? It's an Olimpico at the Stadio Olimpico of course! How good.
Kyra Cooney-Cross, Melbourne Victory vs. Sydney FC | 2020-21 A-League Women
Kyra Cooney-Cross turns 22 today, which is all the excuse we need to bring out her Grand Final-winning Olimpico 🏆🚀🔥
Imagine doing this on the biggest stage at 19 🤯 What a talent.
Happy birthday, Kyra 🙌 pic.twitter.com/LCJ8Gdnh9A
— Ninja A-League (@aleaguewomen) February 15, 2024
In the 120th minute of the A-League Women Grand Final, 19-year-old Cooney-Cross stepped up to take a corner ... and wrote her name into Australian football folklore.

items.summary:
