items.text:
WASHINGTON -- The Kansas City Current lay claim to some of the most passionate home supporters in the NWSL. Their 33-match regular-season unbeaten run at CPKC Stadium speaks to this.
However, the Current has had to adopt a new identity this postseason: that of road warriors.
That spirit was plain to see as Kansas City captured its first NWSL Championship with a 2-1 win over the Washington Spirit at Audi Field, with their path to the title including two back-to-back road victories.
The match was poised to be a homecoming for the Spirit, who have now lost three successive NWSL Championships. The Current was eager to play the role of spoilers, and Saturday's win marked just the second time Kansas City have claimed a victory at Audi Field.
The partisan atmosphere did not intimidate a battle-tested Kansas City side. Set pieces have been their bread and butter this postseason, edging Angel City in the quarterfinal and Gotham FC in the semifinal off of set piece goals.
The Current stuck true to the formula again Saturday night. Vanessa DiBernardo's exquisite goal directly off a corner kick proved to be the early difference-maker. It was the first Olimpico in championship history and second goal from a corner kick Washington conceded in as many weeks. It was also Kansas City's first goal in a championship.
Kansas City fans were the silent minority up to that goal and had been drowned out by the deafening cheers of Washington's home fans. After DiBernardo's goal, though, it was the traveling Kansas City fans whose cheers reverberated around a subdued Audi Field.
Debinha's stoppage-time goal appeared to be the icing on the cake, sending some Spirit fans toward the exits. However, the Spirit kept things interesting with an immediate reply following the restart. The Current, though, rode out the final nervy moments to officially spoil Washington's party.
While Washington entered Saturday's game with the heavy burden of expectation, Kansas City has also dealt with its fair share of postseason disappointments.
The team featured in its first NWSL Championship (also at Audi Field) in 2022. However, it came up short against the Portland Thorns in a 2-0 loss.
One year later, its home venue CPKC Stadium was designated the predetermined venue for the NWSL Championship. However, the Current failed to make it to the game.
In 2025, the club set a new watermark in the regular season last year and amassed what was arguably the most dominant regular season in NWSL history. The Current set new records for the most points (65), most wins (21), fewest goals allowed (13) and most shutouts (16). They also became the earliest team to clinch the NWSL Shield, with five games remaining.
However, No. 1 Kansas City was shockingly eliminated by 8-seed Gotham FC at home in the first round of the 2025 playoffs. Gotham FC went on to win the NWSL Championship.
The Current got its revenge this season. In a role reversal, they defeated 2026 NWSL Shield winners Gotham FC by the same score (2-1) away as the lower-seeded team. The players insisted the victory was "personal."
The Current found strong form and health at the right time this year. The team's frontline of 2026 Midfielder of the Year Croix Bethune, two-time NWSL MVP Temwa Chawinga, Michelle Cooper and Haley Hopkins fully clicked into gear.
Bethune (who drew the most vociferous jeers from the Audi Field crowd) provided her typical creative spark and defensive effort against her former side Saturday. Chawinga proved to be a threat throughout the game and led her team with six shots.
They continued to ride that momentum into Saturday's championship match. They finish the 2026 season on an eight-match win streak and have not lost a game since mid-September.
The silverware is just reward for a team that's had its fair share of challenges. Former U.S. men's national team player and MLS head coach Chris Armas took the reins from previous manager Vlatko Andovoski this offseason when Andonovski joined the front office. Andonovski then announced his departure as sporting director in September.
Armas endured a baptism of fire. The Current met defeat in five of their opening seven games this year -- including a four-game losing streak. The team's early struggles only served to sharpen their resolve. The Current faced more friction during the regular season than they had throughout their historic 2025 campaign.
"I do believe we are peaking at the right time, and that almost carries more weight than last season because it's all about how you respond to those struggles throughout the entirety of the season," Armas said before the game.
On Saturday, Kansas City responded to the adversity of being underdogs in a hostile environment with conviction and resilience.
"For our team, in this story of 2026 KC Current, it was one built on a lot of adversity and a lot of joy through it all," Armas said.

items.title: DiBernardo's Olimpico goal leads Kansas City to 1st NWSL Championship
items.summary:
WASHINGTON -- The Kansas City Current won their first NWSL Championship on Saturday, defeating the Washington Spirit 2-1 at Audi Field to hand the Spirit a third consecutive loss in the league final -- this time at the Spirit's home field.
Current midfielder Debinha scored the winning goal in the se
items.text:
WASHINGTON -- The Kansas City Current won their first NWSL Championship on Saturday, defeating the Washington Spirit 2-1 at Audi Field to hand the Spirit a third consecutive loss in the league final -- this time at the Spirit's home field.
Current midfielder Debinha scored the winning goal in the seventh minute of second-half stoppage time on a counterattack as she dribbled around Spirit goalkeeper Sandy MacIver.
The goal briefly gave Kansas City a 2-0 lead and appeared to seal the game, but Spirit forward Trinity Rodman scored on a header one minute later, and Washington pushed for an equalizer as the sellout home crowd urged on the Spirit.
Kansas City held on in the final moments to secure its first title after falling short in last year's playoffs as the No. 1 seed.
"It took literally every single person, everyone in teal, it honestly probably took those years to build that grit," Current captain Lo'eau LaBonta said. "It took us years to get here so I'm glad we finally got the trophy."
Kansas City midfielder Vanessa DiBernardo scored an Olimpico -- a goal directly from a corner kick -- in the 54th minute to give the Current the lead. Kansas City defender Kayla Sharples jumped for the ball in front of MacIver, who attempted to punch the ball with her right hand and missed.
DiBernardo is a 12-year veteran of the league who returned from maternity leave in July. She had never won an NWSL Championship after twice losing in the final with the Chicago Red Stars (now Chicago Stars).
DiBernardo was named the game's MVP, to chants from teammates of "MOM-VP."
"It's really special to be a part of," DiBernardo told CBS. "I felt like we were so close last year, and we really just stuck together as a group. And I think the challenges that we faced this year, we really stuck together, and I feel like we really deserved this."
With her goal Saturday, the 34-year-old DiBernardo briefly became the oldest goal scorer in NWSL Championship history before Debinha, 35, took the record with the winner.
Kansas City is the seventh different franchise to win the NWSL Championship (counting the Western New York Flash and North Carolina Courage together after relocation).
The title comes in Chris Armas' first year as head coach.
Current midfielder Croix Bethune also got her hands on the trophy for the first time after being on the losing roster with the Spirit for the past two seasons before making the move to Kansas City in February.
"I'm very, very confident, to the point where people might think it's cocky," she told ESPN. "And at the beginning of the year, I knew that we would get here. I knew that we would win. It doesn't matter how you start; it matters how you finish. And I think throughout the year, we just kept climbing. And we got here and we got the job done."
And Bethune was unfazed by the reception from her former home crowd.
"Expected the boos, maybe some cheers, but more boos," she added. "Honestly, I live for that, because I'm gonna eat it up. It's my job, but it's also entertainment, and I love to do that."
Saturday's final was a chippy, choppy final reminiscent of the 2017 NWSL Championship between the North Carolina Courage and Portland Thorns, a match that Portland won 1-0 and was marred by fouls and injuries.
Kansas City and Washington combined for 19 fouls in the first half, the most in any half of an NWSL Championship, according to ESPN Global Research.
Rodman sustained an apparent upper left arm injury just five minutes into the game after she was fouled from behind by Kansas City defender Laney Rouse. Rodman returned to the field after two minutes of treatment on the sideline, but she continued to favor her left arm throughout the first half.
Rodman went down hard again in the final moments of the game in a collision with Kansas City goalkeeper Lorena, but she stayed on the field.
The volume of fouls called made it difficult for either team to sustain possession. Most opportunities came in transition moments.
Current forward Temwa Chawinga slipped in behind Washington's defense for an open shot on goal in the 11th minute, but MacIver came off her line and saved Chawinga's shot.
Kansas City found Chawinga in transition again in the 33rd minute, when forward Haley Hopkins ran onto a ball over the top from LaBonta before finding Chawinga with a low cross. Chawinga pushed her right-footed shot wide.

items.title: Columbus coach says Messi should've got red card: 'Everyone knows'
items.summary:
MIAMI -- Columbus Crew head coach Laurent Courtois said Lionel Messi should have received a red card for throwing the ball into the face of Gonzalo Tapia during the Crew's 3-0 victory over Inter Miami on Saturday night at Nu Stadium.
With Tapia not backing off the required distance, Messi took a qui
items.text:
MIAMI -- Columbus Crew head coach Laurent Courtois said Lionel Messi should have received a red card for throwing the ball into the face of Gonzalo Tapia during the Crew's 3-0 victory over Inter Miami on Saturday night at Nu Stadium.
With Tapia not backing off the required distance, Messi took a quick throw-in straight into the face of the Crew forward from just a couple of feet away.
Messi and Tapia both received yellow cards from referee Allen Chapman for the incident, which occurred in first-half stoppage time of Game 1 of the best-of-three round one playoff series.
Had Messi received a red card, he would have been suspended for at least the next game.
"Everyone knows that was more than a yellow card," Courtois told reporters after the match.
The Crew coach added that the entire situation is "sad," when asked if he thought Major League Soccer should review the incident.
Tapia, who scored twice for Columbus in the win, did not weigh in on the referee's decision.
"It's a play in the match. I don't know if it's a red card, but I am not the referee to say," he said. "It stays there."
Inter Miami head coach Cristian "Kily" González adopted a similar tone when asked about the incident.
"I have to think about the situation, the card doesn't change much," he said in his postgame news conference. "The referee saw a yellow and that is it, we can't blame the referee. Sometimes they make mistakes, sometimes they don't like each one of us and we have to accept it."
Miami, the 2026 MLS Cup winner, now faces the possibility of a first-round elimination after entering the playoffs as the second seed in the Eastern conference.
Miami must win in Columbus on Friday to earn a third match at Nu Stadium to keep its playoff hopes alive.
"Pressure? Of course there is pressure," Miami's Brazilian defender/midfielder Casemiro said. "Inter Miami always plays to win and we know if we lose the next game we are out. So, that's the pressure.
"The most important thing now is to be calm. We know we have to do better, because we can do better. We were second on the table and so the next game we'll use it to show the rest how strong we are."
Ahead of kickoff on Saturday, Inter Miami co-owner Jorge Mas presented Messi with the 2026 Golden Boot award, which the star won earlier this month.
Messi also won the Golden Boot last year, becoming the first player to win the award given to the league's top scorer in consecutive seasons.
He had 26 goals during the regular season, along with 17 assists -- second-most in the league. He's just the sixth MLS player to win multiple Golden Boots. He is also expected to win his third straight MLS MVP award.
Information from The Associated Press contributed to this report.

items.title: Rodman on 3rd straight NWSL Championship loss: 'This one hurts way worse'
items.summary:
WASHINGTON -- Forward Trinity Rodman smiled and said she was proud of the Washington Spirit's season after a third consecutive NWSL Championship loss but she acknowledged that Saturday's defeat on home soil hurt the most.
The Kansas City Current defeated the Spirit 2-1 on Saturday at Audi Field in f
items.text:
WASHINGTON -- Forward Trinity Rodman smiled and said she was proud of the Washington Spirit's season after a third consecutive NWSL Championship loss but she acknowledged that Saturday's defeat on home soil hurt the most.
The Kansas City Current defeated the Spirit 2-1 on Saturday at Audi Field in front of a sellout crowd of mostly Spirit fans. Washington also lost the previous two NWSL Championship matches by one goal.
"Obviously, this one hurts way worse than any of the other ones," Rodman told reporters after Saturday's loss. "I don't even think you have words in this moment. It's too fresh, but I mean, we're all proud of each other. We're all going to be together no matter what.
"At the end of the day, I think there's so much to celebrate on the season that we had. It obviously sucks to lose, but you've got to give credit to Kansas [City]. They were very dominant. They were very together and they finished their chances."
Rodman scored the Spirit's goal deep in stoppage time, her 15th of the season including the playoffs, to give a glimmer of hope to the home team one minute after Current midfielder Debinha appeared to seal the game.
Kansas City midfielder Vanessa DiBernardo gave her team the lead just after halftime by scoring directly off a corner kick.
Saturday's defeat was the Spirit's first in nine home playoff games.
Rodman's night appeared to be in jeopardy only a few minutes into the match when Current defender Laney Rouse tackled her hard from the side right in front of the team's benches.
The United States star appeared to have a serious upper left arm injury, but she returned to the field after several minutes of medical attention. She favored her left arm throughout the first half but continued to play. Rodman created one of the Spirit's best opportunities of the game in the second half when she surged past two defenders and passed to forward Clara Luvanga, but Luvanga pushed her shot wide.
Rouse's foul set the tone for a physical match that ended with 35 combined fouls. The 19 combined fouls in the first half set a record for an NWSL Championship.
"In the sense that it hurt really bad, yeah," Rodman said of Rouse's tackle. "I mean, yeah, as a team, you always want to put the first tackle out. You're taught to make the first hit. Again, credit to that, because I wish I was the one that put her on the ground.
"But at the end of the day, I think they did a really good job at setting the tone and controlling the first half."
After the game, Rodman said her shoulder felt "phenomenal."
Rodman acknowledged the difficult job the referees have, but the choppy flow of the game "100%" disrupted how the Spirit wanted to play.
"It felt like we couldn't play more than two minutes without a whistle," she said. "We were fouling. They were true calls, for sure. But I think you lose control of the game really quickly that way.
"I think we could have been smarter, because there's the balance between setting the tone with a tackle and doing it too much, so I think we could have definitely managed that better. So, I would say that definitely it messed with our rhythm a little bit."
Spirit defender Esme Morgan dropped to the ground at the final whistle after her third straight defeat in a final. Her eyes were red from tears when she spoke with reporters in the tunnel moments later.
"I think it was a difficult game to manage," Morgan said. "I think they came with a game plan to kind of disrupt the flow, stop us from getting any momentum, a lot of very, very soft fouls. But I think we did a good job of not getting drawn into the chippiness of it."
Washington has now lost four NWSL Championship games, including a loss in 2016.
The Spirit's lone NWSL Championship victory came in 2021, Rodman's rookie year.
Rodman said that she was optimistic about how 2026 went despite another defeat. She spoke frequently throughout the week about how she was grateful to have stayed healthy this season after managing back pains and a knee injury in the previous two postseasons.
"I'm so freaking grateful that I was able to even get to this point and play as many minutes as I did and contribute the way that I did," Rodman said. "So, honestly, I'm not even faking a smile. I genuinely am really happy with where I ended as an individual and just proud of the team.
"At the end of the day, everything happens for a reason. God has plans."

items.title: Messi, Miami staring at early playoff exit after Columbus rout in Game 1
items.summary:
Defending champion Inter Miami and star Lionel Messi are facing the prospect of an early exit from the MLS playoffs after a 3-0 home loss to the Columbus Crew in Game 1 of their first-round series Saturday.
Gonzalo Tapia scored twice for Columbus on either side of a goal from Taha Habroune to stun a
items.text:
Defending champion Inter Miami and star Lionel Messi are facing the prospect of an early exit from the MLS playoffs after a 3-0 home loss to the Columbus Crew in Game 1 of their first-round series Saturday.
Gonzalo Tapia scored twice for Columbus on either side of a goal from Taha Habroune to stun a star-studded Miami team that played most of the game with 10 men after a 36th-minute red card for defender Gonzalo Luján.
Inter Miami must now win when the best-of-three series heads to Columbus, Ohio, for Game 2 on Friday to force a decisive Game 3 back in Miami on Dec. 2.
"Pressure? Of course there is pressure," Miami's Brazilian defender/midfielder Casemiro said. "Inter Miami always plays to win and we know if we lose the next game we are out. So, that's the pressure.
"The most important thing now is to be calm. We know we have to do better, because we can do better. We were second on the table and so the next game we'll use it to show the rest how strong we are."
Second-seeded Miami, boasting Golden Boot winner and prohibitive MVP favorite Messi, finished 13 points clear of seventh-seeded Columbus in the regular season.
The Crew were in last place in the Eastern Conference on Sept. 1 but entered the MLS postseason having won their last six regular-season matches -- the longest active streak in the league.
It was another disappointing performance for Inter Miami in their first season playing at Nu Stadium, the 26,700-seat venue that opened this year. Miami won just six of 17 regular-season matches at its new home since playing its first game there in April and was shut out for the first time at the venue on Saturday.
"The team created four or five clear-cut chances to put the game away, but we couldn't convert, and their goalkeeper made the saves," Miami coach Cristian "Kily" González told reporters. "Then came the red card, which completely changed the nature of the match.
"But focusing on the 11 versus 11, we created plenty of chances; it was just one of those games where nothing goes your way, you just have to bite your tongue and endure it. There's still another leg to play -- we have to go there, win and then come back and define it at home. I take full responsibility."
From early on, Miami played a major role in its own downfall.
Goalkeeper Dayne St. Clair committed an unforced error by bringing down Tapia in the box after rushing off his goal line to concede a penalty just eight minutes in. The Columbus forward made no mistake from the spot to put Miami in an early hole.
Miami had chances to pull level, with Messi being spectacularly denied by Columbus' United States international goalkeeper Patrick Schulte and Luis Suárez poking a shot just wide of the post with the goal at his mercy.
At the other end, though, Miami was grateful for St. Clair partially redeeming himself with some smart saves of his own.
But the home side's hopes of a comeback were dented further when Luján was sent off in the 36th minute after being shown two yellow cards.
Messi, too, was showing signs of frustration and was given a yellow card after taking a throw-in straight into the face of Tapia from just a couple of feet away.
The scoreline being just 1-0 at the interval was perhaps the only silver lining for Miami from the first half.
But it didn't stay that way for long. Exploiting glaring deficiencies in the Miami defense, Columbus scored twice in six early second-half minutes.
First, Habroune feasted on a through ball from Brais Méndez to side-foot home past St. Clair before Tapia grabbed his second after easily turning Yannick Bright and running clear to score.
Columbus' dominance was such that interim coach Laurent Courtois could afford to take off Tapia with more than 30 minutes to go in an effort to preserve his legs and ensure he didn't receive a second yellow card that would rule him out of Game 2.
Courtois has overseen a dramatic turnaround for the Crew just to make it this far.
Miami, in contrast, limped into the playoffs and must now produce an immediate resurgence of its own after a loss that leaves it with just five wins in its past 18 MLS matches.
ESPN's Lizzy Becherano and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Irrespective of res
items.text:
'He will see what Man Utd are made of' - Pulis on Pochettino's first game
- Published
Stepping into a job like Mauricio Pochettino has done at Manchester United, where managers have come and gone frequently, will always lead you to wonder why the others have not lasted very long.
Irrespective of results, you face these first few days in your new post with suspicion.
So, while what happens in Pochettino's first game against Liverpool on Sunday is important, it will not define his early opinions of the club - good or bad.
Whenever you take over a team in mid-season, which I did on a few occasions, you don't usually get much time to work with your players before your first game.
Jumping straight in and going straight to the heart of a two-day preparation for a game, like Pochettino has done before United go to Anfield, is so difficult and I am not sure any manager can honestly make a profound difference.
A change of voice helps, I'm sure, but so does showing strength and confidence in your own principles and making sure the players understand you demand complete and utter commitment in all the games you face, starting with this one.
With time on the training ground being so limited, my initial work would focus on us being a team and working up and down the pitch together, by breaking down different scenarios inside the game and what we should do in them.
I'd keep the focus on hard work and making us difficult to beat - clean sheets are so under-rated.
Then, on the day, your first pre-match speech is always a massive one, and it will be the same for Pochettino too.
My first team talk would always focus on generating an 'us against the world' mentality. As a manager coming in now, you've usually got the job because the team has struggled, so you can play on that to motivate the players.
You can use media reports and stories to show the negativity against them - but then counter that by producing a real 'stand-up and be counted' kind of rallying call, before sending them out on the pitch, while mentioning your faith in them to succeed.
'What your own eyes tell you is most important'
I would have selected my team before I met the players, through my own knowledge and also with help from within.
Whichever club I went in at, I'd expect to know something about most of the players within the group in terms of their position and ability, but understanding the character of the squad was vital too.
The existing staff would know more about the lads' qualities in that respect than myself or anyone who had just arrived with me, so I'd always discuss that with the people I had inherited, from fitness coaches to the medical department.
It's what your own eyes tell you that is most important, however. Going into your first game gives you the opportunity to see for yourself what your players are made of - and it can be a completely different view from what other people see.
Most of the early games I managed would be hit and miss in terms of selection, but I would quickly work out the strengths and weaknesses of the group.
As I've mentioned in previous columns, one of my first aims at any club where I was manager was about putting out a team, not a group of individuals.
It does not take long to see when that is not happening. I can remember my first game of my first spell at Stoke, a 4-2 defeat at Walsall in the Championship.
I wasn't universally enamoured by certain crowd favourites in that team and, while any manager knows that leaving some of them out could have an adverse effect on the supporters' view of yourself, you have to stand up and make decisions based on what you see.
It is the same if there are other issues with the squad you have inherited too.
West Brom's first game after I was appointed manager was a draw with West Ham on New Year's Day 2015.
I sat in the stands at Upton Park with my son, Anthony, who was concerned how different the Albion team was compared to Crystal Palace, the last team I had managed in the Premier League.
He was right to worry about it, but we still found a way - a totally different way of playing, but still a way to win that suited the group.
All your staff have to understand your objectives
My initial aims after arriving at any club mid-season were pretty direct and also pretty basic too.
The staff I inherited did not just know the players, they were also the first group who had to understand my objectives and also my principles - like the work ethic I expected, for example.
Irrespective of what they were used to doing, it was imperative they followed my lead.
One of the clubs I arrived at were struggling at the foot of the table and also suffering from a glut of injuries.
In my opinion, the players were taking advantage of a very honest and hard-working medical department, who were quite accommodating on the treatment times for the lads.
I changed that immediately, so injured players were treated at 9am, 2pm and 4pm, with sessions in-between those times for strength and recovery workouts.
This did not go down well with the players because it impeded on their social lives and, in one case, a player whose injury record was not exactly brilliant came to me complaining that his wife expected him to pick his children up from school and being asked to be in at 4pm affected his private life too.
I did not budge, and funnily enough the player in question recovered quite quickly - as did the majority of the other injured players.
'Clear the treatment rooms, and make sure the players are fit'
Asking injured players to be at the training ground all day was by far the best way of getting them fit, in my experience, and the medical departments I managed were all working well past 4pm anyway so it was no hardship to them.
Just on that side of things, I would sometimes get the feeling some medical departments thought that, if they weren't treating players, then they weren't doing their jobs.

Max Verstappen wins wild Las Vegas Grand Prix; Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri claim double podium for McLaren after late Mercedes collapse saw George Russell and Kimi Antonelli drop back; Charles Leclerc penalised for causing collision with Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton
Sunday 22 November 2026 05:56, UK
Max Verstappen produced a remarkable drive to win a wild Las Vegas Grand Prix that saw him withstand extreme pressure from George Russell and Kimi Antonelli before a late Mercedes collapse.
Pole-sitter Verstappen retained the lead at the start but the enormous power of a slipstream on the long straights of the Las Vegas Strip Circuit made it impossible for the leader to pull clear.
First Russell, and then later newly crowned world champion Antonelli were each able to pass Verstappen on several occasions but the Red Bull driver calmly retook the lead within a few corners every time, expertly managing the deployment of his power.

items.title: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to standardize parts to lower costs
items.summary:
- Toyota, Nissan, and Honda will begin standardizing some vehicle parts in an effort to lower production costs, according to a report by Automotive News.
- The automakers will start with equalized quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics, and a universal color-coding scheme for
items.text:
- Toyota, Nissan, and Honda will begin standardizing some vehicle parts in an effort to lower production costs, according to a report by Automotive News.
- The automakers will start with equalized quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses.
- Discussions are starting with Japan’s domestic suppliers, though international suppliers will be looped in soon.
Japan’s three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to Automotive News. The outlet reports that Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, who is also the vice chairman of Toyota, announced the decision at a news conference in Tokyo this week.
In the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car. The three areas were chosen as the first to be standardized because they are parts that are generally not noticed by consumers, and they shouldn’t have an impact on any brand’s individual identity. All three are also areas that account for significant production costs for the automakers, meaning they can have an immediate impact.

The first discussions of standardization are set to include Japan’s domestic automotive parts suppliers, though international suppliers will be brought into the fold in time. The first standardization efforts are set to go into place next year, according to the AN report.
The push to simplify and lower costs comes as Japan’s seven automakers, including Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Suzuki, work to fend off the increasingly competitive list of Chinese automakers. The automakers are said to hope that they can channel the money saved by homogenizing into new innovations.
“We all share this strong sense of crisis, creating a momentum for change,” Sato said. “Based upon our sense of a crisis, we decided to choose these three areas.”

items.title: Champion’s corner: KC Current win first NWSL Championship with 2-1 stunner over Spirit
items.summary:
It took five years, 90 minutes and a goal for the ages, but the Kansas City Current have their first-ever NWSL championship.
Riding a wave of momentum created by a 54th-minute Olimpico from midfielder Vanessa DiBernardo, and capping it off with an all-important breakaway winner from Debinha, the Cur
items.text:
It took five years, 90 minutes and a goal for the ages, but the Kansas City Current have their first-ever NWSL championship.
Riding a wave of momentum created by a 54th-minute Olimpico from midfielder Vanessa DiBernardo, and capping it off with an all-important breakaway winner from Debinha, the Current silenced the partisan, sellout crowd at the heavily-favored Washington Spirit’s home ground with a 2-1 victory on Saturday.
The Spirit, heartbroken at the final whistle, have now lost three consecutive NWSL Championships.
“Obviously this one hates way worse than any of the other ones,” forward Trinity Rodman said afterward. “I don’t even think you have words in this moment — it is too fresh.”
DiBernardo’s goal was stunning, a driven, bent corner kick played to the far post that eluded Spirit goalkeeper Sandy MacIver, her defenders and Current forward Haley Hopkins, potentially DiBernardo’s intended target. The Spirit’s players and fans alike pleaded with center referee Joshua Encarnación, suggesting he examine the play on VAR for obstruction, as MacIver had potentially been screened. The review never came.
Whether played directly on goal intentionally or otherwise, the effort will go down as one of the most memorable in NWSL Championship history. At 34, DiBernardo becomes the oldest player in league history to score in a final, and was later named the match’s MVP.
“I’ve been to the game a few times and haven’t won, but this one just felt a little lighter,” said DiBernardo, who gave birth to Charlie, her first child, in January and took time off before returning to the Current in March. “I think just having Charlie, it just brings a different perspective on life. I knew the game was big and it was a big moment, but just kinda having her, just spending the day with her, it just felt really special.”
The game’s early phases were forgettable save for one incident which would go on to affect the remainder of the match: a bruising, high-speed tackle on Rodman by Current defender Laney Rouse in the fifth minute. The challenge sent Rodman flying and appeared to injure her left elbow; the Spirit forward, nearing tears, spent much of the first half in visible pain and seemingly never fully recovered. Rouse was not cautioned for the challenge.
“[It helped set the tone] in the sense that it hurt really bad, yes,” Rodman said. “As a team, you always want to put the first hit in. You’re taught to do that. Credit to them. I wish I was the one who put her on the ground. They did a really good job at setting the tone and controlling the first half.”
It was far from the game’s only physical moment. Neither team managed to settle into any meaningful rhythm during an opening 45 that felt at times more like a title fight than a title match. Encarnación, involved in his first NWSL final, called a very tight match and the near-constant stoppages in play were the defining characteristic of a sometimes ugly opening phase. In many ways it was not entirely his fault: the message-sending start from KC and the Spirit’s subsequent response often compelled him to act. The 19 combined first-half fouls between both sides were the most in any half of any NWSL title match in league history.
“It felt like we couldn’t play more than two minutes without a whistle,” Rodman said. “We were fouling, they were true calls for sure — but I think you lose control of the game really quickly that way ... It definitely messed with our rhythm a little bit.”
Paradoxically, though, the match was won with speed. Deep into second-half stoppage time, the Current found their eventual match-winner on a breakaway. After doggedly winning back possession after a Spirit free kick late on, Kansas City forward Debinha streaked upfield from just beyond the center stripe, looking off a wide-open Temwa Chawinga and rounding MacIver who looked on hopelessly as the Brazilian slotted it home.
Moments later, Rodman – somehow still in the match after not only the early challenge but a later high-speed collision with Current goalkeeper Lorena – pulled one back for the Spirit. Falling away from goal 10 yards out, Rodman got her head on the end of a Tara Rudd cross, placing it perfectly over Lorena’s outstretched arms and into the far-side netting. The ensuing five minutes – the game ended in the 102nd – were chaotic but the Spirit couldn’t quite find the equalizer.
After a slow start, the Current were well-managed by former Major League Soccer and US national team member Chris Armas. Armas was widely considered a controversial selection at the time of his appointment but proceeded to lead the club to their first championship in his first season, doing so by beating Gotham FC and now the Spirit, two sides picked by many as potential league-winners.
“I think from the front to the back we made it a point that every person on this team defends and if somebody is going to make a mistake the other person is going to have their back,” Current defender Izzy Rodriguez said. “We try and turn every 1v1 situation into a 1v2 for us, and I think that showed up today. We were winning our duels and second balls and those are things that win games.”
For the Spirit, the loss is devastating. They become the first American professional club – men’s or women’s – to lose three consecutive finals since the New England Revolution of Major League Soccer, who did so in the mid 2000s. In their five Championship appearances, the Spirit have won just one time, in 2021.

items.title: Lionel Messi at center of red-card controversy as Inter Miami face early MLS playoff exit
items.summary:
Columbus Crew coach Laurent Courtois said Lionel Messi should have been sent off after throwing a ball into an opponent’s face as Inter Miami crashed to a 3-0 defeat in the MLS Cup playoffs on Saturday.
Messi’s frustration boiled over on the stroke of half-time when he hurled a throw-in into the fac
items.text:
Columbus Crew coach Laurent Courtois said Lionel Messi should have been sent off after throwing a ball into an opponent’s face as Inter Miami crashed to a 3-0 defeat in the MLS Cup playoffs on Saturday.
Messi’s frustration boiled over on the stroke of half-time when he hurled a throw-in into the face of Columbus forward Gonzalo Tapia, with 10-man Miami trailing 1-0 at the time.
Messi and Tapia were both shown yellow cards for the incident by referee Allen Chapman, but Courtois said afterwards that the Argentina superstar should have been given a red card.
“Everybody knows that he deserved more than a yellow card,” Courtois said at a post-game press conference when asked about the incident. “It’s just really sad.”
Chapman later defended his decision to show Messi only a yellow card.
“The force used was negligible and the offense did not reach the level of violent conduct,” Chapman told a pool reporter.
Miami had already been reduced to 10 men when the incident occurred and were trailing 1-0 after an early penalty from the Chile international Tapia.
The reigning MLS champions went on to suffer a 3-0 defeat, with Taha Habroune doubling Columbus’s lead shortly after half-time before Tapia added his second at Miami’s Nu Stadium.
The result means seventh-seeded Columbus, the 2023 champions, can eliminate Messi and Miami from the playoffs with a victory in Game 2 of the best-of-three series in Ohio next Friday.
“It was a game where nothing went right for us, and we effectively created their chances for them,” Miami coach Kily González said afterwards.
“We didn’t produce the great performance we had hoped for. Everything went wrong, but we have to learn from it because next time, if we don’t win, we’re out.
“There’s no better challenge for us as a team than this. It’s a test of character, and I know my team has that character.”
FC Dallas 3-0 Portland Timbers
Joaquín Valiente scored twice in the space of two minutes as FC Dallas beat the Portland Timbers 3-0 in the opening game of their best-of-three Western Conference first-round series.
The 25-year-old Uruguayan midfielder broke the deadlock in the 53rd minute, volleying home a rebound after Daniel Job’s shot was parried by Portland goalkeeper James Pantemis.
Valiente doubled the lead two minutes later, timing his run to meet another pass from Job before redirecting the ball between Pantemis’s legs.
Samuel Sarver completed the scoring in the fourth minute of stoppage time, finishing a cross from Logan Farrington on the counterattack.
Dallas goalkeeper Daniel de Sousa Britto, known simply as Daniel, made four saves, while Pantemis finished with five for Portland.
The Timbers also lost Ariel Lassiter to an apparent injury in the 33rd minute.
Second-seeded Dallas can advance to the Western Conference semi-finals with a victory in Portland next Saturday.
New England Revolution 2-0 Philadelphia Union
Teenager Peyton Miller scored one goal and helped create another as the New England Revolution beat the Philadelphia Union 2-0 in the opening game of their Eastern Conference first-round series.
The 19-year-old Miller became the fifth-youngest goalscorer in MLS Cup playoffs history when he volleyed home a cross from Jack Harrison in the 73rd minute, his effort bouncing off the crossbar and into the net.
New England had taken the lead in the 10th minute when Miller’s shot from the edge of the penalty area deflected off Philadelphia defender Nathan Harriel for an own goal.
Harrison, who came on as a substitute in the 62nd minute, was making his first appearance since 9 September after missing more than two months with a quadriceps injury.
Philadelphia nearly equalized in the 37th minute when Cavan Sullivan turned and fired a shot from outside the penalty area that struck the left post.
The Union fielded the youngest starting lineup in MLS Cup playoffs history, with an average age of 23 years and 207 days, breaking the record set by the New York Red Bulls in 2022.
Matt Turner made two saves to preserve the shutout for New England, who can advance to the Eastern Conference semi-finals with a victory in Philadelphia next Saturday.

items.text:
Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers
OpenRouter ·
Earlier this week, security researchers reported that certain inference providers had data compromised or otherwise shown evidence that their data policies were not being upheld. We have been collaborating closely with the researchers and with providers to understand the findings and encourage the providers to address them.
These findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter. The results of this testing revealed new findings about specific inference providers. A live list of the security announcements we have received from providers is below.
As the operating layer between customers and a fast-moving ecosystem of models and providers, we take data policy enforcement very seriously. We have taken the following actions:
- Off-boarded three providers from OpenRouter, based on the results of our investigations.
- Removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention (ZDR) eligibility. The removals included providers flagged by researchers, plus additional endpoints that we removed as a precautionary measure.
- Notified all potentially affected customers.
The following work is underway:
- We are adapting the researchers’ testing approach so we can run these checks on an ongoing basis.
- We are conducting technical verification of network paths to identify instances where requests and responses may be being forwarded to third parties.
- We are requiring appropriate assurances and validation before restoring ZDR eligibility to any endpoint removed in this review.
We are grateful for the Dragos report. As we integrate similar testing techniques into OpenRouter, we will keep raising the bar, and providers that want to be on OpenRouter will need to meet it.
Provider security announcements
- Novita: Privacy notice regarding MiniMax requests on Novita
- Phala: November preliminary incident report
- Together: Security event: prompt leakage for requests in June and July of 2026
Not all affected providers have posted publicly. We have notified affected users regardless of whether there is a public post. We are encouraging all providers to create incident write-ups and will keep this list updated.

items.title: Supersub Espí's 'most special' goal earns win for Madrid and praise from Nadal
items.summary:
MADRID -- Real Madrid supersub Carlos Espí said his 85th-minute winner against Celta Vigo was his "most special" goal yet for the club after earning his team all three points at the Bernabéu on Saturday.
Celta's Pablo Durán put the visitors ahead after just six minutes, before a late rally saw Jude
items.text:
MADRID -- Real Madrid supersub Carlos Espí said his 85th-minute winner against Celta Vigo was his "most special" goal yet for the club after earning his team all three points at the Bernabéu on Saturday.
Celta's Pablo Durán put the visitors ahead after just six minutes, before a late rally saw Jude Bellingham level for Madrid, and then Espí -- who was introduced on 79 minutes by coach José Mourinho -- score from close range, after Vinícius Júnior's cross, to seal a 2-1 victory.
- Madrid chief Pérez: "outrageous" that LaLiga president Tebas hasn't resigned
- Hunter: Has Vini Jr. finally put summer transfer saga behind him? Real Madrid need him at his best
Espí, 21, has played just 44 minutes for Madrid in LaLiga this season but he's now scored three, crucial goals to secure victories against Espanyol, Elche and Celta, as well as netting in the club's 4-3 Champions League comeback win away at Roma.
"I think it's the most special," Espí told reporters on Saturday, when asked about his first goal scored in front of the Bernabéu crowd.
"Honestly, it's a day I'll never forget ... I can't even count how many times I've dreamed of scoring here, celebrating with the fans, and hearing them chant my name."
Espí said coach Mourinho was "euphoric" after his late winner, and described meeting Rafael Nadal post-match, after the tennis legend was voted onto Madrid's board of directors earlier on Saturday.
"I went over to see [Nadal], and he was very proud of me," Espí said. "Having a legend like Rafa Nadal there, talking to me, it made me incredibly happy."
Mourinho cited the return from the international break as a factor in Madrid's lackluster first-half performance, which saw them trail at halftime.
"If you look at the big teams that played today: Arsenal didn't win, [Manchester] City didn't win, Chelsea didn't win, Bayern [Munich] didn't win," Mourinho said. "It's difficult."
Mourinho confirmed that Vinícius -- who he brought off the bench after 57 minutes on Saturday -- would start in Madrid's Champions League game with PSV Eindhoven on Tuesday.
The coach also revealed why Espí is unlikely to start many games alongside first-choice center forward Kylian Mbappé.
"It's possible, but when we lose the ball, I -- on the touchline -- would have to run onto the pitch during the transition, and clatter someone on the opposing team," Mourinho joked.
"Playing with two pure forwards means your wingers have to be very capable of defending in central areas. And that wouldn't be Vinícius, for sure. Arda [Güler] might do it a bit, Brahim [Díaz] a bit, but given the characteristics of our wingers, we aren't built to play in a traditional 4-4-2."

- Man City at a crossroads as a sh

Home defeats to big rivals. Injuries to key players. One of the worst defenses in the Premier League.
Another crisis might be unfolding at Chelsea, just a few months into Xabi Alonso's tenure.
- Raya exits with injury as Arsenal held by Newcastle: 'Never good news'
- Man City at a crossroads as a shell of themselves
- VAR review: Should Haaland's goal vs Fulham have been disallowed
"We're in a fragile moment," Alonso said Saturday after seeing his team overrun in a 4-1 home loss to Leeds, who hadn't won at Stamford Bridge this century.
"We need to be tougher," he added. "It's something mandatory in this competition.
Already without major players in striker João Pedro and defender Maxence Lacroix because of injuries, Chelsea fell apart against Leeds following the enforced withdrawal of Moisés Caicedo in the 22nd minute after the Ecuador midfielder landed awkwardly on his back while making a challenge.
Despite going ahead within three minutes through Emmanuel Emegha on his first start, Leeds equalized almost immediately through Noah Okafor and dominated the second half, scoring through Dominic Calvert-Lewin -- via the penalty spot -- Okafor again and then U.S. midfielder Brenden Aaronson.
Leeds -- whose rivalry with Chelsea dates back to the 1960s and early '70s -- last beat the London club away in 1999. Less than a month ago, Tottenham won at Stamford Bridge for the first time since 2018. Before the international break, Chelsea lost 1-0 at Sunderland, which started that match in last place.
Chelsea, one of the biggest spenders in Europe in recent seasons, has tumbled toward midtable and are putting in lethargic performances even though the team doesn't have the hindrance of European competition this season.
"After we lost Moises, we lost completely the momentum," Alonso said. "Until then we were doing OK, but from that moment they started believing and we started not believing. After that, we never got the good feeling and were not able to come from the pressure. It completely changed.
"I'm not feeling [let down]. We do it as a team, as [a] collective. We need to support each other. We need to find solutions to do better because this will happen. There were moments that we were not competing at the level required. But the physicality, the duels, it's not the only explanation. The mentality part we can do better."
Chelsea has now conceded 20 goals in 11 games, with only last-place Crystal Palace and promoted teams Ipswich and Coventry letting in more.
Information from The Associated Press and PA contributed to this report.

items.title: Milan boss Amorim heaps praise on Pulisic: 'The player we cannot replace'
items.summary:
AC Milan head coach Ruben Amorim has heaped praise on Christian Pulisic, calling him "the player we cannot replace."
The 28-year-old is in sparkling form, having scored three goals in two games for the United States men's national team -- including a stunning bicycle kick -- and three in four in Ser
items.text:
AC Milan head coach Ruben Amorim has heaped praise on Christian Pulisic, calling him "the player we cannot replace."
The 28-year-old is in sparkling form, having scored three goals in two games for the United States men's national team -- including a stunning bicycle kick -- and three in four in Serie A prior to the international break.
"I can tell you today that Pulisic, maybe, is the player that we cannot replace," Amorim told a news conference ahead of Milan's game against Frosinone on Sunday.
"The characteristics of turning between the lines, we don't have another Pulisic. There are some moments in Europe, in this last schedule, we had to save -- a little bit -- Pulisic.
"There is nothing that I can say better than saying that Pulisic has some characteristics that, if we don't have it on the pitch, the team feels a lot that Pulisic is not there. From that, you can understand how important Pulisic is for us.
"He's not that kind of guy that speaks a lot, but [he] speaks on the pitch, without speaking. He wants the ball all the time and you can feel it against Genoa. If you see all the plays, Pulisic is the guy that pulls the team up. Him and [Adrien] Rabiot."
The former Borussia Dortmund and Chelsea winger has been with the Italian club since 2023 and recently signed a new deal through 2031.
"I think it helps any player to feel the confidence from the club," Amorim said on Saturday.
"I think [that] was clear [when] the club showed him a new contract. That helps always a player."

The Portuguese coach added: "When he was not playing [at the beginning of this season], I said 'Pulisic is really important for us.'

items.summary:
Paris Saint-Germain forward Désiré Doué was carried off on a stretcher with a serious knee injury late in the first half of the team's 3-2 win at Nice in Ligue 1 on Saturday.
The defending champions' 12th straight win in all competitions was soured by yet another injury.
"We will have to wait until
items.text:
Paris Saint-Germain forward Désiré Doué was carried off on a stretcher with a serious knee injury late in the first half of the team's 3-2 win at Nice in Ligue 1 on Saturday.
The defending champions' 12th straight win in all competitions was soured by yet another injury.
"We will have to wait until tomorrow to know the exact nature of the injury. But it is a serious injury, we have seen the images," PSG coach Luis Enrique said after the game. "That's the life of a professional footballer, you have to realize that this is part of a career and you have to accept it."
It happened when he turned to shield the ball from Nice midfielder Sofiane Diop and his fully-extended leg buckled under him without any contact from Diop.
The France forward fell to the ground clutching his right knee in the 39th minute and looked in severe pain as he cried out. Moments later he was taken off on a stretcher and placed both hands on his face.
"He is sad and worried," Luis Enrique said. "He will come back twice as strong, I have no doubt."
The 21-year-old Doué -- who shot to prominence with an outstanding performance in the 2025 Champions League win against Inter Milan -- had scored his second league goal of the season earlier in the first half.
Spain forward Ferran Torres replaced him and scored the third goal. Senny Mayulu got PSG's opening goal.
Two-time defending champions PSG face Roma in the Champions League on Wednesday.
Doué missed stretches of last season with a calf strain and a thigh injury and had a bothersome ankle injury the previous season.
His latest injury is a concern for Enrique, after Khvicha Kvaratskhelia tore the ACL in his right knee against Barcelona on Oct. 20 and Ousmane Dembélé and captain Marquinhos tore thigh muscles in that game.
Dembélé came off the bench against Nice in the second half for PSG.
Information from The Associated Press contributed to this report.

The Spain goalkeeper walked off holding his left arm and looked in discomfort as he did so. He was replaced by Kepa Arrizabalaga.
"Unfortunately, he had to come off which is never good news," Arsenal
items.text:
David Raya was forced off with an injury during Arsenal's 2-2 draw at Newcastle United on Saturday.
The Spain goalkeeper walked off holding his left arm and looked in discomfort as he did so. He was replaced by Kepa Arrizabalaga.
"Unfortunately, he had to come off which is never good news," Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta said. "He will get assessed now and he will probably have an MRI tomorrow to see what it is exactly because at the moment I don't know.
"It was a knock. I don't know how it happened or what the injury is at the moment so we'll have to see wait and see tomorrow.
"We know how important David is for us but tomorrow we will have more news."
The 31-year-old had played every minute of Arsenal's Premier League and Champions League games this season up to that point.
He also played 37 out of Arsenal's 38 games as they lifted the Premier League last season.
Raya has won the league's Golden Glove award in each of the last three seasons, and Arsenal have conceded the joint-fewest goals so far this Premier League season.
The Spaniard could join Bukayo Saka and Martín Zubimendi on the sidelines, although Saturday's game did see William Saliba feature in a Premier League squad for the first time this season.

items.text:
Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?
- Published
Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.
At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.
He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.
"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.
But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.
Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.
The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.
His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.
Of the 18 presidential candidates, only one is under 40 - Moses Olusoji Adebisi, a 35-year-old businessman representing the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA).
Although he says he is confident of winning, few Nigerians appear to know much about him and he has not been seen much on the campaign trail.
The contrast is striking in a country with one of the world's youngest populations, where young people have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to shape political debate and mobilise for change.
In the previous election, Obi, then 61, galvanised millions of young Nigerians through a social media-driven movement known as the "Obedients".
His campaign promised a break from the established political order, appealing particularly to young people struggling to find jobs and earn a decent living.
But his failure to win the presidency left many of his supporters disillusioned.
"At the time we were so hopeful, but unfortunately the result wasn't what we wanted, which made many lose hope in the system," former Obedient Nonso Chukwudi tells the BBC.
The movement had built on the momentum of the EndSars protests in 2020, which grew into one of Nigeria's biggest youth-led movement in decades.
Initially sparked by anger over police brutality, the demonstrators developed into a wider call for political reform, accountability and greater youth participation in governance.
But the protests were eventually crushed by the authorities. About 56 were reportedly killed, although officials dispute this figure, while hundreds were arrested and some had their bank accounts frozen.
Both EndSars and the Obedients demonstrated the capacity of young Nigerians to mobile around political causes.
But turning that enthusiasm into sustained electoral participation has proved much harder.
Hajara Musa, 33, is among those who have lost faith in the political system. She has no plans to register or vote in the near future.
"I just feel like things are already determined and I'll just be wasting my time. It is going to be the same people all over again," she tells the BBC.
The electoral register appears to reflect this growing disillusionment.
Although the number of registered voters has increased by 10 million to over 103 million since the last election, enrolment of those under 35 has actually fallen, by about seven million.
Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.
Nigeria's electoral commission, Inec, says it has made efforts to encourage more young people to register ahead of the 2027 general elections.
This includes appointing nine ambassadors from the entertainment industry, spanning film, music and comedy, to reach younger audiences.
But the figures suggest these efforts have yet to make a significant difference.
Dalhatu says he understands the frustration but argues that young Nigerians cannot expect change, if they stay away from the political process.
"Unfortunately, many prefer to just post on social media" instead of getting involved, he says.
Of course being young does not mean you are necessarily the best candidate.
For those who want to participate, there is a formidable obstacle to getting into politics - money.
Dalhatu dreams of becoming president one day, but says he has previously had to abandon campaigns because he could not raise enough funds.
The cost of running for office in Nigeria is notoriously high.
Under the Electoral Act, presidential candidates were allowed to spend up to 5bn naira (£2.8m; $3.7m) on campaigns ahead of the 2023 elections. That spending limit has since been doubled.
The cost of nomination forms alone puts the presidency beyond the reach of most aspiring young Nigerians.
The ruling All Progressive Congress (APC), along with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) have each set their presidential nomination fee at 100m naira ($74,000; £56,000), making it extremely hard for new challengers to emerge.
Since the return to democracy in 1999, only two parties have governed Nigeria - the PDP from 1999 to 2015 and the APC since 2015.
These parties, alongside the ADC, formed last year by politicians who had defected from the other two, have established nationwide network of branches, supporters and campaigners.
Those aspiring candidates without the financial resources to secure nomination forms and compete in the internal party contests of the main parties have little chances of becoming president.
The barriers are also evident in the National Assembly.
Not one of Nigeria's 109 senators is under 40, while only 14 of the 360 members of the House of Representatives fall into that age group.
"I have been in politics for many years and I will tell you that young people in this country lack the resources to become president," says Dalhatu, who is running under Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.
Fatima Zahra Umar, a young politician in the APC who has previously tried to run for a seat in the House of Representatives, agrees.

Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability t
items.text:
Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.
Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”
“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”
Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.
That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

items.title: A tale of two Nvidias
items.summary:

items.text:
We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.
Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.)
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China. This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.
What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.
A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.
Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.
Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China.
And again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be — if Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line.
Kirsten: Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline.
It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.
So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way.
Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him.
It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.”
So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen.
Kirsten: Sure, never say never.
Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks.
Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there.
Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that.

items.title: The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’
items.summary: One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiat
items.text:
One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.
The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’
Countries agree to ‘start discussing options’ for rules around autonomous weapons.
According to NPR:
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.
The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”
Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan.
According to NPR, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions:
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

items.text:
Ireland beat world champions South Africa in thriller
- Published
Nations Championship
Ireland (17) 20
Tries: Baloucoune 2, Kelleher Con: Prendergast Pen: Prendergast
South Africa (10) 17
Try: Van den Berg, Marx Cons: Feinberg-Mngomezulu 2 Pens: Feinberg-Mngomezulu
Ireland exacted revenge on world champions South Africa with a thrilling win in Dublin after England's victory over New Zealand dashed Andy Farrell's side's hopes of reaching next weekend's Nations Championship final.
With banned South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus hosting a watchalong stream from his team's hotel, the Springboks fell to back-to-back Test defeats for the first time since November 2022 after last week's loss to France in Paris.
A losing bonus-point, however, is enough for South Africa to top the southern hemisphere table and secure a place in the final against France, who beat Argentina 45-17 later on Saturday.
Ireland, who were shown five cards during last year's 24-13 loss to the Springboks in Dublin, led at the break after two tries from Robert Baloucoune and a Ronan Kelleher score, with Morne van den Berg crossing for the visitors.
After Canan Moodie had a try ruled out early in the second half, Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast - who was cleared to play by a disciplinary panel earlier this week - stretched Ireland's lead with a penalty.
However, hooker Malcolm Marx's 57th-minute try hauled South Africa back into it before yellow cards for Ireland captain Dan Sheehan and Springbok replacement Marco van Staden - the latter upgraded to red - set up a nail-biting denouement in the final 10 minutes.
But amid a hair-raising atmosphere inside Aviva Stadium, Ireland held on for a much-needed win after six successive double-digit defeats by the Springboks, New Zealand and France.
France's win meant that Ireland had to settle for third place in the table, and they will face Australia in a fifth-place play-off at Twickenham on Friday at 20:10 GMT.
Ireland narrowly beat Australia 33-31 in Sydney in July, but the Wallabies have since had a change of head coach after Les Kiss replaced Joe Schmidt.
Ireland front up to SA after Erasmus-dominated build-up
After an explosive build-up headlined by Erasmus, who was banned for six matches on Tuesday after questioning the integrity of match officials in last week's game against France, Saturday's contest in Dublin had a lot to live up to.
But it delivered emphatically during a breathless first half as Ireland fronted up impressively to South Africa's immense physicality.
In last year's meeting in Dublin, Ireland ended a nightmarish first half with 12 players on the field as South Africa - and their mighty scrum - played the game on their terms.
Fuelled by the pain of that encounter, Ireland attacked the game with real gusto and while South Africa fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu kicked the first points of the game, Ireland bossed possession and territory for much of the opening half.
There were plenty of moments for the sold-out crowd to cheer, with perhaps the biggest roar reserved for the hosts winning a rare scrum penalty after 26 minutes.
Baloucoune was exceptional, too. In addition to faring well in the aerial battle, the rapid Ulster wing displayed his finishing skills to get Ireland on the board, slipping past Damian Willemse and touching down after being picked out by Stuart McCloskey.
While Baloucoune - who also crossed twice against Fiji last week - was denied a second try by a superb piece of last-ditch defending by Springbok number eight Cameron Hanekom, Joe McCarthy won a turnover to deny the visitors momentum.
From there, Ireland kicked to the corner and eventually worked the ball back to Baloucoune on the right, who dived over in the corner for his second.
But with both conversion attempts missed by Prendergast, Ireland were pegged back when South Africa won a penalty inside green territory, with Van den Berg dotting down off the back of a scrum.
Unlike last year, though, Ireland had the final say of the half and restored their lead when Kelleher scored off a well-worked line-out.
South Africa's frustration deepened early in the second half when Moodie's fine finish in the corner was ruled out after the replacement back was pushed into touch by Mack Hansen.
Ireland pulled further clear when Prendergast atoned for his missed kicks at goal with a penalty to put the hosts 20-10 up.
But after world player of the year Marx forced his way over with more than 20 minutes remaining, Ireland were denied a fourth try when Sheehan - in his first Test start at number eight - was held up on the line.
Sheehan was then yellow-carded at the same time as Van Staden, for a croc roll and dangerous clear-out respectively, and while South Africa pushed for a late winner, Ireland held on for a statement win.
Reacting from what looked like a conference room at his team's hotel, Erasmus slammed a table in frustration at full-time before his stream ended, spelling a miserable end to a tumultuous week for the two-time World Cup-winning coach.
Line-ups
Ireland: Keenan; Baloucoune, Henshaw, McCloskey, Hansen; Prendergast, Gibson-Park; Porter, Kelleher, Furlong, McCarthy, Beirne, Baird, Van der Flier, Sheehan (capt)
Replacements: Stewart, O'Toole, Clarkson, Ryan, Timoney, Casey, Frawley, Aki
Sin-bin: Sheehan (73)
South Africa: Willemse; Arendse, Kriel, De Allende, Hooker; Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Van den Berg; Nche, Marx, Louw, Etzebeth, Mostert, Kolisi (capt), PS du Toit, Hanekom
Replacements: Wessels, Steenekamp, T du Toit, De Jager, De Villiers, Van Staden, Williams, Moodie

Assistant referees: A Gardner (RA) & A Woodthorpe (RFU)
